World.title: Three quarters of Poles support cooperation with Ukraine against Russia despite historical dispute
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A new study shows that, while most Poles were angered by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s recent decision to name a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, they still overwhelmingly support cooperation with Ukraine and believe that Russia benefits from the dispute. The study, carried out by Polish state research agency CBOS, also finds that a large majority of Poles believe good relations with Ukraine will only be possible once historical issues are resolved. The polling was carried out this month in response to the ongoing diplomatic crisis that began in May, when Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. The UPA is widely revered in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-backed Soviet rule. However, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians – mostly women and children – were slaughtered during World War Two, often with great brutality. Zelensky’s decision sparked anger in Poland, where the massacres are regarded as a genocide (though Ukraine strongly rejects that label). In June, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest honour, which he had received in 2023. In its new survey, CBOS found that 59% of Poles support Nawrocki’s decision, while only 28% oppose it. However, they were divided over the consequences, with 41% saying it would bring Poland more losses than benefits and the exact same proportion saying the benefits would outweigh the costs. More broadly, 84% said the Polish state should react when another country glorifies historical figures responsible for crimes against Poles. However, when asked if Ukrainians have the right to honour their own historical heroes, even if those figures left a negative mark on Polish history, 44% agreed and 42% disagreed. At the same time, over three quarters of respondents (77%) said that good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past, but a similar proportion (73%) also believe that politicians on both sides “fuel conflicts between Poles and Ukrainians for their own political gain”. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Yet the survey also showed that, for Poles, historical disputes have not displaced security concerns, and in particular the view that, for Poland and Ukraine, Russia is a shared enemy. Some 75% of respondents agreed with the statement that “Poland and Ukraine should, above all, cooperate in the face of the threat from Russia, rather than focus on the issues that divide them”. The most frequently cited priorities in relations with Kyiv were security cooperation (61%), building good neighbourly relations (46%), commemorating victims of the Volhynia massacres (43%), strengthening Poland’s regional leadership (41%), and ensuring Polish companies participate in Ukraine’s reconstruction (40%). Just over half of Poles (52%) agree that “Poland and Ukraine have more common aims and interests than conflicting ones”, while 32% disagreed. A huge majority (80%) agreed that “Russia benefits from the Polish-Ukrainian dispute”. W ocenie społecznej zdecydowanym priorytetem w relacjach z Ukrainą powinna być współpraca na rzecz bezpieczeństwa – wskazało ją 61% badanych.📊 ➡️Więcej w komunikacie #CBOS "Wokół polsko-ukraińskiego sporu o imponderabilia i nie tylko":https://t.co/pIvYbu8gyz#Ukraina #relacje pic.twitter.com/LOpmAKNnXn — CBOS (@CBOS_Info) July 23, 2026 Based on the answers in the survey, CBOS identified three broad groups of respondents classified by their views of the dispute. The largest, described as “moralists”, accounted for 46% and placed greater emphasis on historical grievances. Among this group, 99% supported Nawrocki’s decision and said good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past. “Pragmatists”, who made up 34% of respondents, placed greater emphasis on future cooperation. Some 96% said Poland and Ukraine should cooperate against the Russian threat rather than focus on historical disputes. The smallest group, labelled by CBOS as “withdrawn”, represented 20% of respondents who were more likely to lack a clear view on Polish-Ukrainian relations. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Recent weeks have seen moves from Ukraine towards finding a diplomatic solution to the crisis. In early July, foreign minister Andrii Sybiha visited Warsaw to propose an “anti-crisis package” of measures. Last week, Zelensky himself outlined a five-point plan to alleviate the dispute, including opening up Ukrainian historical archives and permitting more exhumations of victims of the massacres, most of whom remain buried in mass graves in Ukraine. The Polish authorities have cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement, though also emphasise that they are waiting to see concrete action. Meanwhile, there is no indication that Zelensky will change his decision to name a unit after the heroes of the UPA. World.title: Poland bans chaining of dogs and cats
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Keeping dogs and cats chained up at home will be banned in Poland from next year, after President Karol Nawrocki signed into law a bill prohibiting the practice. His decision ends a long-running dispute over the issue, after Nawrocki last year vetoed a previous proposal to ban chaining because it also included what he argued were excessive and unrealistic additional measures on minimum kennel sizes for dogs. Zawetowana w listopadzie 2025 r. ustawa łańcuchowa była źle przygotowana i przeregulowana, ponieważ nakładała na obywateli obowiązki, których wielu nie byłoby w stanie spełnić. Dzisiaj otrzymujemy ustawę lepszą, z pozytywnym głosem takich podmiotów jak rolniczy samorząd.… pic.twitter.com/h7kIAI77KR — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 24, 2026 The new law bans owners from tethering dogs and cats at home. Animals must be kept either inside the house, in a fenced garden or, if that is not possible, in a kennel “large enough for the animal to move freely and satisfy its natural needs”. Dogs kept in kennels must be provided with daily exercise outside of it. Dogs and cats can still be put on leashes in certain situations, such as when they are being walked, but also during transport, while participating in shows, performances or training, if they are at vets or groomers, or if they represent a danger to humans or other animals. Those who are found to have violated the new law can be fined between 1,000 and 100,000 zloty (€232-23,166). If they are deemed to have acted with “extreme cruelty”, they can also face a prison sentence of up to five years, reports the Forsal news service. Now that the bill has been signed by Nawrocki, it will be published in the official Journal of Laws (Dziennik Ustaw), after which it goes into force 12 months later. The new measures represent a successful second attempt to introduce a leashing ban. A previous bill was approved by parliament last September. However, in December, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, announced that he was vetoing it. The president argued that, “although the intention – protecting animals – is just and noble, the law itself was poorly drafted”. In particular, he said that elements introducing minimum sizes for dog kennels were unrealistic and would “harm farmers, breeders and ordinary rural households”. After an attempt by parliament to overturn the veto failed, legislators went back to the drawing board and, following discussions with the president’s chancellery and animal rights groups, drafted a compromise bill that was approved by parliament earlier this month. The bill received support from the current ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, as well as most MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party. The far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) voted against it. Thousands of people have protested in Warsaw against President @NawrockiKn's veto of a law that would have banned the chaining up of dogs Parliament will vote on Wednesday on whether to overturn Nawrocki's veto, which would require a three-fifths majority https://t.co/0GRup2sppb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 “We now have a better law, with positive feedback from entities such as the agricultural chamber,” said Nawrocki today. “It demonstrates that the pressure of the presidential veto makes sense. My previous decision to refuse to sign this bill forced the government and parliament to work harder.” However, although Nawrocki said the new law would no longer entail “rigid and costly requirements” for kennels, his office noted in a separate statement that the legislation requires the agriculture minister to issue a regulation establishing “minimum kennel area, taking into account the dog’s size”. It remains unclear if and how that would differ from the requirements Nawrocki previously vetoed. The presidential chancellery also noted that the law itself already outlines that kennels must be made of “wood or wood-like material with thermal insulation”, must be insulated from the ground, and must have openings on at least two sides to allow light and air to enter. A dog who throws a ball to passers-by from a balcony above one of Poland’s most famous streets and waits for them to throw it back has become a star. Videos of her game have been viewed millions of times and people visit in the hope of playing with her https://t.co/A9p9t0hWSD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 9, 2024 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Police and park rangers step up joint patrols in Poland’s Tatras after series of tourist offences
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Police officers and rangers have stepped up joint patrols in Poland’s mountainous Tatra National Park during the peak summer season, following a spate of rule-breaking including swimming in the park’s lakes and ponds, driving cars and going off marked trails. Meanwhile, national park authorities have repeated warnings that bathing, littering and breaking other rules can damage the park’s fragile ecosystem. Local police officers have joined Tatra National Park rangers on patrols on popular tourist routes. On one such patrol last week, officers focused on education and prevention, reminding visitors not to leave marked trails or litter and explaining how to behave safely and responsibly in the mountains. They also checked that organised groups were accompanied by qualified mountain guides, as required by law. Fines for such offences range from 50 zloty (€11.55) to as much as 1,000 zloty (€231) in the event of environmental damage or multiple offences. Police said that all visitors encountered during the patrol were complying with the park’s regulations. However, they added that similar patrols would continue on a regular basis. The Tatra National Park, home to Poland’s highest peaks, and the nearby mountain resort of Zakopane are among the country’s most popular holiday destinations, with crowds taking to park trails in the summer season. The park, the most visited of Poland’s 23 national parks, welcomed a record 5.3 million visitors in 2025 and offers 275 km of marked hiking trails, including high-altitude routes that connect at several points with the adjacent national park in Slovakia. 🚨 Ukraiński Influencer wjechał nielegalnie samochodem na Morskie oko 🗣️: Jesteśmy pierwszymi ludźmi w historii, którzy wjechali samochodem nad Morskie Oko. To było jedno z miejsc, do których chcieliśmy dotrzeć podczas tej podróży i wszyscy znajomi oraz przyjaciele mówili, że… pic.twitter.com/tA9shZ6Rqk — Pigułka 💊 (@informacyjnie) May 23, 2026 This season has already seen a number of high-profile cases of transgressions of the park’s strict rules. In May, a Ukrainian social media influencer sparked outrage after driving a sports car along a road closed to traffic to Morskie Oko, a picturesque lake nestled between the mountains. As a result, he was banned from entering Poland and other Schengen Area countries for five years. Tourists have also been filmed entering Morskie Oko and other protected lakes and ponds, which is not permitted in the national park. This month, a group of young Dutch tourists were filmed bathing in Przedni Staw Polski in the Valley of the Five Lakes, one of the Tatras’ best-known hiking destinations. Witnesses repeatedly warned the group that entering the lake was prohibited, but they ignored the warnings, reports Gazeta Wyborcza. Park authorities have responded to such incidents by reminding visitors of the reasons for the strict rules. “Tatra ponds are incredibly delicate ecosystems. Cosmetics, UV filters, insect repellents, and bacteria entering the water can have a long-lasting impact on its chemical composition and the organisms living in the lakes,” they warned. A national park in Poland’s southern mountains has completed testing of an electric bus that could replace horse-drawn carriages carrying tourists to a famous lake. World.title: Polish opposition PiS party set to split, with over 30 MPs being expelled
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. More than 30 MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party, have effectively resigned after refusing to sign a loyalty pledge, party leader Jarosław Kaczyński has announced. The dispute centres around a more moderate faction in the party aligned with former prime minister and deputy PiS leader Mateusz Morawiecki, who is one of those now set to be expelled from the party. They have for months been unhappy with PiS’s move in a hard-right direction. 💬 Prezes PiS Jarosław Kaczyński @OficjalnyJK. 👉 Udostępnij pic.twitter.com/bycjE0Yq0f — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) July 24, 2026 “Around 30-something…of our group’s MPs have resigned,” revealed Kaczyński at a press conference on Friday. He added that their departures would be formalised at a meeting of the party’s political committee scheduled for Tuesday next week. Kaczyński’s announcement came after a deadline expired at midnight on Thursday for its MPs to sign a pledge of loyalty to the party that included a commitment not to be members of any external political associations. That measure was aimed in particular at an association called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) founded by Morawiecki in April. The former prime minister had always insisted that his organisation was intended as complementary to PiS, rather than a rival to it. However, many figures in the party saw it as an attempt by Morawiecki to create a separate centre of power, and potentially to use the association as a launchpad for creating his own party ahead of the autumn 2027 parliamentary elections. The right-wing opposition PiS party has threatened disciplinary action, including exclusion from electoral lists, against dozens of its MPs who have joined a new internal group led by former PM @MorawieckiM and intended to appeal to more moderate voters https://t.co/y62Cm361U2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 17, 2026 After PiS issued a resolution on Wednesday last week requiring that its parliamentarians pledge to withdraw from any such associations, most of its 186 MPs quickly complied. However, a group of between 30 and 40 who are part of Development Plus refused to do so. “Everyone knew what they were supposed to sign, and knew the consequences of not signing,” said Kaczyński on Friday. “And so they made the decision they did.” “In this situation, we cannot view the [Development Plus] association as anything other than a component of a plan…to split our party,” he added. However, although its supporters will now leave PiS, “we want to part ways without any animosity”, said Kaczyński. After Kaczyński’s announcement, senior figures from Development Plus made clear that no one from their association had resigned from PiS. They had simply not signed the declaration of loyalty demanded by the party. Later, Morawiecki himself held a press conference in parliament surrounded by his supporters. He claimed that an unnamed “small group of schemers” within PiS had been seeking to turn Kaczyński against him and push him out of the party. “We fought for the unity of Law and Justice until the very end,” declared Morawiecki, who said that his group included 40 MPs, one senator and three MEPs. However, three of the MPs are not members of PiS, and therefore were not expected to sign the loyalty declaration. Szanowni Państwo! 🟦Do ostatniej chwili walczyłem o jedność Prawa i Sprawiedliwości. Nie o stanowiska. Nie o osobiste ambicje. Nie o wpływy. 🟦Walczyłem o jedność obozu, który przez osiem lat zmieniał Polskę – budował jej bezpieczeństwo, rozwijał gospodarkę i przywracał godność… pic.twitter.com/PP7sOkzMHp — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) July 24, 2026 If the expulsion of Morawiecki’s supporters is confirmed, it will mark a major shake-up of Poland’s political landscape. PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right, including periods leading governments in 2005-2007 and 2015-2023. However, since losing power at elections in 2023, when the party won 35% of the vote, PiS has seen its average support in polls fall to around 23-24%, the lowest level in 14 years. Meanwhile, it has been challenged by the rise of the far right, where two parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), now together poll a similar combined level of support to PiS. In response, Kaczyński in March named a hardline figure, Przemyszław Czarnek, as PiS’s candidate for prime minister in next year’s elections. Czarnek was seen as someone who could appeal to far-right voters, while also potentially working with the far right if a coalition was needed after the elections. Support for PiS has fallen to its lowest in 14 years, as the party grapples with internal division, the rise of far-right challengers, living in President Nawrocki's shadow, and the unpopularity in Poland of PiS ally Donald Trump, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/QRScBpEQQG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 2, 2026 However, there has been no rise in support for PiS since Czarnek was named, prompting growing concern from more moderate figures within the party, led by Morawiecki. They argue that PiS has wrongly disowned many of the successes of its time in office before 2023, and they fear that its rightward shift damages its chances of winning over more centrist voters. Morawiecki, who was an international banker before joining PiS to become finance minister and then prime minister, wants the party to focus on more technocratic issues, such as economic development, rather than Euroscepticism and culture wars. That has led to frequent public sparring between his supporters and others in the party. In April, PiS threatened disciplinary action against members of Development Plus. Kaczyński and Morawiecki then reached an agreement that allowed the association to continue. But that uneasy truce has now fallen apart. World.title: Polish president renews bid for referendum on EU climate policy
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Karol Nawrocki has submitted a second request to parliament for a nationwide referendum on whether Poland should continue implementing the European Union’s climate policies, which he argues are too costly. Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, first proposed a referendum in May. But it was rejected by the Senate, the upper house of parliament, where the more liberal government has a majority. Senators argued that the proposed referendum question was “absurd”. The president has now submitted a revised proposal featuring a simplified question and again proposed holding the referendum on 27 September this year. Nawrocki’s originally proposed question was: “Are you in favour of implementing EU climate policy, which has led to an increase in citizens’ cost of living, energy prices and the cost of running business and agricultural activity?” However, following criticism in the Senate that the question was clearly intended to elicit a specific answer, this time he has proposed a more neutral one: “Are you in favour of Poland implementing the European Union’s climate policy?” “I’m looking for compromises, looking for solutions,” said Nawrocki on Thursday while announcing the new referendum bid. “The Senate wasn’t satisfied with the [previous] question”, so “we prepared a different one…[that] does not suggest anything”. However, the president has also proposed that the ballot paper would include information on what answering “yes” or “no” would mean in practice. Voters would be told, for example, that maintaining EU climate policy would result in, among other things, “Poland bearing costs estimated at 3.5 trillion zloty by 2040”, “burdens on agriculture”, “increasing costs for industry” and “obligations for owners of buildings”. By contrast, voting “no” would mean “negotiating exceptions and exemptions for Poland with the relevant EU bodies that will protect Polish industry and citizens from the burdens of climate policy”. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 Under Poland’s constitution, the president may call a referendum with the approval of a majority of senators in a vote where at least half of all members of the 100-seat chamber are present. The ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk controls 63 seats in the Senate, making approval of proposals brought forward by Nawrocki, who often clashes with the government and regularly vetoes its bills, unlikely. While the government is generally pro-EU, it has also been critical of Brussels’ green policies, arguing that they place too great a burden on Poland. After the European Commission last Friday unveiled changes intended to soften the impact of the Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS), the EU’s flagship climate policy, they were welcomed by the Polish government as a step in the right direction. Dzisiaj robimy milowy krok w zmianie systemu ETS. Po raz pierwszy Komisja Europejska proponuje rozwiązania, które łagodzą, a nie zaostrzają wpływ systemu na gospodarkę i obywateli. To efekt konsekwentnych działań Polski i zbudowania silnej koalicji państw w UE. Dzisiejsza… pic.twitter.com/5AMd9KCBVa — Ministerstwo Klimatu i Środowiska (@MKiS_GOV_PL) July 17, 2026 However, in his written justification for the new referendum proposal, Nawrocki wrote that, while he had “given the government time” in its push for ETS reform, the final result was simply “technical adjustments” that postpone some elements but do “not change the direction” or ultimate outcome. “ETS will remain an increasingly expensive, increasingly extensive system, and increasingly burdensome for the Polish economy,” wrote the president. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), which is the main opposition and supported Nawrocki’s bid for the presidency last year, wants Poland to unilaterally withdraw from ETS. Government figures warn, however, that there is no way to do so without either accruing enormous fines or leaving the EU entirely. When in power, PiS launched a revolution in Poland's energy transition. But now, in opposition, it has disowned those achievements and returned to an emphasis on coal. This could be a missed opportunity to win back centrist voters, writes @OrzelBartlomiej https://t.co/8cGvubn7N2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 29, 2026 Nawrocki’s new referendum proposal was met with criticism by figures from the ruling coalition. “There is no possibility of one country suspending part of EU law,” wrote Stanisław Gawłowski, a senator from Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO) party. “This referendum is pure fraud.” Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, also from KO, wrote that, “as the Brits have learned, the Europhobe’s dream world, in which one enjoys all the privileges of EU membership without any obligations, does not exist”. However, Nawrocki’s initiative was welcomed by Przemysław Czarnek, deputy leader of PiS, who wrote that, “on such fundamental matters as climate policy, Poles should decide, not Brussels bureaucrats”. Zaproponowane przez @NawrockiKn pytanie referendalne jest wybiórcze. Kontrpropozycja: „Czy jesteś za likwidacją unijnych dopłat do inwestycji i dla rolników?” Jak przekonali się Brytyjczycy, świat eurofoba, w którym ma się same przywileje członkostwa w UE, nie istnieje. — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) July 23, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland appoints new human rights commissioner
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government’s majority in parliament has chosen Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram as Poland’s new human rights commissioner. She will take office after the five-year term of the incumbent, Marcin Wiącek, expires today. Gregorczyk-Abram is a prominent lawyer and activist, who is particularly well known for opposing the overhaul of the judiciary by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. PiS, which is now the main opposition party, strongly opposed her election, arguing that she is politically aligned with the current, more liberal government. Gregorczyk-Abram herself, however, has pledged to “put all my beliefs and views aside” when she takes up the new role. Senat wyraził zgodę na powołanie Sylwii Gregorczyk-Abram na Rzecznika Praw Obywatelskich. pic.twitter.com/gz3rwGy3hi — Senat RP 🇵🇱 (@PolskiSenat) July 22, 2026 The commissioner for human rights (widely known by its Polish initials, RPO) is appointed by a resolution of the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, with the consent of the upper-house Senate. Candidates must meet certain requirements, including not belonging to any political party and having legal expertise and relevant experience. As well as acting as a watchdog for human rights, the RPO also has the power to submit motions to the Constitutional Tribunal to assess the constitutionality of laws and to file so-called cassation appeals to the Supreme Court and Supreme Administrative Court against rulings by lower courts. Poland’s human rights commissioner has written to the government expressing concern that a "temporary" ban on asylum claims by most migrants who irregularly cross the border from Belarus remains in place after more than a year https://t.co/9SA2TypQdK — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 28, 2026 Gregorczyk-Abram was last month nominated as a candidate to be the new RPO by the main ruling party, Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO), along with one of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica). PiS proposed a rival candidate, Adam Borowski, a veteran of Poland’s anti-communist struggle in the 1980s. However, critics argued that Borowski, an activist and former PiS election candidate, does not appear to have the requisite legal knowledge and experience. In a Sejm vote last Friday, the ruling coalition supported Gregorczyk-Abram, who won 233 votes to Borowski’s 177. On Wednesday, her candidacy was also supported by the Senate, with 59 votes in favour and 25 against, confirming that she will become the new RPO. Gregorczyk-Abram is best known as one of the founders and leaders of the Free Courts (Wolne Sądy) initiative launched in 2017 amid a wave of protests against the then-PiS government’s efforts to take greater control over the judiciary. Free Courts was prominent in efforts to defend the rule of law. Many of its leading figures are now associated with the current ruling coalition: Maria Ejchart is a deputy justice minister, while Michał Wawrykiewicz is a member of the European Parliament representing KO. In April last year, Gregorczyk-Abram was made chairwoman of a commission established by the current government to look into cases of abuse of power against civil society under the former PiS administration. In September, her commission published its first findings, in which it said that public media outlets under PiS control had “carried out systematic repressive and defamatory actions against activists, non-governmental organisations, and civil society”. Poland's public media “carried out systematic repressive actions against activists, NGOs and civil society” during the rule of the former PiS government, a report commissioned by the new government has found https://t.co/S2MO9KGssC — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 26, 2025 PiS argues that Gregorczyk-Abram’s previous activity makes her unsuitable as a suitable candidate for RPO, which is meant to be a non-partisan role. They also point to claims that she was involved in a group of legal figures that discussed the Tusk government’s controversial takeover of public media in December 2023. “[She] is a discredited and extremely politicised person who should be brought to justice, and not receive the laurels of the commissioner for human rights,” former PiS justice minister Marcin Warchoł told the Do Rzeczy weekly last month. After a Sejm committee hearing on Gregorczyk-Abram’s candidacy earlier this month, former PiS deputy justice minister Sebastian Kaleta criticised her for ignoring questions over her alleged “role in the illegal takeover of public media”. Zadałem Sylwii Gregorczyk-Abram serię pytań o jej działania i możliwe spotkania z Ewą Wrzosek w sprawie przejęcia TVP, w tym możliwego tworzenia dokumentów prokuratorskich w prywatnej kancelarii. Kandydatka ostentacyjnie zdecydowała się ignorować te pytania. Ma bardzo dużo do… — Sebastian Kaleta (@sjkaleta) July 15, 2026 Speaking to state broadcaster TVP on Wednesday after her appointment was confirmed by the Senate, Gregorczyk-Abram declared that, “from the moment I take the oath and assume the position of commissioner, I will be independent and sovereign”. She pledged to “put all my beliefs and views – because each of us has them – aside and become an advocate for all citizens, regardless of what they believe in, how they live, or who they vote for”. Gregorczyk-Abram said that among her priorities as RPO would be the justice system, supporting the rights of disabled people and their carers, protecting older people, and fighting hate speech. With regard to the last of these issues, she noted that certain politicians present some groups as “enemies”, pointing to how this previously happened with LGBT+ people and judges, and is now being directed towards Ukrainians. Those are all groups who have at various stages been targeted by PiS and other right-wing parties. The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: President to swear in new judge to Poland’s disputed constitutional court

President Karol Nawrocki has agreed to swear in a new judge to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), ending weeks of doubt as to whether the opposition-aligned president would accept the judge appointed by the government’s parliamentary majority. Although Sławomir Patyra will now be accepted onto the court, four other judges appointed by parliament earlier this year continue to be excluded after Nawrocki refused to receive their oaths and the TK’s chief justice, also aligned with the opposition, blocked them from taking office. W najbliższy wtorek 28 lipca Prezydent Karol Nawrocki działając na postawie art. 4 ust. 1 ustawy o statusie sędziów Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, przyjmie ślubowanie od prof. Sławomira Patyry i tego samego dnia wręczy powołania czterem nowym sędziom Sądu Najwyższego. W przyszłym… — Zbigniew Bogucki🇵🇱 (@BoguckiZbigniew) July 22, 2026 Under Polish law, when a vacancy emerges among the 15 positions on the TK – for example when a judge’s nine-year term expires – the lower house of parliament, the Sejm, chooses who should fill it. However, to take office, the judge must swear an oath before the president. In April, after the Sejm had chosen six candidates to fill vacancies on the court, Nawrocki took the unprecedented step of inviting only two of them to be sworn in. He argued there were doubts over the legality of how all six had been chosen, but decided to accept two to ensure the TK had the necessary quorum to function. Those two have been able to take up their seats on the court, but the other four remain in limbo. Although they arranged their own private swearing-in ceremony without the presence of Nawrocki, the TK’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, has refused to accept them. In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the quartet be allowed to take up their positions. But the TK – where judges appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government retain a majority – issued its own ruling endorsing Nawrocki’s right not to swear in the new judges. On 11 June, the Sejm then chose another judge, Patyra, to fill a newly opened vacancy on the court. In his case, the legal doubts Nawrocki had expressed regarding the previous appointments, which in some instances were made more than a year after the vacancies had arisen, did not seem to apply. Yet for weeks the president refused to confirm whether he would swear him in. That prompted Patyra to write to Nawrocki in early July and then again this week, asking the president to indicate a date on which he could take his oath. Patyra himself has also made clear on which side of the dispute he stands. In an interview with news website Onet in May, he accused Nawrocki and Święczkowski of “blatantly unlawful actions” in deciding which TK judges can and cannot take office and suggested that the police should intervene. Sędzia TK prof. Patyra po raz kolejny zaapelował do Prezydenta o wyznaczenie mu terminu na złożenie przysięgi. Ignorowanie sędziego TK przez Prezydenta jest kolejnym przykładem psucia państwa. To pokazuje, jak bardzo siły anty-demokratyczne boją się odbudowy niezależnego TK.… — Dariusz Mazur (@_Dariusz_Mazur) July 21, 2026 Finally, on Wednesday this week, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, announced that Nawrocki had invited Patyra to the presidential palace on Tuesday next week to take his oath. Speaking to Polsat News, Bogucki said that, in the case of Patyra, initially “there were some doubts, but the president dispelled them”, without specifying what they were. In the end, they concluded that “we had a fundamentally clean situation here” and Patyra was chosen “in accordance with all procedures”, unlike the six new judges chosen by the Sejm in March to fill longstanding vacancies. “It was not President Nawrocki or the current opposition who destroyed and are destroying the tribunal; it is the government that is doing it,” he added. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. World.title: Best Petting Zoos in Prague for Families with Kids (2026 Guide)
World.content:
Prague Zoo gets all the attention — and fair enough, it’s consistently ranked among the top zoos in the world — but the city is also full of smaller, low-key spots where kids can get hands-on with animals.

These mini farms and forest parks are perfect for a relaxed weekend outing, most are free or nearly free, and several are just a short metro ride from the centre.

Here’s our pick of the best small zoos and petting farms around Prague.

1. Milíčovský dvůr – Prague 11

Right on the edge of Milíčov forest, this outdoor farm is home to a horse, an ostrich, a fox, goats, sheep, pigs, rabbits and more. Feed dispensers let kids feed the animals directly, and there’s a sandpit, a wooden playground and a small snack stand on site. Entry costs just 20 CZK. Closed Mondays.

📍 K Milíčovu 100/8, Prague 11 — nearest metro: Háje

2. Chuchle Grove Mini Zoo – Prague 5

Set on a hillside inside the Chuchle Grove nature park, this zoo run by Prague’s city forestry service cares for injured and orphaned wildlife. Expect to see mouflons, deer, wild boar, owls, lynxes and more — though petting isn’t allowed here, since the focus is conservation and education. Free entry, open 24/7, with a playground and refreshment kiosk nearby.

📍 V Lázních 8, Prague 5

3. Station of Young Biologists – Prague 5

A mix of indoor and outdoor spaces near Anděl, with a tropical terrarium (crocodiles, monkeys, boas), an aviary, and outdoor pens with kangaroos, llamas, ponies and goats. Regular workshops and interactive shows run alongside the animal exhibits. General entry is free; the terrarium and greenhouses cost a small fee (20–40 CZK).

📍 Drtinova 1A, Prague 5 — near Anděl metro

4. Toulcův dvůr – Prague 10

An 8.5-hectare environmental education centre in Hostivař with cows, horses, chickens, pigs, sheep and goats, plus a cherry orchard, wetlands and a farm-to-table restaurant. Petting and feeding aren’t permitted, but it’s a beautifully kept site for a nature walk.

📍 Kubátova 1/32, Prague 10

Honourable mentions

If you’re just after a nice walk with a chance of spotting animals, these free spots are worth a detour:

Wild Garden Hostivař (Prague 15) — rare white fallow deer and mouflons roam near a flooded quarry, with a playground and lakeside walk.

(Prague 15) — rare white fallow deer and mouflons roam near a flooded quarry, with a playground and lakeside walk. Kunratice Forest (Prague 4) — sheep, dwarf goats and pigs can be fed at the “Na tý louce zelený” restaurant, with spotted deer and mouflons visible along the trails.

(Prague 4) — sheep, dwarf goats and pigs can be fed at the “Na tý louce zelený” restaurant, with spotted deer and mouflons visible along the trails. Kamýk Forest (Prague 12) — a small goat enclosure and pheasant aviary tucked next to the gamekeeper’s lodge, surrounded by walking and cycling trails.

World.title: Stromovka: A Green Paradise in the Heart of Prague
World.content:
Stromovka is one of the largest and most popular parks in Prague, drawing visitors with its beautiful nature, rich history, and numerous activities.

Let’s explore what Stromovka offers and how to get there.

Why Visit Stromovka?

Looking for a break from the city’s hustle and bustle or the perfect spot for a picnic with friends? Stromovka is your ideal choice. This vast park features green meadows, shady alleys, and ample opportunities for sports and cultural events.

What is Stromovka?

Stromovka, officially known as Královská obora, spans more than 95 hectares, making it one of Prague’s largest green spaces. Located in Prague 7, the park is a favorite among joggers, cyclists, families, and anyone looking to escape into nature without leaving the city.

It’s perfect for walks, picnics, sports, or simply relaxing on the grass.

A Brief History

Stromovka’s history dates back to the 13th century when it was established as a royal hunting ground. Over time, it evolved and expanded, becoming a public park in the 19th century. The park is home to the original Vltava Creek and several ponds, which host various water birds.

Throughout its history, Stromovka has undergone many changes, shaping it into the popular relaxation spot it is today.

Activities in Stromovka

Stromovka offers a wide range of activities for all ages. Here are some ideas:

Walking and Running: Enjoy the scenic trails.

Cycling: Explore the park on two wheels.

Picnics: Large meadows and shady spots are perfect for a picnic.

Sports: Play football, volleyball, and other sports.

Cultural Events: Attend various events hosted in the park.

How to Get to Stromovka

By Metro: The nearest metro station is Nádraží Holešovice (line C). From there, it’s just a few minutes’ walk to Stromovka.

By Tram: Trams also reach the park. The nearest stops are Výstaviště Holešovice (lines 6, 12, 17) and Planetarium Prague (line 6).

By Bike: Cycling enthusiasts can easily access Stromovka by bike. Bike-sharing stations like Rekola and Nextbike are available around the park, allowing you to ride directly into this natural haven.

World.title: August 12-31: Prague to Host Festival of New Circus Letní Letná
World.content:
The international festival of new circus and theatre, Letní Letná 2026, will take place in Prague on August 12-31.

The festival will feature over 200 performances, workshops, concerts, and various acts by circus artists from 14 countries, including a special program for children.

This year marks the 23rd edition of the festival. Letenské sady park will once again be the main venue, with tents set up to create a mini-town complete with a coffee shop and an evening bar.

Many performances will be free of charge. Additionally, the festival will offer a rich and varied daily program: children’s shows, circus, juggling and acrobat workshops, music concerts, exhibitions, lectures, creative workshops, and more.

One of this year’s highlights is Wolf by Australia’s renowned Circa ensemble. The international lineup also includes Switzerland’s Accademia Teatro Dimitri, presenting its graduate production La Grinta, and Seismic, a collaboration between French choreographer Marie Gourdain and German artist Felix Baumann, featuring Czech performers.

The Czech program includes the premiere of Vertige by AirGym Art Company, Enola by Eliška Brtnická, new productions from Losers Cirque Company, and Hey, Earth! by Cirque La Putyka.

Emerging talent will also take center stage, with performances by CZirkidz Dance Company, Teens Cirkabaret, and recent graduates of international circus schools.

Audiences will have the chance to experience works in progress, including K voknu by Michaela Stará and Filip Zahradnický, followed by discussions with the artists.

For adults, Světla a stíny by Silk&Steel explores the darker sides of human experience through aerial and ground acrobatics, while family-friendly performances include the popular (Not Only) Juggling Galashow and Orbiting Zero by Czech juggler Aleš Hrdlička.

Beyond the performances, visitors can enjoy free workshops, children’s activities, concerts, open-air events, food stalls, bars, and relaxation areas throughout the festival grounds. Babysitting is available during selected performances, and the venue is fully accessible, making Letní Letná a festival for all ages.

World.title: New Railway Tunnel to Cut Prague to Pilsen Journey to 45 Minutes
World.content:
The Czech government has approved the next phase of one of its largest railway infrastructure projects: a new tunnel connecting Prague and Beroun.

Construction is expected to begin in 2032, with completion scheduled for 2044.

The 24.7-kilometre double-track tunnel will significantly shorten travel times on one of the country’s busiest rail corridors.

Once completed, trains will travel between Prague-Smíchov station and Beroun in around 13 minutes, reducing the current journey time by more than 30 minutes.

The project will also improve connections towards western Czechia and neighbouring Germany. The journey from Prague to Pilsen is expected to take approximately 45 minutes, while international rail services to Munich and Nuremberg will become faster and more reliable.

New railway line designed for speeds of up to 200 km/h

The planned railway route will include a new high-speed section designed for trains travelling at up to 200 km/h. The tunnel will begin near Prague-Smíchov station, pass beneath the Barrandov area, and emerge near Beroun.

A separate connection on the Prague side is also planned, linking the new line with Braník Bridge and Prague-Krč. The additional infrastructure will improve connections within the capital while increasing capacity on the wider railway network.

Construction preparation underway

Preparatory work for the tunnel is already in progress. Geological surveys and technical documentation are currently being completed, with the application for a construction permit expected to be submitted between 2028 and 2029.

After the approval process, Správa železnic will launch a tender to select the construction company responsible for building the tunnel.

The Czech Railway Administration estimates the total cost of the project will continue to rise due to inflation and increasing construction expenses. However, its director general Tomáš Tóth said the estimated cost of around CZK 3 billion per kilometre remains comparable with similar railway tunnel projects abroad.

The project is expected to increase railway capacity towards western Czechia, improve timetable reliability, and strengthen connections between Prague, Pilsen, and major German cities.

World.title: Thailand Brings Its Culture and Flavours to Prague at Thai Market 2026
World.content:
The colours, flavours, and warm spirit of Thailand return to the capital on Friday, 4 September 2026, as the Royal Thai Embassy proudly hosts Thai Market 2026 at the historic Písecká brána.

Organised alongside Team Thailand—comprising the Thai Trade Centre and the Tourism Authority of Thailand in Prague—this year’s flagship event is held in active cooperation with the Prague 6 Municipality.

“Thai Market has become a meaningful platform to bring Thailand closer to the Czech public through friendship, creativity, and people-to-people connections,” said H.E. Mr. Pichit Boonsud, Ambassador of the Kingdom of Thailand to the Czech Republic.

“This year, we are thrilled to celebrate Prague 6 Day with our Thai Market to show our true partnership with the local municipality. This event is a heartfelt cultural exchange and our way of actively engaging with the wonderful community that hosts us.”

Open to all ages with free admission, the event will offer a full day of authentic Thai experiences, from traditional cuisine and refreshing drinks such as Thai iced tea to popular desserts including Mango Sticky Rice and Thai tea ice cream.

Visitors can also take part in interactive workshops, including a mini Loy Krathong celebration with origami lotus basket-making, traditional Thai clothing photo sessions, and postcard design with Thai stickers.

The programme will also feature live stage performances, premium Thai products from Czech importers, traditional Thai massages, and activities where guests can win vouchers to spend at the event.

A dedicated tourism section will provide inspiration and information for those planning their next trip to Thailand. Thai Market 2026 promises to be a vibrant celebration of Thai culture, flavours, and community in the heart of Prague.

Event Details Event:

Date: Friday, 4 September 2026

Time: 11.00-17.30

Venue: Písecká brána, K Brusce 5, 160 00 Prague 6 – Hradčany

Admission: Free entry

World.title: Future of Prague’s Výtoň Bridge Could Be Decided by the End of This Year
World.content:
The Railway Administration (Správa železnic) is expected to decide on the future design of Prague’s Výtoň Railway Bridge by the end of this year.

If the final plan is approved, construction could begin in 2028.

The long-delayed project has become the centre of a dispute between transport authorities and heritage experts. While railway officials argue that a new three-track structure is necessary to meet future transport demands, conservationists continue to push for the preservation of the existing historic bridge.

The Railway Administration has warned that the current condition of the bridge requires a final decision soon.

Dispute over historic structure

The main proposal currently under consideration is the construction of a new three-track railway bridge. Správa železnic selected a project team last year, but the plan remains controversial due to opposition from heritage authorities and groups seeking to preserve the original structure.

The debate has also attracted international attention. UNESCO representatives are preparing a Heritage Impact Assessment (HIA), which will examine how the planned changes could affect Prague’s cultural heritage.

The Transport Association supports the construction of a new bridge, arguing that rebuilding the existing structure would be more expensive and would not provide enough additional capacity.

Construction could start in 2028

According to earlier plans from Správa železnic, work on the project was originally expected to begin sooner. A tender process was completed in 2025, with companies SUDOP Praha and TOP CON SERVIS selected for the preparation of the three-track bridge project.

The estimated cost of the entire project is around CZK 3.4 billion.

Because of the bridge’s deteriorating condition, trains currently operate on only one track and must reduce speed when crossing the structure. The construction of the additional third track alone is expected to cost approximately CZK 129 million.

World.title: Prague Compared to 11 European Cities: Housing, Jobs, Transport,
World.content:
A new report from the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR) compares life in Prague with 11 other European cities, following a typical resident’s day—from housing and commuting to work, education, and leisure.

Based on verified data collected directly from partner cities, the study highlights both Prague’s strengths and its biggest challenges.

Prague Has Some of Europe’s Least Affordable Housing

The report found that Prague has the least affordable owner-occupied housing among the cities compared.

Buying an apartment requires more than 13 years of gross salary, placing Prague alongside cities such as Barcelona, Munich, and Amsterdam. Unlike many Western European cities, Prague also lacks relatively affordable rental housing.

Renting a 60-square-meter apartment costs around 40% of the average salary in Prague. By comparison, the same apartment would consume about 28% of average income in Munich and just 14% in Vienna.

Strong Job Market, But Lower Incomes

Prague continues to have one of the lowest unemployment rates in Europe, making it relatively easy to find work.

However, real incomes remain below those of most Western European capitals. Workers in Munich earn roughly 50% more than those in Prague, while wages in cities such as Copenhagen have grown steadily over the past decade.

Although Prague residents now work fewer hours than they did ten years ago—less than 39 hours per week on average—they still work around three hours more each week than people in many Western European cities.

Public Transport Is One of Prague’s Biggest Strengths

Prague ranks among Europe’s top cities for public transport.

Around 70% of residents use public transport regularly, while 87% report being satisfied with the service. The city’s extensive tram, metro, and rail networks make commuting easy, and the system stands out for its reliability, dense coverage, and affordability.

A monthly public transport pass costs less than 1% of the average monthly income, making Prague one of the most affordable cities for public transport after Barcelona.

Car Ownership Continues to Rise

Despite having one of Europe’s best public transport systems, Prague continues to see a steady increase in car ownership.

Together with Warsaw and Bucharest, Prague is one of the few cities in the study where the number of registered cars is still growing significantly. By contrast, cities such as Stockholm, Copenhagen, and Vienna have between one-third and one-half fewer cars per capita and a much higher share of electric and hybrid vehicles.

The report warns that increasing car ownership contributes to traffic congestion, road accidents, poorer air quality, and greater pressure on public space.

World.title: Meet the Four Prague Pizzerias Recognized in 50 Top Pizza Europa 2026
World.content:
Prague’s growing pizza scene gained international attention after four local restaurants were recognized in the 50 Top Pizza Europa 2026 guide.

The biggest success went to Pizza Nuova, which secured 30th place among the best pizzerias in Europe outside Italy. While the restaurant slipped a few places compared with last year’s ranking, it remains the only Czech establishment to appear in the guide’s main European list.

Located near Prague’s Kotva department store, Pizza Nuova has built its reputation on authentic Neapolitan pizza made with premium Italian ingredients. The restaurant also holds certification from the Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana, an organization that promotes traditional Neapolitan pizza-making standards.

Prague’s recognition extended beyond a single restaurant. Three additional venues received the guide’s Excellent Pizzerias distinction, awarded to restaurants that consistently demonstrate outstanding quality.

This year’s recipients are Da Pietro, Sasy The Original, and Diskotéka in Prague’s Dejvice district.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pizzeria Da Pietro Praha (@dapietropraha)

Diskotéka is one of this year’s notable newcomers. Shortly after opening, the restaurant attracted attention for its distinctive interior, centered around a large silver pizza oven designed to resemble a disco ball.

Alongside its food, the venue hosts DJ nights and combines a traditional pizzeria with a relaxed social gathering space.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Diskotéka Pizza (@diskoteka.pizza)

The annual 50 Top Pizza rankings are compiled by anonymous inspectors who visit restaurants without prior notice. Their assessments go well beyond the pizza itself, taking into account ingredient quality, dough preparation, baking technique, service, beverage selection, atmosphere, and the overall dining experience.

World.title: Putin’s ally urges the Russian president to ‘freeze’ Ukraine war
World.content:
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev on Saturday met with Russian President Vladimir Putin, urging him to “freeze” the Ukraine conflict and return to what he described as the “Istanbul Formula 2.0,” where “significant results were achieved.”

During a meeting with Putin in the Russian city of Omsk, Tokayev said Kazakhstan was not an outsider to the ongoing conflict but would not seek to play a mediator role, expressing confidence that “a great country,” Russia, would resolve issues on its own.

“Perhaps this conflict should be frozen, and we should return to the ‘Istanbul Formula 2.0,’ since significant results were achieved there,” Tokayev said. “Then, naturally, under guarantees from the major powers, including Russia, we can move toward the long-awaited peace.”

Tokayev said he had received numerous signals from Europe and the United States regarding the conflict, which he described as an interstate war.

He also praised what he called Putin’s “maximum diplomatic flexibility” during the summit in Anchorage, Alaska, between the Russian president and US President Donald Trump in August last year.

“And all of this must be stopped, because what is happening, in my convinced opinion, is to the advantage and delight of the opponents of both Russia and the Ukrainian state,” he added.

Tokayev did not clarify his remarks concerning the “Istanbul formula,” but the Turkish metropolis has hosted peace talks between Russia and Ukraine, first in the initial weeks of the ongoing war, which produced a framework for a possible deal.

In mid-2025, three rounds of renewed peace talks were also held in Istanbul — on 16 May, 2 June, and 23 July — which produced major prisoner swaps and draft memorandums outlining positions of both sides for a potential peace deal.

Astana International Forum 2025, Kazakhstan. Photo: Kazakhstan Presidential Press Office

Developing ties

Tokayev further commented on Kazakh-Russian ties, saying Russia is effectively becoming the leading investor in his country’s economy, with volumes reaching nearly $30 billion.

“Interestingly, through joint efforts, we have identified a pool of 177 promising industrial projects, 122 of which have already been implemented, with a total project value of $53 billion,” Tokayev said.

Defining this to be a significant number “given the challenging geopolitical conditions of the current era,” Tokayev went on to speak about Kazakhstan’s project of building its first nuclear power plant. Tokayev stated he has been informed that field work on the site near Lake Balkhash is nearing completion.

“This project isn’t just about producing a new form of energy in Kazakhstan. It’s a project that will bring our countries and, most importantly, our peoples, particularly the younger generation, closer together,” Tokayev said.

“After all, we’re talking about training technical personnel with Russia’s help, local Kazakh personnel who would then be capable of working in this very complex field, the nuclear industry. Therefore, I believe all other issues are progressing quite well,” he added.

For his part, Putin praised the development of Russian-Kazakh ties, describing them as “truly strategic in nature—not just in words, but in deeds.”

“This is evidenced by the growing level of trade turnover. Last year, we had almost $28 billion, $27.8 billion, to be precise—a decent figure,” he said.

Describing this as a “positive trend” indicating they have good prospects, Putin said these prospects are determined, among other things, by investment.

“Here, too, we have something to brag about: we have 70 projects involving Russian companies and Russian businesses, totalling approximately $30 billion,” Putin said, noting Russia is the largest investor in the Kazakh economy in this sense, and in a wide range of sectors.

He also said that they actively cooperate internationally and are actively involved in all regional organisations, including the Collective Security Treaty Organisation and the Eurasian Economic Union.

Concerning the topic of Ukraine, Putin later told his Kazakh counterpart that he would inform him about it in detail during their conversation.

Russia: Kazakh proposal impossible due to Kyiv’s position

The Kremlin said on Saturday that Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s proposal to “freeze” the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war is “impossible” given Kyiv’s position. “Freezing (the war) as such is not possible,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted as saying by Russian media outlets, including state news agency Tass.

Peskov was quoted as saying that Russia’s conditions for a halt to hostilities are clear and the war could end “by the end of the day” if Ukraine makes the “appropriate decisions,” referring to Moscow’s demand for a Ukrainian withdrawal from the Donbas region, as well as Kyiv’s abandonment of plans to join NATO.

“For us there is one main condition –- we must achieve our goals,” Peskov went on to say, adding Russian President Vladimir Putin provided Tokayev with a detailed update on the progress of what Moscow calls its “special military operation” in Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin on 17 June 2026. Photo: Anadolu Agency

Kyiv welcomes Kazakh president’s call to freeze the war

Ukraine on Sunday welcomed Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s call to “freeze” the war Russia launched in 2022, with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha describing the suggestion as “realistic, timely, and wise.”

“We appreciate President @TokayevKZ telling Putin it is time to stop the war. A realistic, timely, and wise message,” Sybiha wrote on US social media platform X.

We appreciate President @TokayevKZ telling Putin it is time to stop the war. A realistic, timely, and wise message. Ukraine has proposed stopping the war along current frontlines and turning to diplomacy, but the Kremlin continues to reject this clear path to peace. Putin’s… — Andrii Sybiha 🇺🇦 (@andrii_sybiha) July 26, 2026

He said Ukraine proposed halting the fighting along the current front lines and turning to diplomacy, claiming that the Kremlin “continues to reject this clear path to peace.”

“Putin’s spokesman has already dismissed the Kazakh President’s proposal as well,” Sybiha added. “The bottom line: Moscow must feel more pressure before it accepts realistic peace proposals.”

World.title: Budapest Mayor calls for renewal of Népliget as opportunity comes with government change
World.content:
Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony has welcomed the government’s willingness to consider renovating the long-abandoned Budapest Planetarium and the Népliget, while sharply criticising the previous Orbán administration for allowing the landmark educational attraction to fall into disrepair.

In a Facebook post published over the weekend, Karácsony said the Planetarium, located in the Népliget (People’s Park in English), had been an important place of learning for generations before closing in 2017. Since then, he said, the building’s condition has steadily deteriorated.

“Among the Orbán government’s many failures was allowing the Planetarium in Népliget to decay,” the mayor wrote.

Minister signals support for renovation

Karácsony revealed that he had recently raised the Planetarium’s future with Zoltán Tanács, Hungary’s Minister for Science and Technology, who announced on Friday that he intends to recommend to the government that the building be renovated and given a new purpose.

The mayor described the announcement as encouraging, arguing that the future of the Planetarium cannot be separated from the wider regeneration of Népliget. “The renewal of the Planetarium and Népliget is inconceivable without one another,” he said.

Hungary’s largest historic public park

Karácsony described Népliget as Hungary’s largest historic public park, stressing that its restoration is not merely a Budapest issue but a project of national importance encompassing urban development, environmental protection and cultural heritage.

The park, jointly owned by the capital, the state and the district authority, has suffered decades of decline despite its valuable tree stock and protected status as a historic garden since 2005. According to the mayor, the deteriorating condition of the Planetarium has contributed to the park’s broader decline.

Masterplan already prepared

The Budapest Municipality says it has spent several years preparing a comprehensive redevelopment strategy for Népliget as part of its Radó Dezső Plan.

The project has included public consultations, cooperation with government bodies and district authorities, the preparation of a strategic development plan and a landscape architecture design competition held in 2022. Based on the winning proposals, the city is now finalising an implementation plan that would guide the park’s gradual transformation.

The plans include renovating green spaces throughout the park, improving pedestrian, cycling and public transport access, expanding recreational and leisure facilities, calming traffic on roads that currently divide the park, demolishing abandoned pavilions, and resolving long-standing land ownership issues. Here are the original plans from 2022:

Transport improvements could transform the park

Karácsony also highlighted several major transport projects that could significantly improve access to Népliget. The Hungarian Museum of Transport will remain adjacent to the park, while the planned development of Budapest’s Orbital Railway (Körvasút) is expected to include a new railway station serving the area.

Combined with existing metro, tram, bus and cycling links, these investments could make Népliget one of the capital’s most accessible public parks, opening up new opportunities for recreation and tourism.

Funding dispute with previous government

The mayor argued that the first phase of the regeneration could have been financed through European Union funding, but claimed the previous government blocked the project for political reasons. He expressed hope that Hungary’s new government would instead become a partner in delivering both the Planetarium’s restoration and the wider renewal of Népliget.

Karácsony said he has already sent the detailed redevelopment plans to Science and Technology Minister Zoltán Tanács, seeking cooperation on what he described as a historic opportunity to restore one of Budapest’s most significant public spaces.

More on Budapest: Easier after dark: Budapest expands night transport to a lot more suburbs

A park with more than 120 years of history

Népliget’s origins date back to the late 19th century, when landscaping began on the site of a former sand quarry and landfill. Its development accelerated ahead of Hungary’s Millennium celebrations in 1896, providing new green space while nearby City Park was occupied by exhibition grounds.

The park enjoyed its heyday between the two world wars, featuring amusement attractions and entertainment venues, while prestigious motor races were held there until the 1970s. From 1977 until its closure in 2017, the Budapest Planetarium became one of the city’s best-known educational attractions, introducing generations of visitors to astronomy and space science.

World.title: PM Magyar presents Hungarian Grand Prix trophy to Lando Norris after record-breaking race
World.content:
Lando Norris received the prestigious Herend porcelain winner’s trophy from Prime Minister Péter Magyar after claiming victory at the 41st Hungarian Grand Prix at the Hungaroring on Sunday.

The McLaren driver finished ahead of Max Verstappen and Kimi Antonelli in front of a record crowd at the Hungarian circuit. As part of the traditional podium ceremony, Magyar also presented Norris with the winner’s medal.

PM congratulates drivers and event organisers

Following the race, the prime minister shared photographs with all three podium finishers on Facebook.

“Incredible excitement, a fantastic race and a record number of spectators,” Magyar wrote. “Congratulations to all the drivers and to the thousands of our fellow Hungarians who helped organise the event.”

Awarding trophies at Formula 1 races by local political leaders is a long-established tradition. Previous Hungarian Grands Prix have featured senior government officials presenting the trophies, and this year Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai also took part in the podium ceremony alongside the prime minister.

Norris avoids repeat of 2023 trophy mishap

Norris handled the famous Herend porcelain trophy with extra care this year, avoiding a repeat of the memorable 2023 podium incident when Max Verstappen accidentally smashed his Herend trophy during the celebrations.

Hungary aims to secure Formula 1 beyond 2032

Before the race, Magyar held talks at the Hungaroring with Formula 1 President and CEO Stefano Domenicali. Following the meeting, the prime minister said negotiations would continue over extending Hungary’s place on the Formula 1 calendar after the current agreement expires in 2032.

“Our goal is to ensure that the Hungaroring continues to host Formula 1 under the best possible conditions,” Magyar said, adding that the government remains committed to maintaining the race in Hungary for years to come.

The Hungarian Grand Prix, first held in 1986, was the first Formula 1 race staged behind the Iron Curtain and remains one of the championship’s most historic venues.

World.title: PM Magyar holds talks with F1 CEO: Here’s what he said about keeping Formula 1 beyond 2032
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has confirmed that Hungary wants to remain on the Formula 1 calendar well beyond the current contract, following talks with Formula 1 President and CEO Stefano Domenicali at the Hungaroring during the 41st Hungarian Grand Prix.

Speaking after the meeting in Mogyoród on Sunday, Magyar said the government’s objective is to ensure that Formula 1 continues to be held in Hungary under the best possible conditions after the current agreement expires.

Hungary and Formula 1 discussing the future

Hungary’s contract with Liberty Media currently runs until 2032, but Magyar revealed that discussions have already begun about a possible five-year extension included as an option in the agreement.

“We agreed with Formula 1’s leadership to continue negotiations. The goal is to secure the best possible conditions so that the Hungaroring and Formula 1 remain in Hungary,” the prime minister said.

He described the Hungarian Grand Prix as a major success, noting that a record number of spectators attended the event, Sunday’s race was sold out, and tickets had been unavailable for some time.

Photo: MTI

More than just a race weekend

Magyar said discussions with Domenicali also focused on extending Formula 1 weekends into longer events that generate greater economic and tourism benefits for host countries.

He pointed out that the temporary facilities in the paddock also serve as venues for business leaders holding investment talks during the race weekend, creating additional economic opportunities beyond motorsport.

According to the prime minister, Hungary should make the most of both the tourism and investment potential generated by Formula 1.

Péter Magyar (l), Czech President Petr Pavel (c) and International Automobile Federation President Mohammed Ben Sulayem (r). Photo: MTI

Hungaroring support remains unchanged

Magyar stressed that the change of government will not affect support for the Hungaroring. However, he said the new administration intends to review the previous government’s spending on the circuit’s redevelopment. Under the existing contract, approximately HUF 90 billion was spent on renovating and constructing facilities at the venue.

“At first glance the investment appears successful, but the devil is in the details,” Magyar said, adding that the government wants to examine how public funds were used and whether costs could have been managed more efficiently.

He also announced that Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai, who is responsible for sport within the government, will conduct a detailed review of the financial figures in the coming days.

Have you read this? Two centuries of history: Why the Hungarian Grand Prix trophy is so iconic

Hungarian fans and a historic circuit

Reflecting on Formula 1’s place in Hungary, Magyar said he had been a supporter of Nigel Mansell, later cheering for Ayrton Senna and Michael Schumacher.

He added that he would like to see more Hungarian fans attending the race, even though 70–80% of spectators currently come from abroad, making the event an important tourism and country-branding asset.

Magyar also highlighted Hungary’s historic place in Formula 1, recalling that the 1986 Hungarian Grand Prix was the first Formula 1 race held behind the Iron Curtain.

According to the prime minister, Domenicali praised the enthusiasm of Hungarian fans and acknowledged the long-standing popularity of Formula 1 in the country. Magyar concluded by saying the championship benefits from a highly professional team and that Hungarians should be proud of the significant contribution made by local professionals to the success of the event.

World.title: Transport Minister Vitézy vows to end bus shortages across Hungary
World.content:
Hungary’s Minister for Transport and Investment, Dávid Vitézy, has pledged that by September no Volánbusz service should be cancelled because of spare parts shortages, after inheriting what he described as a severe maintenance and procurement crisis.

During a visit to one of Volánbusz’s largest maintenance depots in Fót, Vitézy said the number of buses out of service due to missing spare parts had already fallen significantly, but warned that further work is needed to restore the country’s ageing fleet.

Idle buses reduced from 290 to 170

According to the minister, when the new leadership took office in May, 290 vehicles were unable to operate because replacement parts were unavailable. He said that figure has since fallen to 170, with the government aiming to eliminate service cancellations caused by spare parts shortages before the new school year begins in September.

“Volánbusz’s problems did not emerge overnight, and unfortunately they cannot be solved overnight either,” Vitézy wrote on Facebook. He added that crisis management over the past two months had prevented the country’s long-distance bus network from facing a much more serious disruption during the hectic summer season.

Vitézy blames predecessor János Lázár

The minister placed responsibility for the crisis squarely on his predecessor, János Lázár, arguing that excessive centralisation of procurement within the MÁV Group had crippled the supply chain.

According to Vitézy, all purchasing, logistics, warehousing and spare parts management for Hungary’s state transport companies had been concentrated in a single organisation, resulting in widespread shortages once existing supply contracts expired in April and May.

He claimed that by the end of May more than half of the required spare part types were unavailable at Volánbusz maintenance facilities, preventing mechanics from repairing broken-down vehicles. Vitézy also alleged that replacement procurement procedures had not been launched in time before previous contracts expired, leaving workshops without the components they needed.

Round-the-clock repairs

Speaking from the Fót depot, Vitézy praised maintenance staff, saying mechanics have been working 24 hours a day, seven days a week alongside ministry officials and MÁV Group employees to return buses to service.

He thanked workers for preventing what he described as the potential collapse of Volánbusz operations during one of the most occupied periods of the year, when additional transport capacity is required for major events such as the Hungarian Grand Prix. According to the minister, around 40 vehicles were being used to support Formula 1-related passenger transport over the weekend.

Long-term problems remain

While progress has been made in restoring spare parts supplies, Vitézy acknowledged that the challenges facing Volánbusz extend beyond procurement.

He said maintenance workshops continue to suffer from staff shortages, while much of the national fleet is reaching the end of its operational life. In particular, the motorway-capable coaches used on longer-distance routes have each travelled more than one million kilometres and are overdue for replacement.

More on public transport: Budapest public transport explained — Tickets, passes, fines and airport connections

Fleet renewal already under way

The government is already continuing a major fleet modernisation programme launched by the previous administration. Between 2025 and 2027, Volánbusz is expected to receive 1,000 new Hungarian-built vehicles, many of them air-conditioned, low-floor vehicles equipped with modern passenger information systems.

Earlier this year, MÁV Group took delivery of its 500th new bus, with the 700th expected before the end of 2026 and the remaining 300 scheduled to enter service by 2027.

Vitézy said that after stabilising day-to-day operations, the government’s priority will be restoring reliable spare parts supply chains, strengthening maintenance capacity and completing the long-term renewal of Hungary’s ageing bus fleet.
