World.title: Viktor Orbán shares his plans after politics: family, football, teaching
World.content:
Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has revealed that if he eventually steps away from frontline politics, he would like to work at the football academy he founded, while also spending more time with his six grandchildren and returning to teaching.

Speaking in an exclusive interview with Hungarian tabloid Blikk following his speech at the Bálványos Summer Open University in Baile Tușnad (Tusnádfürdő), Orbán discussed his political future, reflected on his election defeat earlier this year, and shared rare details about his personal ambitions beyond public office.

“I’ll stay as long as I can”

Asked how long he intends to remain at the helm of Fidesz, Orbán said his departure would depend on both his own abilities and public support.

“As long as I can, and as long as people don’t say the old man has become too tired to give advice and would be better off staying at home.”

He added that although such a moment may eventually come, he believes he would be able to accept it when it does.

Football academy and grandchildren

Looking beyond politics, Orbán said retirement would not mean inactivity. He pointed first to his family, noting that he already has six grandchildren and hopes for more in the future. His second priority would be the football academy he established.

“There is a football academy that I founded. If I could, I would gladly work there.”

The remarks refer to the Puskás Academy, founded in Felcsút, which has long been one of Orbán’s flagship sporting projects.

Teaching remains a passion

Orbán also said he still enjoys teaching and expects to continue giving lectures in the future. He revealed that he previously taught several classes as a guest lecturer at the Reformed University for one semester but never accepted a full-time academic position.

“My mother was a teacher,” he said, explaining that he finds satisfaction in helping younger people understand the world better. Rather than traditional university lectures, however, he envisages speaking at public events and international engagements.

“I’m certain I will teach again. I have something to say to young people.”

Why he stayed out of Parliament

Orbán also explained why he chose not to take up a parliamentary seat after Fidesz lost the general election. He said he had originally planned a gradual leadership transition within the party by 2030, but the election defeat accelerated those plans.

According to Orbán, he believed he could have a greater impact by working behind the scenes rather than participating in parliamentary debates, arguing that meaningful dialogue with the country’s new prime minister would not be possible.

Instead, he said younger politicians should take the lead in parliamentary confrontations while he focuses on rebuilding and supporting the party from outside the chamber.

Lessons from defeat

Reflecting on the election result, Orbán admitted he had underestimated the need for generational renewal before the vote. He suggested he should have recognised earlier that younger voters were no longer responding to him as they once had, saying that leadership renewal should perhaps have begun sooner.

Despite the setback, he insisted defeat represents “the beginning of something else” rather than the end, adding that he believes productive work should continue regardless of political success or failure.

This might interest you: Orbán changes tone at Tusványos: Fidesz recast its role as “resistance politics” shifts into gear

A passion for sailing

Away from politics, Orbán also spoke about his growing enthusiasm for sailing along Croatia’s Adriatic coast. He described discovering the country from the sea as “love at first sight” and said he prefers small sailing boats and wild anchoring in secluded bays rather than luxury yachts and marinas.

His long-term dream, he added, would be to explore the entire Mediterranean coastline by sea, following the routes of ancient Greek and Roman civilisation.

World.title: Don’t try to swim here! Bathing banned at five Lake Velence beaches
World.content:
Bathing has been temporarily banned at five popular beaches on Hungary’s Lake Velence, as well as one beach on the Danube, after routine water quality tests detected bacterial contamination above legal limits. The restriction will remain in force until follow-up laboratory tests confirm the water is safe again.

The Fejér County Government Office has ordered a temporary bathing ban at six natural bathing sites following the latest official water quality monitoring. According to the authority, laboratory tests found bacterial contamination exceeding permitted levels, prompting the immediate precautionary measure.

The ban affects five beaches on Lake Velence, one of Hungary’s most popular summer destinations, as well as the Szalki Island Free Beach in Dunaújváros.

Which beaches are affected?

The following beaches are currently closed to swimmers:

Agárd Park Beach Camping (Gárdony-Agárd)

Tini Beach (Gárdony)

Velence North Beach

Velence Korzó and Free Beach

Velence Resort & Spa Beach

Szalki Island Free Beach (Dunaújváros)

Officials stressed that the restriction is temporary and will be lifted as soon as repeated laboratory tests confirm that water quality once again complies with microbiological standards.

Enterococcus bacteria detected

According to reports, self-monitoring water samples collected by beach operators on 21 July showed Enterococcus bacteria levels above the legal threshold at several Lake Velence beaches. As a result, the microbiological quality of the bathing water no longer met public health requirements.

The government office has ordered operators to suspend bathing, inform visitors about the restrictions and ensure the ban is enforced until the water is declared safe.

Alleged failure to enforce the closure

The situation has also sparked controversy in the town of Velence. According to the municipality, the operator of Velence Korzó and Free Beach allegedly failed to comply with the official order, FEOL writes. Local authorities said they instructed the operator to close the beach immediately, install warning signs and prevent bathing, but claimed they received no response.

During a site inspection on 24 July, municipal officials reportedly found that the beach remained open, visitors were still swimming, and information boards continued to display “good” or “excellent” water quality ratings despite the bathing ban.

The municipality has urged visitors to respect the restrictions and choose alternative activities in the area until the water quality improves. Officials highlighted that the Lake Velence region continues to offer hiking opportunities, cultural events, restaurants, wellness facilities and other leisure activities.

If you missed it: Lake Velence property prices defy climate change, but can they stay up forever?

Drought adds to Lake Velence’s problems

The closures come as Lake Velence is already facing severe environmental stress from prolonged drought. Low water levels have significantly altered parts of the lake, with some areas appearing unusually dry after months of exceptionally hot and arid weather.

The authorities are continuing control water quality tests, and the bathing bans will be lifted without delay once the results confirm the affected beaches meet the required health standards again.

World.title: Hungarian forint is the weakest since elections, still manages to hold on
World.content:
The Hungarian forint strengthened on Friday against all three major foreign currencies, recovering from recent losses and ending the week on a firmer footing. While the domestic currency remains weaker than it was at the start of June, it has posted solid gains since the beginning of the year.

Forint rebounds after recent pressure

The Hungarian forint started Friday on a positive note in the interbank foreign exchange market, reversing some of the weakness seen earlier in the week.

During Thursday’s trading, the euro briefly climbed close to HUF 365, raising concerns that the forint’s recent decline could continue. However, sentiment improved overnight, allowing the Hungarian currency to recover.

By 9 AM on Friday, the euro had fallen to HUF 363.10 from HUF 364.58 on Thursday evening. The US dollar slipped from HUF 320.50 to HUF 318.65, while the Swiss franc eased from HUF 392.24 to HUF 390.54, writes Tőzsdefórum.

Stronger finish by the afternoon

The forint continued to strengthen throughout the day. By 6 PM, one euro was trading at HUF 362.19, compared with HUF 364.12 early in the morning. The US dollar fell from HUF 320.04 to HUF 318.12, while the Swiss franc declined from HUF 391.48 to HUF 389.55.

Market data also showed an even stronger late-afternoon performance, with the euro briefly trading around HUF 361.05, the dollar at HUF 317.55, and the Swiss franc at HUF 388.16. Overall, the forint gained around 0.5% against both the euro and the Swiss franc during the day, while strengthening 0.6% against the US dollar.

Still below June levels, but ahead for the year

Despite Friday’s recovery, the Hungarian currency remains weaker than it was at the beginning of June. Compared with the start of the month, the forint is still down by 1.7% against the euro, 1.8% against the US dollar and 0.9% against the Swiss franc.

The broader picture for 2025, however, remains considerably more positive. Since the beginning of the year, the forint has appreciated by:

5.8% against the euro,

2.8% against the US dollar,

5.7% against the Swiss franc.

This might also interest you: The art of selling property in Hungary — Getting the best price in 2026

Key economic data could drive next moves

Friday’s trading session was expected to remain sensitive to fresh macroeconomic data. Hungary’s Central Statistical Office (KSH) was due to release employment figures, while the afternoon brought purchasing managers’ index (PMI) data from both the eurozone and the United States.

These indicators are closely watched by investors and could influence currency markets in the short term. And although the forint has regained some lost ground, analysts will be watching whether the latest rebound marks the beginning of a more sustained recovery or merely a temporary correction.

World.title: Romanian Air Force shoots down three drones in three consecutive days
World.content:
A Romanian F-16 aircraft shot down a drone on Sunday, July 26. It was the third time that this happened in three consecutive days, after similar incidents on Friday, July 24, and Saturday, July 25.

The drone was shot down at 10:13 AM, July 26, above Romania’s territorial waters, in the Sulina–Chilia area, according to Romanian president Nicusor Dan.

The president’s announcement came about half an hour after the drone was shot down. “I congratulate the Romanian pilots and the ground crews for the professionalism, courage, and efficiency with which they carry out their missions. Through their actions, they contribute to the defense of the national territory and the safety of Romanian citizens,” he stated on Facebook.

Dan specified that the first drone shot down on Friday was a Shahed model used by the Russian military and said that Romania will initiate a diplomatic protest against Russia.

“According to the investigation carried out by the General Prosecutor’s Office, the drone shot down on Friday morning is a Shahed type, used by the Russian Federation in its war of aggression against Ukraine. The investigations into the drones shot down yesterday and today are ongoing. Romania’s diplomatic protest against the Russian Federation will be based on these investigations. It is unacceptable and intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romania’s airspace, which is at the same time NATO and European Union airspace,” he added.

The drone was neutralized “under safe conditions,” at a distance of approximately 12 kilometers northeast of Sulina, above Romania’s territorial waters, the Ministry of Defence also said in its press release. The institution noted that “four of the five drones shot down so far on the territory of EU countries in NATO have been neutralized by Romanian military pilots.” Back in May, a Romanian F-16 Fighting Falcon fighter jet deployed as part of NATO’s enhanced air policing mission in the Baltic region shot down a drone in Estonian airspace.

Since the outbreak of the war in Ukraine, more than 100 attacks have been recorded on Ukrainian territory near the border with Romania. During the same period, 33 incursions of Russian drones into Romania’s airspace were recorded. Authorities have also identified drone fragments or entire drones on Romanian territory in approximately 50 cases.

The most recent incursion sparked reactions from the Romanian government, which has upped spending on defense in recent years. Interim PM Ilie Bolojan condemned the drone incursion, emphasizing that the incidents of recent days are the consequence of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.

Interim foreign minister Oana Ţoiu, in turn, announced that the Russian ambassador to Bucharest had been summoned to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs following the repeated violations of Romania’s airspace by the Russian Federation.

World.title: Romanian director Alina Șerban’s debut film “I Matter” to premiere at Venice Film Festival
World.content:
“I Matter” (“Eu contez”), the feature film debut of Romanian director Alina Șerban (in photo), will have its world premiere at the 83rd edition of the Venice International Film Festival, taking place from September 1-12.

Written and directed by Alina Șerban, one of the few Roma female directors in the world, “I Matter” is a co-production between Romania (microFILM), Germany (2Pilots Filmproduction), and Belgium (Frakas Productions, Lemming Film), exploring themes such as overcoming fear, hope, and self-acceptance, according to the press release.

Spoken in Romanian and Romani, the film tells the story of Rebeca, a young Roma woman who is about to leave the foster care center where she grew up.

“We very rarely see Roma characters who live complex human experiences beyond stereotypes. And stories about what it means to be a girl, Roma, and part of the child protection system are almost nonexistent. Through ‘I Matter’ I wanted to build a bridge toward a deeper understanding of these experiences and, above all, to tell a story about humanity. The fact that this film is beginning its journey in Venice means a great deal to me,” said Alina Șerban.

The film was developed over more than four years together with young people from the social protection system. During this period, Alina Șerban created several documentary short films and theater performances alongside them.

The film’s cast includes Denisa Farcaș, Sorin Mihai, Angelina Pavel, Vanessa Dancea, Raisa Mihai, Juno (Alexandru Stancu), Alina Berzunțeanu, and Natalia Călin. Alongside them, 16 children and young people residing in the Casa Iosif and Casa Sara foster centers, part of the Măgurele Christian Social Ensemble in Bucharest, also appear in the film.

The Venice International Film Festival / Mostra Internazionale d'Arte Cinematografica will take place from September 2-12, 2026. “I Matter” has been selected alongside seven other titles in the Spotlight section, dedicated to audience films characterized by innovation and creativity in the way they engage with viewers. The film is competing for the Audience Award offered by Armani Beauty and the Luigi de Laurentiis Award for Best Debut, awarded by an international jury.

Winner of the Best Actress award at the German Actors’ Association Awards for her role in Gipsy Queen (2019), Alina Șerban is a graduate of the prestigious Tisch School of the Arts (New York), Royal Academy of Dramatic Art – RADA (London), and UNATC. In 2024, she was decorated by the president of Romania with the Order of Cultural Merit, in the rank of Knight.

She is the first Roma film and theater director in Romania and, for more than a decade, has developed artistic projects dedicated to children and young people from disadvantaged backgrounds, as well as Roma communities.

World.title: Anti-corruption prosecutors detain three directors of state-owned Romanian defense companies
World.content:
Romania’s National Anticorruption Directorate (DNA) officially announced on Friday, July 24, that it has detained three directors from companies within Romania's defense industry, all accused of taking bribes.

The three are Mihai Rafiu (general manager of Uzina Mecanică București), Tiberiu Alexandru Pîrvu (general manager of Uzina Mecanică Plopeni), and Liliana Sorescu (commercial director of Uzina Mecanică Plopeni).

Alongside the three, an administrator of several commercial companies was also detained, accused of giving bribes and complicity in giving bribes.

During searches, prosecutors found EUR 500,000 in cash at the home of Tiberiu Pârvu Alexandru. Authorities say Rafiu, for his part, allegedly received RON 48,000 from the businessman detained in this case, divided into 12 installments, according to the official DNA statement.

Tiberiu Pârvu Alexandru also allegedly received RON 25,900 from the same businessman "related to contracts concluded with the commercial companies effectively managed by defendant V.M."

The same businessman allegedly also bribed Liliana Sorescu. According to DNA, the total amount she allegedly received as bribes was RON 24,250, in several installments.

In addition, DNA also claimed that another businessman, who owns a company with contracts with Uzina Mecanică Plopeni, allegedly gave Liliana Sorescu USD 3,800, for "placing orders and carrying out the formalities necessary for the acceptance of the goods delivered by the respective companies."

Liliana Sorescu allegedly claimed that the dollars she received were counterfeit and requested the same amount once again, which she allegedly received in lei. "The contracts concluded by the two factories with the aforementioned commercial companies mainly concerned maintenance services, the purchase of materials, and the provision of services," DNA emphasized.

Reacting to the detention of the three directors, economy minister Irineu Darau said that "in general, the defense industry is an extremely sensitive subject. I am convinced that for some it is also a subject of temptation. A strong Romanian state must identify anyone connected to the defense industry who engages in dishonest activities.”

ROMARM, Romania's national state-owned defense company and the country's primary producer and exporter of military equipment, said in connection with the detention that it will support any legal action aimed at strengthening and reviving the defense industry.

The company noted that the problems within its subsidiaries have been known for some time and have been repeatedly brought to the attention of the Ministry of Economy, without answer.

The company's general manager, Răzvan Pîrcălăbescu, said in a statement cited by Digi24 that the reform plan was drafted by ROMARM's management, discussed with institutional partners, approved by the Board of Directors, and submitted to the Ministry of Economy for final approval, but so far the institution has made no decision.

World.title: Asia-born home improvement chain MR.DIY opens location at Bucharest’s Colosseum Mall
World.content:
MR.DIY, one of the world’s leading home improvement and lifestyle retailers, announced the opening of a location at Bucharest’s Colosseum Mall on Thursday, July 23.

Spanning over 800 sqm and developed following an investment of nearly half a million euros, the new MR.DIY store represents one of the most important openings within the retailer’s current national expansion plan, according to the press release.

The store offers a comprehensive one-stop-shop format offering customers access to thousands of practical everyday products across categories such as home improvement, household items, home organization, hardware and tools, stationery, toys, decorations, electrical accessories, car accessories and lifestyle products.

The opening is part of a process of diversification ongoing at the mall. Earlier this spring, Colosseum Mall also welcomed dm dogerie markt and Planeta Arthur bookstore.

The new store has been designed to deliver an accessible and efficient shopping experience, allowing customers to discover a broad assortment of products for everyday needs under one roof.

“This new store reflects our commitment to bringing the MR.DIY concept closer to Romanian consumers through accessible locations, a broad product assortment and affordable prices. Romania is an important market in MR.DIY’s European expansion strategy, and each new opening represents another step in building a strong long-term presence locally,” said Cătălin Secăreanu, representative of MR.DIY in Romania.

Established in Malaysia in 2005 with a single hardware store in Kuala Lumpur, MR.DIY has grown into one of Asia’s leading home improvement and lifestyle retailers, with a continuously expanding international presence across multiple markets. Today, MR.DIY operates in 15 countries worldwide, with more than 5,700 stores across Asia, Europe and other international markets.

World.title: EUR 80 million refinancing for Bucharest underground telecommunications network operator Netcity
World.content:
Meridiam and its partners have successfully closed the EUR 80 million refinancing of Netcity Telecom, the operator of Bucharest's underground telecommunications network, the company announced.

According to the company, the refinancing operation, led end-to-end by Meridiam, represents the first project finance bond issuance in the country, and establishes a new market record with tenors of up to 26.5 years, surpassing Meridiam's previous 18-year market benchmark achieved in 2022.

The operation also provides flexibility to support a future expansion of the Netcity Telecom network and new digital infrastructure developments across Bucharest, Meridiam said.

Netcity Telecom has been operating the underground telecommunications network in Bucharest since 2008, in a 49-year concession agreement with the Bucharest City Hall.

It has so far developed more than 3,000 kilometers of underground telecommunications infrastructure across Bucharest, while removing overhead cables. Today, the network serves around 70,000 buildings, representing approximately half of all buildings in the city, and provides internet access to nearly 600,000 homes and office premises.

Netcity Telecom has worked with several districts of Bucharest in designing and deploying dedicated fiber networks for municipal CCTV projects. The company has also contributed to the implementation of the pilot phase of the new Bucharest Traffic Management System, and is currently involved in Smart School initiatives.

Meridiam has an 80% stake in Netcity Telecom, alongside E-INFRA Group (20%), a Romanian group active in the energy, construction, and telecommunications sectors.

Meridiam, an independent investment Benefit Corporation and asset manager, was founded in 2005 by Thierry Déau. The firm specializes in the development, financing, and long-term management of public infrastructure across three sectors: sustainable mobility, critical public services, and innovative low-carbon solutions. With offices in Addis Ababa, Amman, Dakar, Istanbul, Johannesburg, Libreville, Luxembourg, Paris, Vienna, and Washington, Meridiam manages USD24 billion and more than 130 projects to date.

World.title: Romanian manufacturer TeraPlast inaugurates polyethylene pipe factory in Spain
World.content:
Romanian building materials manufacturer TeraPlast Group inaugurated its TeraPlast Iberia polyethylene pipe factory in Spain, strengthening its expansion into Western European markets. The facility, located near Bilbao, is expected to serve customers across Spain, France, and North Africa.

The factory, inaugurated on July 23, is located in Okondo, in Spain's Álava province, about 20 kilometers from Bilbao. It has an annual production capacity of 16,000 tonnes and employs 79 people.

The opening follows TeraPlast's acquisition of the facility and forms part of the group's international expansion strategy after earlier investments in the Republic of Moldova, Hungary, Austria, and Croatia.

“Romanian industry can compete and thrive at European level, and we demonstrate it through actions, not idealistic speeches. Following our expansion into the Republic of Moldova, Hungary, Austria and Croatia, our entry into the Spanish market marks another important step in our international growth strategy,” said Dorel Goia, chairman of the TeraPlast Board of Directors.

The company plans to invest EUR 4 million in the Spanish factory over the next three years to increase production by 60% and achieve an EBITDA margin of more than 10%.

“The expanded production capacity will serve the markets of Spain, France, and North Africa. This will enable us to reduce leverage while generating returns on our investment for the benefit of the group's shareholders," Goia added.

According to the company, the factory has an established customer base in Spain, France, and Germany and will serve as a regional hub for the group's operations in Western Europe.

TeraPlast Group is the largest polymer processor in Southeastern Europe and operates production facilities in Romania, the Republic of Moldova, Hungary, Austria, Croatia, and Spain. Its parent company, TeraPlast SA, is listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange under the symbol TRP.

World.title: Otokar starts deliveries of Romanian-built Cobra II armored vehicles
World.content:
Turkish defense manufacturer Otokar has begun delivering Cobra II tactical armored vehicles manufactured locally to the Romanian Armed Forces, marking the start of serial production at its plant in Mediaș. More than 780 of the 1,059 vehicles ordered by Romania are scheduled to be built at the local facility over the next five years.

The company said the first Cobra II vehicles manufactured entirely in Mediaș left the factory this week. A total of 216 vehicles, including four different variants, are scheduled for delivery in 2026.

The vehicles are being produced at Automecanica Mediaș, which has become Otokar's first manufacturing facility in the European Union. According to the company, the factory carries out the entire production process rather than only final assembly, giving Romania the capability to manufacture 4x4 armored vehicles locally.

“Romanian-made Cobra II deliveries have just begun. The first Cobra II vehicles manufactured entirely in Mediaș left the factory gates yesterday heading to the Romanian Armed Forces,” said Yusuf Fettahlıoğlu, General Manager of Automecanica Mediaş.

The Mediaș plant covers around 140,000 square meters and has been equipped to manufacture the vehicles to the same production standards as Otokar's facilities in Türkiye.

“Beyond the production line, the investment brings Romania what matters over the long term: advanced production know-how, technology transfer and engineering capabilities. The Mediaș plant is becoming a regional land-systems hub, capable of supporting not only production for the Romanian armed forces but also future export opportunities linked to NATO and European Union defence programmes,” stated Yusuf Fettahlıoğlu.

The Cobra II is a modular 4x4 tactical armored vehicle introduced in 2013 and currently used by more than 20 military and security organizations across 13 countries, including NATO members. For Romania, Otokar is producing several variants, including personnel carrier, reconnaissance, remote weapon station, CBRN reconnaissance, and ambulance versions.

The project has also expanded employment at the Mediaș facility, where the workforce now exceeds 300 people and is expected to grow to nearly 400 as production ramps up.

World.title: Romania wins one gold, seven silver medals at first Central European Olympiad in AI
World.content:
The Romanian delegation to the first Central European Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (CEOAI), held in Cluj-Napoca between July 14-19, won one gold medal and seven silver medals, according to the Ministry of Education.

The event represented a historic moment for the international AI community, bringing together more than 90 contestants from over 20 European countries, along with invited delegations from around the world.

During the competition, contestant had to design, train, and optimize their own artificial intelligence models, starting from completely new datasets and requirements. In the two competition days, students tackled problems in diverse fields, such as artificial intelligence model interpretability, optical character recognition (OCR), mathematical and physical modeling, computer vision, and the security of machine learning models through steganography techniques. The competition tested not only the participants' technical knowledge but also their creativity, analytical ability, and rapid adaptation to problems without standard solutions, according to G4Media.

Following the interest shown by high school students from across Europe, the competition, initially known as the Central European Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (CEOAI), received a new name, becoming the European Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (EUROAI).

Emil-Andrei Burloi, a student at the International Computer Science High School of Bucharest, ranked third in the overall competition standings, winning Romania's first gold medal in international AI competitions in 2026. Subsequently, following the decision of the Ministry of Education and Research for the Romanian delegation to participate as a guest delegation, the official ranking was adjusted in accordance with the competition regulations.

Silver medals went to Ciortea-Suciu Andrei from the "Silvania" National College, Zalău, Morariu Tudor from the International Computer Science High School of Bucharest, Ilie-Goga Radu from the "Tudor Vianu" National College of Computer Science Bucharest, Dobre Darius-Adrian from the "Matei Basarab" National College of Computer Science in Râmnicu Vâlcea, Apostol Mihnea-Petru from the same highschool, Nistor Iulian from the “Tiberiu Popoviciu" Computer Science High School in Cluj-Napoca, and Asandei Ștefan-Alexandru from the Iași National College.

The national team was coordinated by Miron Radu (Alexandru Ioan Cuza University of Iași) and Ciprian Păduraru (University of Bucharest). The national team's qualification was achieved following the ROAI stages, organized in partnership with Genesis College and the "Tudor Vianu" National College of Computer Science, with the support of the Nitro Association, Babeș-Bolyai University, the University of Bucharest, and Alexandru Ioan Cuza University of Iași.

Throughout the selection stages, hundreds of students from across the country solved original machine learning and deep learning problems, training their own models and demonstrating advanced skills in a field at the intersection of computer science, mathematics, and research.

World.title: Serbian Flag on Cocaine Haul from Ecuador is a Clue – Not Proof
World.content:
On July 21, the Italian authorities seized 650 packages with more than 770 kilograms of cocaine at the port of Vado Ligure. The drugs were hidden among pallets of bananas in a refrigerated container from Ecuador.

Concealing cocaine in commercial shipments of fresh fruit, particularly bananas from Ecuador, is a well-known method used by criminal actors, including groups from the Balkans.

The Vado Ligure seizure, therefore, fits a broader pattern of maritime cocaine trafficking into Europe.

In Serbia, however, it wasn’t the size of the seizure or its route that attracted most attention but the Serbian flag displayed on some of the packages.

Although the comments posted under the media reports offer only a snapshot of public opinion, they reveal two recurring reactions.

World.title: Law and Justice Suffers Split Ahead of Poland’s 2027 Election
World.content:
Following a months-long power struggle, more than 30 MPs – including former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki – are set to be expelled from the Law and Justice party, in the biggest rupture seen on the Polish right in many years.

Law and Justice, or PiS, is Poland’s largest opposition party and one of the country’s two dominant political forces, alongside the governing Civic Coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. The split could sharply reduce PiS’s chances of returning to power in next year’s parliamentary election.

On early Friday afternoon, PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski announced that “around 30-something” of the party’s 186 MPs had effectively chosen to leave after refusing to sign declarations of loyalty. The documents required them to state that they did not belong to any political associations operating within the party – an obvious reference to Development Plus (Rozwoj Plus), an organisation created by Morawiecki, until now one of PiS’s deputy leaders.

“Everyone knew what they were supposed to sign, and knew the consequences of not signing,” Kaczynski said. “And so they made the decision they did.”

Kaczynski has been PiS’s undisputed leader and chief power broker for more than two decades, selecting loyal candidates for prime minister who largely continued to defer to him once in office. Morawiecki was initially one of them, serving as prime minister between 2017 and 2023.

But in recent years, Morawiecki – an economist, former banker and comparatively moderate conservative – has grown increasingly impatient with Kaczynski’s dominance. He has pushed for changes to both the party’s internal structure and its political program, arguing that PiS was failing to speak convincingly to younger voters and entrepreneurs.

Friday’s rupture was the culmination of months of increasingly open conflict.

“Until the very last moment, we fought for the unity of the Law and Justice camp,” Morawiecki said at a press conference. “We could not accept being forced to sign a loyalty pledge.”

He accused the party leadership of using ultimatums and political blackmail to discard a strategy that had been agreed only recently.

Morawiecki did not formally announce the creation of a new party. He did, however, declare the beginning of “a new chapter in Poland’s political history”, promise a major nationwide tour and announce that his camp would soon present a new political program.

He said his political circle now included 40 MPs (which stands at odds with Kaczynski’s estimate), one senator and three members of the European Parliament, describing it as a “very strong representation”. Its offer, he said, would reach beyond PiS’s traditional base and target young people, entrepreneurs, local-government officials and even some voters currently supporting the governing coalition.

Morawiecki presented his project as a modern, patriotic and pro-state conservative force, capable of responding to social and economic change without falling back on outdated ideas.

The electoral consequences could be enormous. An Opinia24 poll conducted before the split tested precisely such a scenario. With PiS united, the party would receive 23 per cent of the vote, behind Civic Coalition on 31.6 per cent. When respondents were offered a separate Morawiecki-led Rozwoj Plus list, support for PiS fell to 17.7 per cent, while Morawiecki’s group received 6.2 per cent. Civic Coalition remained clearly ahead on 30.9 per cent.

Tusk responded with a single cutting line: “They are fighting so hard for party unity that there won’t be one stone left standing.”

Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski was blunter: “Kaczynski went all in and lost.”

World.title: Week in Review: A Fighting Spirit
World.content:
Turkey’s opposition political scene is heating up. On July 21, Ozgur Ozel announced that he was leaving the main opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP, to establish a new party.

The news followed a crisis triggered two months ago, when a court annulled Ozel’s election as CHP leader at an earlier party congress, restoring his predecessor, Kemal Kilicdaroglu, as leader. Ozel’s new party looks set to take a majority of the CHP’s MPs and voters. But can it be turned into a political force capable of taking on the ruling party?

World.title: Turkey Gets New Main Opposition Party Following Opposition Split
World.content:
Opposition leader, Ozgur Ozel, waves to crowds during a rally in Izmir, Turkey, 26 May 2026. Photo: EPA/STRINGER

Former party chairman Ozgur Ozel announced on Friday that he and 90 lawmakers had resigned from the Republican People’s Party, CHP, to establish the New Party.

Ozel’s decision marks the latest stage in a crisis that began on May 21, when a court annulled the CHP congress that had elected him chairman and reinstated his predecessor, Kemal Kilicdaroglu.

Ozel said he hoped the New Party would “be beneficial for our country, our nation, our party, and all of us”, as he signed the document for the foundation of his new party.

Meanwhile, 90 other MPs also resigned from the CHP, making the New Party Turkey’s new main opposition party. The CHP lost its main opposition role after 23 years, retaining only 44 MPs.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, has the largest number of seats in parliament, with 277.

The court in May cited alleged voting fraud as the reason for reinstating Kilicdaroglu but Ozel and his supporters saw the ruling as blatant judicial interference in the party’s affairs.

Police entered CHP headquarters four days later to enforce the ruling. Kilicdaroglu’s administration subsequently began disciplinary proceedings against figures associated with Ozel and promised political and organisational “purification”.

Ozel and his allies argue that the judicial intervention and subsequent internal purge have eliminated any possibility of the CHP winning the next elections.

Kilicdaroglu has been removing key CHP figures and local party administration since he took office.

“We opened up a new road because they blocked all the others. We are opening up that road now. Are you ready to march to power? We will march to power,” Ozel said on July 21 in parliament.

Ekrem Imamoglu, jailed Mayor of Istanbul and an opposition presidential candidate, is one of Ozel’s main partners. He is behind bars for alleged corruption – charges he describes as politically motivated. Imamoglu supported Ozel at the 2023 CHP congress and led the internal resistance within the party against Kilicdaroglu.

His jailing and the developments around the CHP come as President Erdogan and his government do their utmost to thwart any opposition challenge to their years-long rule.

In addition to the annulment of the party congress, dozens of CHP mayors and hundreds of party members have been arrested on corruption and terrorism charges in recent years.

Opposition politicians, rights groups and international organisations have accused the government of using the judiciary to crush its political rivals in what they describe as an unprecedented crackdown.

Ozel’s new party is generating excitement in opposition ranks – but according to experts translating a buzz into a political force capable of challenging President Erdogan will not be easy.

World.title: Fake Social Media Accounts Target Albania Protest Supporters
World.content:
After weeks of protests demanding his resignation, Prime Minister Edi Rama accused social media algorithms of having “poured gasoline on the fire” of Albania’s so-called Flamingo Revolution.

“The more views you get, the more influence you have. The more influence you have, the more power you hold. Power over whom? Over the slaves of the algorithms – over all of us,” Rama told parliamentarians from his governing Socialist Party.

Days later, he returned to the theme of social media manipulation after visiting the picturesque mountain village of Theth, where last year the government demolished dozens of illegally built holiday chalets, prompting locals to demonstrate.

Rama posted screenshots on Facebook of what he said were more than a dozen fake accounts who had commented on posts criticising his tourism development plans for Albania’s mountain regions.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Russian Hackers Linked to FSB Target Slovakia
World.content:
Hungary’s chief prosecutor resigns; ex-Austrian chancellor Kurz on MCC’s payroll

Hungary’s chief prosecutor, Balint Gabor Nagy, resigned this week amid mounting pressure from the new Tisza-led government. PM Peter Magyar welcomed the decision. Nagy was appointed by the previous government of Viktor Orban in 2025 for a nine-year term and was regarded as one of its key officeholders. Nagy said he was resigning in order to preserve the dignity and independence of the national prosecutor’s office. “The prosecutor’s office must not become an instrument in conflicts between political actors, nor can it become a battlefield for short-term political interests or power struggles,” Nagy argued in his resignation letter. If accepted, his resignation will take effect on August 25. Magyar has demanded the resignation of key officeholders of the Orban administration following his landslide election victory on April 12. He identified the state president, the chief prosecutor, the president of the Supreme Court and the president of the Constitutional Court as among those who needed to step down in order to achieve genuine regime change in Hungary and dismantle the deep state behind the Orban system. Magyar originally demanded their withdrawal by the end of May, but the process is taking somewhat longer. However, this week he achieved three objectives at once via a constitutional amendment passed on July 13: he secured the departure of the president, the chief prosecutor and the president of the Constitutional Court. Removing the president of the Supreme Court in such a manner could raise rule-of-law concerns but, according to the latest constitutional amendment, he can now be voted out of office by the judges themselves. The move clears the way for potential investigations into Orban’s close business associates or even family members, as Nagy can no longer block them.

It emerged this week that Austria’s former conservative chancellor, Sebastian Kurz, was on the payroll of the Mathias Corvinus Collegium (MCC), a Fidesz-aligned think tank and foundation which in 2020 received a huge endowment from the Hungarian state in the form of assets worth 1.3-1.4 billion euros. Kurz confirmed the information to the Austrian weekly Falter, but said that after Orban’s election defeat he immediately returned around 110,000 euros to the institution. After resigning from office, Kurz maintained close ties with Orban and his Fidesz party. Officially, he served as an adviser to assist the MCC’s acquisition of Austria’s private Modul University in Vienna and received 10,000 euros a month for his involvement, although there is no evidence that he carried out any such work. The MCC acquired a 90 per cent stake in Modul in 2023, while the remaining 10 per cent stayed with the Vienna Chamber of Commerce. Hungary’s new government has already announced it will dissolve the MCC and return its assets to the Hungarian state, which could lead to the bizarre situation where the Hungarian state inherits an Austrian university. Frank Furedi, the head of the MCC’s Brussels branch, which also benefited massively from taxpayer money, has announced earlier this month his institution is seeking new financing but insisted that it operates independently so cannot just be closed down by the Hungarian government. It is becoming increasingly clear that Orban was not only an ideological ally of many far-right and Eurosceptic leaders, but also provided a financial lifeline to many when they were out of office. The MCC also offered lucrative fellowships to Western politicians who praised Orban in the international media and at conferences. Kurz was a regular guest at MCC events and the Orban government firmly believed he would eventually return to government in Austria.

World.title: The Biggest Question Is Not Hungary’s Next President but Its Next Constitution
World.content:
Orban’s shameless resistance – against what exactly?

The former prime minister did not take up his parliamentary mandate after the election that his party so resoundingly lost, but he is still president of the Fidesz party. He declared on Wednesday that after the constitutional amendment removing Sulyok, the rule of law has ceased to exist in Hungary; from now on, there is only tyranny.

After 16 years spent consolidating power and appointing loyal officials to every independent institution, Orban now contends that the actions of the new government are illegitimate because it is seeking to monopolise power. Therefore, Fidesz won’t participate in the election of officials in the place of those who were removed, because it considers the new officials also to be illegitimate. Beyond the state president, this will comprise four constitutional judge vacancies, because the constitutional amendment passed by Tisza also reintroduced the 70-year retirement age for constitutional court judges and four older than that will now have to retire on September 1.

Orban recalled that, according to the constitution, everyone has the right to lawfully resist attempts to secure exclusive control of political power. He promised that Fidesz would support anyone engaged in such resistance. At this point it is worth reminding that at the time he was prime minister, those who expressed similar resistance were usually labelled traitors and foreign agents – but “the times they are a-changin’,” as Bob Dylan sang.

It is likely that with its resistance agenda, Fidesz wants to undermine the new government’s constitution-drafting plans. Prime Minister Magyar has made it explicit that in a constitution-making process seen starting in September Hungarian society would be involved, which is in sharp contrast with the exclusively elite-driven constitution-drafting practices that Hungarians have so far experienced.

By calling on its supporters to resist and depicting the new government’s rule as arbitrary, Fidesz probably also hopes to put people off participating in the constitution-drafting process so that it can label any new constitution illegitimate. Yet this could easily backfire, as the current Fundamental Law was practically written by two Fidesz politicians on a tablet, after a postal consultation with citizens full of biased questions and simplified answer options. This level of transparency and social involvement is not that difficult to surpass, even if Fidesz eventually ends up boycotting the process.

Beyond its legitimacy, the key question about any new constitution is whether and how it will be able to prevent a similar concentration of power to what we witnessed over the past 16 years. This might entail various institutional solutions, depending on the outcome of the consultations in the constitution-making process.

It would be worth considering the reintroduction of bicameralism where, if the right institutional balance is found, the upper chamber could function as a counterbalance to the government and its majority in the lower house. Referendums should also be made functional. Though they currently exist on paper, it is practically impossible to hold a legally binding referendum due to the high turnout threshold and the extensive list of prohibited subjects. Most important of all, the electoral rules and the constitutional provisions governing legislation and institutions must guarantee that no single party can amend the constitution or entrench its priorities in cardinal laws, and that no single party can pack independent institutions with loyalists, hollowing them out from within.

Finding the right constitutional solutions to all these matters is far more important than which person will hold the presidency for an interim period of one or two years.

Bea Bakó is an independent researcher, she holds a PhD in constitutional law and co-authors the Hungarian newsletter Gemišt.

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: Drone Down: Someone’s Messing with Satnav Signals over Protest-Hit Serbia
World.content:
GNSS comprises four major networks: US Global Positioning System, or GPS, the European Union’s Galileo, Russia’s GLONASS, and China’s BeiDou.

They form a critical part of modern infrastructure. Besides guiding aircrafts, ships and vehicles, such systems are used in the energy sector, telecommunications, geodesy, maritime navigation, precision agriculture and numerous industrial systems that depend on accurate positioning and timing.

“It is used by almost every sector of industry,” said a radio frequency and telecommunications expert in Serbia, speaking on condition of anonymity.

“Interference can lead to the collapse of transport, the failure of telecommunications networks, problems in banking systems, while emergency services lose the ability to locate incidents quickly.”

The protest Novak took photos of, in May, wasn’t the only one where jamming and spoofing were detected.

Data from GPSwise and GPSJam show both phenomena occurred between 1 p.m. and 5 p.m. on March 15, 2025, when Serbia witnessed one of the biggest anti-government protests in its history.

According to GPSwise data, fake satellite signals affected several commercial flights, including Pegasus Airlines flights from Paris to Istanbul, London to Istanbul and Amsterdam to Istanbul, a Smartwings Hungary flight from Budapest to Egypt, and Wizz Air flights from Catania, southern Italy, to Warsaw and from Brussels to Craiova, Romania.

A source with expertise in the civil aviation sector, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said pilots landing at Nikola Tesla Airport also reported navigation interference.

“What I know is that the largest number of problems coincided with March 15,” the source told BIRN. “That was when the highest number of reports came in. Five, six, seven aircraft reported problems – it was obvious that something was going on.”

One Wizz Air flight received false navigation data while it was still over Hungary, approximately 250 kilometres from the source of the interference in Belgrade.

The Pegasus flight from Paris to Istanbul was over Krupanj, some 100 kilometres southwest of Belgrade, when it encountered the same problem.

“Since GNSS signals are not selective, interfering with one drone also affects all other systems within a radius ranging from several hundred metres to several kilometres,” said the radio frequency and telecommunications expert. “Their disruption is justified only in extreme security situations.”

“The operational range of such systems can be quite extensive, and to maximise effectiveness, jamming systems generally operate at maximum transmitter power,”

“The aircraft detect lower-intensity interference because each directional jamming beam can still be detected at much lower intensity over considerable distances, particularly in airspace.”

The source with civil aviation expertise said that, while aircraft have other navigation systems, they “primarily rely on GNSS” when approaching airports.

“Today, pilots generally do not fly aircraft manually but rely on computers, whose most important requirement is to know the aircraft’s precise position at all times,” the source told BIRN.

“All major airports, including Belgrade, have precision approach procedures that require certain standards to be met, including reliable satellite navigation. Without it, that level of precision is significantly reduced.”

If navigation systems are disrupted, pilots are obliged to make a report, he said.

Drones grounded

World.title: Croatia Braces for Another Heatwave as Temperatures Could Reach 40°C
World.content:
July the 27th, 2026 – Following a brief but very welcome period of cooler, fresher and somewhat unstable weather, Croatia is set to face another heatwave with temperatures likely to reach 40 degrees.

After a brief spell of unsettled and sometimes stormy weather, Croatia is preparing for another intense heatwave, with temperatures expected to climb steadily throughout the week and potentially reach 40°C in some inland areas. Index reports that meteorologists are claiming that the hottest conditions are likely to arrive during the second half of the week.

above 35 degrees by the end of the week

Weather conditions are expected to stabilise on Tuesday and onwards. Daytime temperatures will rise each day, with much of the country seeing highs above 35°C by the end of the week. Forecasters say isolated locations could even record temperatures of around 40°C if current forecasts hold.

The Croatian Meteorological and Hydrological Service (DHMZ) has already issued an initial yellow heat warning for Thursday, cautioning that the heat could pose a risk to human health. Meteorologists warn that higher-level warnings may be introduced if temperatures continue to increase as expected.

The upcoming heatwave follows an unusual period of unstable weather that brought thunderstorms, strong winds and a series of strange meteotsunamis along parts of the Adriatic coast. Once the current weather system moves away, a strengthening area of high pressure is expected to bring prolonged sunshine and very little rainfall.

records were broken in june

Forecasters also pointed to this summer’s exceptional conditions. During June, fourteen of Croatia’s 35 main meteorological stations recorded new monthly temperature records, while Split reached an all-time record of 40°C at the Marjan weather station. Staggeringly, even sea temperatures climbed to around 30°C in some areas, highlighting the intensity of this year’s hot summer season.

Authorities are advising residents and visitors to stay hydrated, avoid prolonged exposure to the sun during the hottest part of the day and keep a close eye on vulnerable groups, including the elderly, young children and those with existing health conditions, as Croatia prepares for another spell of extreme summer heat.

World.title: Sea Floods Stari Grad on Hvar for the Third Time in Just 10 Days
World.content:
July the 27th, 2026 – The sea has created floods in Stari Grad on the island of Hvar for the third time in just 10 days due to repeated meteotsunamis.

Index reports that visitors and residents of Stari Grad on the island of Hvar have once again found themselves dealing with flooded streets after the sea overflowed onto the town’s waterfront, marking the third such event in just ten days. The repeated flooding has drawn attention to increasingly unusual sea level fluctuations affecting parts of Croatia’s coastline and islands.

Videos shared by residents showed seawater spilling over the promenade and into the historic centre, covering streets and public spaces before gradually receding. Although the flooding caused disruption, there were no reports of serious injuries or major structural damage.

According to meteorologists, the flooding was not caused by rainfall but by a combination of low atmospheric pressure, strong southerly winds and elevated sea levels. These conditions created what is known as a storm surge, pushing large volumes of seawater onto the shoreline and into low-lying coastal areas.

The phenomenon has affected Stari Grad several times over the past two weeks, with each event occurring under similar weather conditions. Locals say the repeated flooding has become a growing concern, particularly for businesses and residents along the waterfront who have had to repeatedly clear seawater from their properties.

Experts note that enclosed bays and historic harbour towns such as Stari Grad are especially vulnerable to this type of coastal flooding. When strong winds coincide with low air pressure, sea levels can temporarily rise enough to overwhelm quays, promenades and streets built just above normal sea level.

As weather conditions improved, the seawater gradually retreated and life returned to normal. However, the latest flooding serves as another reminder of how quickly changing weather patterns can impact Croatia’s coastal communities, with residents hoping calmer conditions will prevent another repeat in the coming days.

World.title: Sveti Ivan Beach: The Hidden Paradise That Requires a 50-Minute Hike
World.content:
July the 27th, 2026 – The entire island of Cres is stunning, but Sveti Ivan beach takes it a step further. If we’re being honest, it takes it many steps further, as a 50-minute hike is needed to reach this hidden paradise. Trust us, it’s so worth it.

Hidden beneath the ancient hilltop village of Lubenice on the island of Cres lies one of Croatia’s most spectacular beaches, Sveti Ivan beach. Putni kofer reveals that it is best known for its white pebbles, crystal-clear waters and particularly dramatic surroundings. It is very often considered one of the most beautiful beaches on the Croatian coast (and that’s a challenging title to receive in itself).

The beach sits in a secluded bay beneath the historic settlement of Lubenice, which is perched high on a cliff overlooking the Adriatic. Surrounded by steep rocks and untouched nature, Sveti Ivan offers the kind of peaceful atmosphere that is becoming increasingly rare on the Croatian coast.

Part of what keeps this beach so special is also what makes it difficult to reach. Visitors who choose to walk from Lubenice must follow a steep trail that takes around 50 minutes downhill, and the return journey can be even more challenging, especially during the intense summer heat. Proper footwear and enough water are essential, and we’d go as far as to discourage anyone doing this during the height of summer.

Because of the demanding access, even during the height of summer Sveti Ivan usually avoids the large crowds found at many other Croatian beaches. Those who make the journey are rewarded with incredible views, peaceful surroundings and some of the clearest waters on the Adriatic.

The beach can also be reached by sea, either with a private boat, organised excursion or water taxi. Nearby is another natural attraction, Plava Grota, a sea cave where sunlight creates beautiful blue reflections inside the cave.

Above the beach sits Lubenice, one of the oldest settlements on the Croatian islands. Located on a 378-metre-high cliff, the village has a history stretching back more than 4,000 years, with archaeological remains from the Bronze and Iron Ages found in the surrounding area.

Once one of Cres’ most important settlements, Lubenice is now home to only two permanent residents. However, during the summer months, visitors arrive to explore its ancient stone streets, admire the views and discover one of Croatia’s most breathtaking beaches down below.

World.title: Should Croatia Charge Tourists Who Need Emergency Help After Excessive Drinking?
World.content:
July the 27th, 2026 – Should Croatia be charging tourists who take it too far and require emergency medical help after excessive drinking or even illicit drug use?

Every single summer, Split in particular faces the same old problem, and that is tourists being found unconscious on city streets after heavy nights of drinking, with emergency services called to help them. The issue has sparked a debate over whether people who put themselves in danger through excessive alcohol consumption should contribute to the cost of medical interventions.

over 50 calls because of alcohol in june alone

During June alone, the Split-Dalmatia County Emergency Medical Service recorded more than 50 calls related to alcohol intoxication. Lukrecija Zderic reveals for Index that medical teams treated 44 people, while eight people were no longer at the location when emergency crews arrived. Among those who received help were also two minors.

Many of these cases involve young foreign tourists visiting Split during the summer season. Locals say it has become common to find intoxicated visitors lying on streets in the early morning hours after nights out and organised pub crawl tours.

The question now being raised is whether tourists who end up needing emergency medical assistance because of extreme alcohol consumption should help cover the cost. Some European countries already charge part of the expense in similar situations, but Croatia currently does not have such a system.

an abuse of already thin resources

Croatia’s emergency services are required to help anyone whose health is at risk, regardless of how the situation happened. However, every intervention requires medical staff, vehicles and resources.

The Croatian Health Insurance Fund explained that emergency medical teams are funded through contracted healthcare costs. A single emergency team consisting of a doctor, nurse and driver represents a significant annual expense for the healthcare system.

For foreign visitors, the final bill depends on their insurance situation. Tourists from EU countries, the European Economic Area and Switzerland with valid European Health Insurance Cards have their costs covered through international healthcare agreements. Visitors from countries without such agreements may have to pay themselves unless they have travel insurance.

irresponsible behaviour should face consequences

However, if a tourist leaves Croatia without paying a medical bill, the unpaid cost can ultimately fall on Croatian public funds. This means taxpayers may end up covering expenses that were never recovered.The debate comes as Split continues to balance the benefits of being one of Croatia’s most popular tourist destinations with the challenges that come from large numbers of visitors, particularly during the peak summer months.

As tourism grows, Croatia faces an ongoing question: should irresponsible behaviour surrounding alcohol and drug use that requires emergency medical intervention come with a financial consequence?

World.title: Search Underway After Skipper Falls Overboard Near Šolta
World.content:
July the 26th, 2026 – A frantic search is currently underway after a skipper fell overboard into the sea not far from Šolta, marking the second serious maritime incident near the island in a short time.

Index reports that a major search and rescue operation is currently underway in the waters off the island of Šolta after a skipper fell overboard from a charter catamaran and disappeared within minutes amid extremely poor weather conditions. The incident was reported at around 09:10, triggering an immediate response from Croatia’s maritime rescue services.

According to the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure, the missing man is an Austrian skipper. At the time of the accident, the sea was being battered by strong winds and rough conditions, making the search particularly difficult.

A large-scale rescue effort was launched involving two rescue boats from the Milna Harbour Master’s Office, one rescue boat from Hvar, three vessels from the Split Maritime and Airport Police, a Pilatus aircraft, and later a helicopter to assist with the aerial search. Authorities also issued a PAN-PAN urgency message via Split Radio, asking all vessels in the area to keep watch for the missing skipper.

The remaining six passengers, all of whom are Austrian nationals, were located unharmed aboard the catamaran. A replacement skipper was transferred to the vessel so it could safely continue to its next destination, where the passengers would disembark.

As of the latest update, the search remains ongoing, with emergency services continuing to comb the waters around Šolta in the hope of finding the missing skipper. Authorities have not released further details while the operation continues.

World.title: Croatian Firefighting Pilots Battle Massive Wildfires in France
World.content:
July the 26th, 2026 – Croatian firefighting pilots are battling massive wildfires in France, which have caused unimaginable destruction in the southwest of the country.

Index reports that Croatian military firefighters are playing a key role in the fight against devastating wildfires sweeping southwestern France, where huge blazes continue to threaten communities near Bordeaux.

Members of the 855th Firefighting Squadron of the Croatian Air Force have been deployed to France as part of an international firefighting effort. They are currently operating in the Biscarrosse area, where large wildfires remain active and conditions continue to challenge emergency crews.

The Croatian crews arrived in France on the 24th of July. On their first day they were assigned to fires near Salernes, before being redeployed to the Bordeaux region as the situation worsened. During their first two days of operations, the crews completed 72 flights, logged a total of 13.5 flying hours, and dropped 402 tonnes of water on the enormous flames.

According to the Croatian Ministry of Defence, the mission remains highly demanding due to the scale of the fires and rapidly changing conditions on the ground. Major Tomislav Vranjić said the situation is still extremely complex, with Croatian pilots making every effort to support French firefighters in bringing the blazes under control.

The deployment comes as France battles one of its largest wildfire outbreaks in decades. The fires in the Gironde region have burned tens of thousands of hectares, forced the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people and prompted international assistance from across Europe.

Croatia’s Canadair crews are among Europe’s most experienced aerial firefighters, regularly assisting other countries through the European Union’s civil protection cooperation mechanisms. Their latest mission once again highlights Croatia’s expertise in tackling large-scale wildfires beyond its own borders.

World.title: Analysis of 1.6 Million Reviews Reveals What Tourists Think of Croatia
World.content:
July the 26th, 2026 – An analysis of a staggering 1.6 million reviews reveals precisely what tourists really think of Croatia in comparison to its competition.

Croatia has triumphantly emerged as the highest-rated major Mediterranean destination based on an analysis of more than 1.6 million online guest reviews, but the data also highlights several areas where the country is falling behind its competitors. This study, as reported by Ivan Ivankovic for Index, examined 1,622,218 reviews written by travellers themselves, offering a broad picture of how visitors perceive Croatia compared with other leading Mediterranean destinations.

greece is still leaving a stronger impression…

The overall results are encouraging. Croatia achieved an average rating of 8.91, narrowly edging out nearby Greece and comfortably outperforming Spain, neighbouring Italy and Turkey in overall guest satisfaction. However, when travellers who had visited both Croatia and Greece were asked which destination they preferred, 11 out of 12 nationalities chose Greece, suggesting that while visitors rate Croatia highly, Greece leaves a stronger overall impression.

One of Croatia’s biggest strengths is its location. Visitors consistently praise the country’s remarkable coastline, islands and natural beauty, while also giving high marks for cleanliness. The analysis found that Croatia is also viewed as one of the fairest destinations in the Mediterranean, with comparatively few complaints about scams, hidden charges or tourist traps.

croatia has the highest number of reviews calling it “too expensive”

The biggest criticism, however, is price. Croatia recorded the highest number of reviews mentioning that it is too expensive, with complaints focusing mainly on restaurants, drinks and other spending outside accommodation rather than hotel prices themselves. Among everyday purchases, tourists most often criticised the cost of bottled water, while cocktail prices were also seen as relatively high. Coffee prices, on the other hand, attracted fewer complaints.

The research also identified several recurring frustrations. Guests most frequently complained about parking, air conditioning, Wi-Fi, noise, cleanliness in some locations and showers or water facilities. Croatia also performed poorly when it came to cashless payments, with many visitors noting that some businesses still accept only cash, which represents a growing inconvenience for international travellers.

croatia performs better outside of the main summer season

Another notable finding is that Croatia receives better reviews during the pre-season and post-season than at the height of summer. This suggests that overcrowding and peak-season prices continue to affect the visitor experience during the busiest months.

The analysis paints a nuanced picture of Croatian tourism as a whole. Visitors continue to love the country’s scenery, safety and overall quality, making it one of the Mediterranean’s top-rated destinations. However, if Croatia wants to remain competitive against rivals such as Greece, the findings suggest it will need to address concerns over pricing, infrastructure and service during the busiest part of the tourist season.

World.title: The Green Cave: One of the Vis Archipelago’s Most Magical Wonders
World.content:
July the 26th, 2026 – The Green Cave is one of the beautiful Vis archipelago’s most incredible natural wonders, and instead of being limited to viewing it by boat, you can swim inside it.

Just off the southern coast of the far-flung island of Vis, the tiny, uninhabited islet of Ravnik is home to one of Croatia’s most spectacular natural attractions, the remarkable Green Cave (Zelena špilja). Putni kofer reveals that unlike very many sea caves in Croatia and indeed elsewhere that can only be admired from a boat, this one offers visitors the rare opportunity to swim inside and experience its unique beauty up close and personal.

This unusual cave gets its name from the remarkable emerald-green glow that fills the interior. Sunlight enters through a circular opening in the cave’s ceiling and reflects off the seabed, which is covered with various types of green algae. Around midday, when the sun is at its highest, the effect is at its most dramatic, bathing the water in an almost unreal green light. Unlike the famous Blue Cave on nearby Biševo, the Green Cave has two large entrances, allowing smaller boats to sail directly inside. Visitors can also jump into the crystal-clear sea and swim beneath the beam of sunlight that shines through the roof, creating one of the Adriatic’s most memorable swimming experiences.

The cave has been protected as a geomorphological natural monument since 1967, while the islet of Ravnik itself is a protected significant landscape. Over the years, the cave has inspired countless visitors, including Emperor Franz Joseph I, who is said to have visited during his tour of the Adriatic back during the 19th century and who was left thoroughly enchanted by it. During World War II, local stories suggest that its spacious interior even provided secretive shelter for small military vessels.

Most visitors reach the Green Cave as part of a boat excursion departing from Vis, Komiža or Hvar, often combined with stops at the Blue Cave, Stiniva Cove and other highlights of the Vis archipelago. Entry is managed under a concession system, with visitors paying a small admission fee before entering or swimming inside the cave.

Although the Blue Cave often attracts the bigger crowds and is definitely much better known globally, many travellers consider the Green Cave an equally unforgettable experience. Its combination of emerald light, clear Adriatic waters and the chance to swim inside a protected natural monument makes it one of the hidden gems of Croatia’s coastline.

World.title: Estonian golfer Kristella Sikk crowned European U16 champion
World.content:
Young golfer Kristella Sikk won the European Under 16 girls' golf title in Spain, finishing as the only player under par.

Sikk is the first Estonian golfer to win an individual European Championship gold. Estonia's only previous individual medal had come last year, when Mattias Varjun returned with silver from the European Mid-Amateur Championship.

"The European Young Masters was a very valuable experience for me because I got to play against very strong opponents and test myself," Sikk said. "The tournament was very well organized and highly competitive. The weather was much warmer than in Estonia, but once I got used to it, it was really pleasant. The course was beautiful and in great condition, and the greens were fast and excellent for putting."

"Our team stuck together and I was very grateful that Kris and Konrad caddied for me on the second and third days. [Coach] Hanna-Maria [Tammo] was a huge help throughout the week. She reminded me to wear sunscreen, drink water and stay in the shade, and she helped me make decisions in difficult situations and calm down. Every day was fun and interesting. There were both good and bad moments, but in the end everything worked out well. Last year I never would have imagined that I would win this tournament myself," Sikk added.

Sikk's three rounds of 69, 71 and 73 across the three days finished with her being three under.

She recorded 21 birdies (one under par) over the three days (including nine in the second round), the highest total of the entire tournament across both the boys' and girls' competitions. Although she carded one costly hole each day, her abundance of birdies made up for every mistake.

For example, her quadruple-bogey eight (a golf score of eight strokes on a hole where the par is four) in the second day came after her ball finished so deeply buried in a bunker that it took three shots to escape. TSecond went to the Czech Republic's Anna Gejdošová (+1), while Spain's Rut Diaz Garcia (+2) claimed third place.

Of other Estonians competing in the girls' event, Nora Marleen Animägi (Estonian Golf & Country Club) produced increasingly mature golf with each round and eventually finished tied for 43rd. Her rounds were 91, 78 and 78 in her debut event.

The best-placed Estonian boy was the youngest member of the national team, 13-year-old Kris Kuusk (Estonian Golf & Country Club), finished tied for 35th after rounds of 77, 74 and 80. Karl Konrad Ranna (Estonian Golf & Country Club) carded rounds of 81, 81 and 80 to finish tied for 49th.

Estonia finished 16th overall, ahead of Scotland, the birthplace of golf, and above neighbors Finland and including golfing nations Portugal and Ireland. France won, followed by Spain and Germany.

World.title: Katri Raik ousted as Mayor of Narva following no-confidence vote
World.content:
Narva City Council ousted Katri Raik as mayor in a no-confidence vote on Sunday, with 16 in favor, 14 opposed and no abstentions.

Jaan Toots (Center) has been elected her successor as mayor.

This followed talk of a change in government in the majority Russian-speaking eastern border town which has been ongoing since April, and was in effect a coup enacted by the Center Party and the Plan B electoral alliance.

Urbo Vaarmann (Plan B) submitted the no-confidence motion while almost immediately after being appointed council chair, as a motion of no-confidence in Mihhail Stalnuhhin in that role had passed earlier Sunday. The city council's deputy chair was also ousted in a motion.

Vaarman said the motion and vote against Raik was prompted by what he called prolonged turmoil in Narva City Council under the leadership of Raik and Stalnuhhin, the latter, Vaarman said, who had engaged in a filibuster lasting 130 days.

The city government had a majority of just one at the 31-seat Narva City Council chamber.

Urbo Vaarmann. Source: Sergei Stepanov/ERR

"As the city government was unable to function, it was also impossible to hold council meetings, and this has resulted in prolonged disorder," Vaarmann said, adding that the mayor had also failed to ensure the proper functioning of the city office and the city secretary's office.

"Second, we consider the mayor's conduct towards city employees and the heads of municipal institutions unacceptable. /.../ Personnel matters have been accompanied by public confrontation, pressure, and damage to people's professional reputation and dignity," Vaarmann went on, referring to Nadezhda Tšerkašina, the head of the Narva keeltelütseum high school.

Tšerkašina, whose dismissal was justified by repeated serious breaches in the school's management, is a Center Party member and also serves on the city council. The opposition, argued that her dismissal was politically motivated.

In her speech, Raik said she was leaving office with a clean conscience, adding that she had never been more satisfied with her work. She also rejected the accusations against her.

The council elected Toots as new mayor, who was voted into office with 16 votes in favor. He had held the position before, 2023-2024.

The council also passed a no-confidence motion against council chair Stalnuhhin. Presenting the motion, Center Party deputy Jaan Toots said the reason was Stalnuhhin's systematic disruption of the council's work by convening meetings and then canceling them. "The council's work must be restored," Toots said.

Vaarmann was nominated as the new council chair, and a secret ballot was held shortly before 12:45 p.m. Sunday He was elected with 16 votes in favor.

A no-confidence motion was also passed against Narva City Council deputy chair Jana Kondrašova, elected on Katri Raik's list at last year's local elections, who was accused of failing to contribute to constructive cooperation. Sixteen councilors voted in favor of her removal, while 14 voted against, so it passed too.

Natalia Umarova was elected as the new deputy chair. Vaarmann also wanted to elect a second deputy chair: Tšerkašina was chosen for that role.

The Center Party and the Plan B electoral alliance says Stalnuhhin had managed to postpone council sessions and delay the no-confidence votes for as long as 130 days.

Mihhail Stalnuhhin Source: Sergei Stepanov/ERR

In late June, a nearly 12-hour Narva City Council meeting was marked by procedural disputes, repeated recesses and agenda disagreements. Stalnuhhin then repeatedly paused proceedings, including multiple one-hour recesses, as opposition members challenged the agenda. The no-confidence motions were at that time submitted against Stalnuhhin, Raik and Kondrašova

Raik had been Narva mayor since late 2024, taking over from Toots following a no-confidence motion. Raik's had previously served as Narva mayor 2020-2021.

Stalnuhhin is a former Center Party member who was expelled from the party in 2022 after referring then-prime minister Kaja Kallas (Reform) and others pressing on with the removal of Soviet-era monuments and other installations in Estonia as "Nazis".
