One widely discussed clue is the Eight Immortals’ temple number — 1350, the same number associated with Sun Wukong, better known as the Monkey King, in the “Book of Life and Death,” a mythical register of the underworld in “Journey to the West,” hinting at his possible appearance later in the story.

The same reinterpretation has also drawn criticism from some viewers, who argue that the film alters the identities and values associated with traditional mythology.

Yang Jian, for example, traditionally portrayed as a righteous war god who protects ordinary people, is reimagined as a figure willing to sacrifice heaven and humanity to save his mother. The film’s other redesigns have also drawn attention, including Cao Guojiu’s portrayal as an overweight, flamboyant official and Lan Caihe’s depiction as a toddler.

The debate also extends to the film’s portrayal of immortality. Through the line, “Only immortals can do good deeds,” it offers a new interpretation that some viewers praised, while others argued it differs from traditional Taoist ideas of attaining eternal life.

The production team, based in southwestern China’s Sichuan province, said the Eight Immortals offer creative space for reinterpretation because many audiences know their famous stories but are less familiar with their broader legends. The filmmakers said they hoped to introduce the figures to a new generation through a fresh retelling.

“We didn’t want to simply bring the Eight Immortals in front of young audiences and tell the same story again,” producer Ying Xujun told domestic media. “We had to create something new for a new generation.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A poster for “All Wishes Come True!” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018802/At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.title: At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018802/At World AI Forum, Four Signs China’s AI Industry Is Growing Up
World.content:
This year’s World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai was larger, more crowded, and more politically prominent than in previous editions.

President Xi Jinping attended the event for the first time, while more than 1,100 companies showcased computing systems, AI agents, robots, and other products aimed at workplaces, factories, and consumers. In-person visits topped 400,000, and tickets were reportedly resold for more than 1,000 yuan.

Xi called for wider access to open-source AI, and China launched a 29-country AI cooperation body, placing issues of governance, access, and international coordination alongside the usual displays of commercial technology.

Beyond the speeches and packed exhibition halls, the most revealing conversations were practical: lowering computing costs, putting AI agents to work, managing new safety risks, and building businesses that can last.

Here are four takeaways from this year’s WAIC.

Computing power gets practical

Computing power was one of the most discussed topics at this year’s WAIC, second only to AI applications by number of related forums. But the focus moved beyond building more data centers or training ever-larger models.

Two questions dominated: what the next generation of computing power might look like, and how to make today’s resources cheaper and more efficient.

At one flagship forum on the future of computing, scientists discussed emerging approaches including quantum computing and space-based computing. Among the speakers was Pan Jianwei, a leading quantum physicist and recent recipient of a top United Nations science award, who outlined recent advances in the field.

Pan also urged caution. Although the field has reached a series of important milestones, he said, building a general-purpose quantum computer capable of quickly solving problems with clear practical value will still require years of sustained research. The academic community, he added, has a responsibility to help the public assess the technology realistically and guard against an industry bubble.

Companies also seemed more focused on improving the efficiency of existing computing resources and reducing the cost of each AI query.

Some were working to improve the performance of models trained mainly on Nvidia chips when deployed on Chinese chips. Others focused on allocating and managing computing resources more efficiently.

Rather than chasing only the most powerful and expensive models, many Chinese AI companies appeared more concerned with making AI cheaper to run.

AI Governance and Safety

AI governance and safety were prominent throughout this year’s WAIC, from high-level forums to the opening ceremony and President Xi Jinping’s speech.

Brian Tse, an AI safety expert and founder and CEO of Concordia AI, said he has seen more discussion in China around cybersecurity and the protection of critical infrastructure, especially the risks posed by frontier AI models.

“The threat landscape is evolving rapidly,” Tse said. “Many experts at the forums expressed concern that threats and potential misuse are developing faster than society’s current defenses.”

The concerns also appeared to be shifting beyond large language models and the harmful content they can generate. More attention was paid this year to the risks posed by autonomous AI agents, which can plan tasks, make decisions, and interact with other tools.

On July 15, just before WAIC, China’s new rules on AI anthropomorphic interaction took effect, targeting services that simulate human personalities and sustained emotional interaction. The rules prohibit providers from offering virtual partners or relatives to minors and bar services from inducing emotional dependence or addiction.

In May, regulators also released guidance on the standardized application and development of AI agents, including plans to explore digital identity management for them.

“China is positioning itself as an architect of multilateral AI governance,” Tse said.

AI lands at work

One phrase heard often at this year’s WAIC was AI’s real-world “landing” — the push to move the technology out of demos and into everyday work. Companies ranging from Tencent and Alibaba to smaller startups showed AI products aimed at offices, factories, and consumer services. AI agents were among the most visible examples.

At booths run by major tech firms, exhibitors demonstrated how agents could be built into corporate workflows, from searching internal documents to generating reports and coordinating routine tasks.

The impact could be broad because many of these companies’ software systems are already embedded in Chinese workplaces. Adding AI agents to existing platforms may prove easier than persuading companies to adopt entirely new tools.

Still, genuinely effective applications appeared limited. Office productivity remained the most obvious use case, while other areas were less developed.

Robotics and embodied AI occupied an entire floor at this year’s WAIC. Visitors could still see robots performing awkward dances or taking six minutes to make a cup of tea. But some companies were beginning to move beyond staged demonstrations, showing robots designed for inspection, manufacturing, logistics, and other industrial uses.

The founder rush

Some of the most revealing conversations at this year’s WAIC took place after the official sessions ended.

Across after-hours gatherings, private meetups, and open-mic sessions, young founders and industry professionals swapped ideas on AI agents, robotics, and productivity tools. Some gatherings ran late into the night, with almost any topic open for discussion.

Many entrepreneurs seemed eager to absorb every new idea, experiment, business opportunity, and professional connection they could find.

But that urgency also carried risks. Some founders said their AI ventures were burning through years of savings. Many still lacked a convincing answer to a basic question: how their projects would generate lasting value and revenue.

That tension ran through WAIC: crowded halls, founders eager to share projects and failures, and a palpable fear of moving too slowly and missing the AI wave. The mood mixed optimism with anxiety, much of it fueled by the speed of the technology and the sheer volume of information surrounding it.

The conversations also suggested a maturing industry. More speakers and founders were asking not only what AI could do, but where it could be useful, how it could be governed, and which businesses could survive once the initial excitement fades.

(Header image: A humanoid robot from a Chinese robotics firm waves Chinese national flags during the 2026 WAIC in Shanghai, July 18, 2026. Ng Han Guan/AP Photo via VCG)

World.title: The Soybean That Built Northeast China
World.content:
In 2020, I traveled to Kaishantun, a town in the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture near the China-North Korea border. It fit every stereotype of the deindustrialized Northeast. Young people had left. The government had built two rows of barracks-style apartment blocks for the elderly residents who remained. Kaishantun railway station had long been abandoned. On the station sign, the space for the next stop was blank. North Korea lay only a few hundred meters away.

On the walk back, I wandered into a derelict movie theater and discovered several reels of old film. Later restored, they revealed something astonishing: clips of a symphony orchestra and a traditional folk orchestra.

What kind of small town could support two orchestras of its own?

As I dug deeper into the history of my home region, Northeast China, I found that part of the answer lay in a crop that today frequently appears in international headlines: soybeans. A century before China became a major importer of American soybeans, it was the world’s leading producer.

In August 1872, three Japanese army officers, disguised as merchants and acting on the orders of General Saigō Takamori, traveled through “Manchuria,” the term they used for Northeast China. Saigō was studying relations between Japan, Korea, and China as he prepared a future campaign against Korea. A year later, the officers submitted their “Report on an Inspection of Manchuria,” one of Japan’s earliest intelligence briefings on China. The report includes a detailed discussion of soybeans:

“From winter through spring, soybeans are continuously transported by inland waterways. Regardless of the cold, day and night, dozens of horse-drawn carts move in a single direction. Large merchants purchase the beans and pile them into circular mountains more than two rooms across and over 6 meters high … The quantity stored is beyond counting.”

In 1885, another Japanese military officer, Kikuchi Setsuzō, passed through Northeast China on his return from the Russian Empire. Along the way, he studied how Qing forces fed their military horses, which he regarded as superior to those of Japan and Russia. Qing troops processed the residue left after soybean oil extraction into pressed soybean cakes for animal feed. Each cake weighed about 12.5 kilograms and could feed three horses for a day. Kikuchi even claimed such soybean resources would be “indispensable” for training military horses.

In the 19th century, Kikuchi was among the few who grasped soybeans’ strategic significance. The crop had reached Europe and North America in the 18th century but remained largely a botanical curiosity. A handful of enthusiasts, such as the Austro-Hungarian agronomist Friedrich Haberlandt, sought to introduce soybeans into Western diets. Yet while they imported the crop, they did not import the culinary traditions that had made it a staple across Asia.

In East Asia, by contrast, people had accumulated more than a thousand years of experience cooking and consuming soybeans. They also recognized the crop’s value as animal feed. After the Meiji Restoration in 1868, Japanese rice farmers gradually abandoned traditional fish-based fertilizers in favor of soybean cake. Between 1882 and 1902, Japan’s soybean imports increased four-hundredfold.

The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05 finally alerted the world to soybeans’ importance. European military observers noted that both sides relied heavily on the crop. Japanese forces consumed soybeans directly and used them in military logistics. Russian forces fed them to cavalry horses. Soybean oil served as a raw material for soap and as a lubricant for artillery equipment and wagon axles.

The soybean trade expanded rapidly. A 1911 report from the Customs Service in Shanghai observed that “It is only in the last three years that soya beans have become important in intercontinental commerce,” calling their rapid emergence from obscurity “one of the most remarkable commercial events of recent times.” In the same year, the U.S. ambassador in Beijing told the State Department that Northeast China had until recently been largely unknown for its commercial potential, despite supplying soybeans to global markets. He observed that its economic trajectory was now drawing attention in major cities including New York, London, Hamburg, and Seattle, and attributed this shift to soybeans, whose rapidly growing demand he characterized as “phenomenal in trade annals.”

Estimates suggest that Northeast China accounted for between 16% and 42% of global soybean production between 1908 and 1930, shipping soybeans, soybean oil, and soybean cakes to the rest of China, Japan, and Europe. Until the eve of World War II, China produced more than 80% of the world’s soybeans. The crop became widely known as the “Manchurian bean.”

Soybeans were also among the most important exports of a then largely impoverished China. After World War I, their importance grew rapidly, and by the 1920s they had overtaken tea and silk to become China’s leading export, accounting for more than 20% of export earnings.

As trade expanded, so did Japan’s territorial ambitions. In the run-up to Japan's formal annexation of Korea in 1910, Yanbian became a frontier along the China-Korea border where Chinese and Japanese spheres of influence met directly. Japanese strategists viewed the wider Yanbian area as a gateway to the interior of Northeast China and sought to build a railway linking the Korean port of Chongjin with China’s inland Northeast. General Hasegawa Yoshimichi, commander of Japanese forces in Korea, regarded Yanbian as a vital supply corridor for sustaining colonial rule on the peninsula. He advocated occupying the region to secure access to strategic commodities such as soybeans.

Over the following three decades, Japan steadily expanded its influence in Northeast China. In 1931, Japanese forces seized the region and took control of its economic resources. This expansion, justified in the name of protecting economic “lifelines,” would later extend across Asia during the Pacific War to the oil fields of Burma, Sumatra, and Borneo; the rubber plantations of Malaya; and the chromium and iron deposits of the Philippines.

In Yanbian, war and colonial rule only reinforced the region’s economic importance. Beyond soybeans, Japanese authorities coveted the region’s timber. In Kaishantun they established the Eastern Manchuria Rayon Pulp Company, whose output eventually surpassed that of most producers in Japan. After the Chinese Communist Party won the civil war and founded the People’s Republic of China in 1949, the new state’s flagship pulp and paper enterprise was established in the same town.

Factories brought more than jobs. They brought hospitals, movie theaters, and even symphony orchestras.

Yet by then Northeast China was no longer the sole center of the global soybean trade. By the early 20th century, American farmers were already familiar with soybeans, using them to replenish soil and support other crops. After the Russo-Japanese War, however, the crop’s industrial potential attracted growing attention.

One unlikely champion was Henry Ford. He used soybean protein and soybean-oil derivatives in automotive components and in 1941 unveiled a prototype car with body panels made largely from soybean-based plastic. To demonstrate its strength, he famously struck it with an axe.

Ford’s soybean car was hardly a commercial success, but it generated publicity for the crop. When Japan severed America’s access to Asian supply routes during the Pacific War, soybeans were transformed from an industrial curiosity into a strategic resource. Combined harvesters and advances in plant breeding helped American farmers scale up production.

By the 1950s, the center of gravity in soybean production had shifted decisively to the Americas.

One final piece was still missing from the modern soybean map: Brazil. In the early 1970s, a major El Niño event, a climate pattern that warms the Pacific Ocean, devastated the Peruvian anchoveta fishery, a key source of animal feed, driving demand for soybean meal. Prices surged, and in 1973 the Nixon administration imposed restrictions on soybean exports.

History then took an ironic turn. Japan, heavily dependent on imported American soybeans, increased its investment in South American agriculture, while Brazil’s agricultural research agency, Embrapa, developed soybean varieties suited to tropical conditions. The result was a dramatic expansion of Brazilian production.

In 2024, more than 70% of China’s soybean imports came from Brazil. When trade tensions between China and the United States intensified in 2025, Brazil became China’s principal alternative for former U.S. suppliers.

Northeast China remains the country’s most important soybean-growing region, producing the beans that become tofu and soy milk on Chinese tables. But it no longer supplies the world with soybean oil and soybean meal. Once-thriving industrial towns have been swept up in the tide of deindustrialization, leaving behind abandoned railway stations and empty movie theaters.

From an unassuming plant in Northeast China to one of the world’s most traded agricultural commodities, the soybean’s history is ultimately a story of globalization. A soybean harvested in Paraguay may be processed in Argentina, sold to China by a trading house in Geneva, and eventually find its way into milk, cakes, or meat products. It shapes what we eat, how we farm, and how nations interact with one another. It also shapes the fate of countless small towns, including places like Kaishantun.

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s SONA 2026
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is set to deliver his State of the Nation Address (SONA) on Monday, July 27, 4 pm, at the Batasang Pambansa in Quezon City.

The situation is markedly different from last year, when Marcos’ erstwhile ally, Vice President Sara Duterte, avoided an impeachment trial after the Supreme Court ruled that the complaint against her was unconstitutional as it is barred by the one-year rule.

This year, as Marcos delivers his fifth SONA, the impeachment trial against the Vice President is in full swing. Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez, the President’s cousin, is no longer House speaker following his resignation after he was implicated in flood control corruption. Marcos himself had announced a crackdown on those involved in the scandal in his SONA last year.

How will Marcos set the tone for the last two years of his presidency? What promises will he declare as fulfilled, and what remains to be done? What will be his new marching order a year since he called for a crackdown on flood control corruption?

Bookmark and refresh this page for updates, analyses, fact checks, and videos as Marcos delivers his fifth SONA.

World.title: Red Sea shipping slows after Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia, data shows
World.content:
2024 RED SEA ATTACK. Greek-registered tanker ship Sounion burns after an attack by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militants in the Red Sea, September 6, 2024 in this satellite image.

Data shows 11 commodity vessels pass through the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Sunday, the lowest level in months

SINGAPORE – Ship traffic through Bab el-Mandeb fell on Sunday, July 26, after Yemeni Houthis attacked Saudi oil installations along the Red Sea coast, while transit through the Strait of Hormuz stayed low over the weekend, shipping data from Kpler showed on Monday, July 27.

Eleven commodity vessels passed through the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Sunday, the lowest level in months, the data showed.

Red Sea traffic has been disrupted off the coast of Yemen since last week by the Tehran-aligned Houthis, who want to blockade Saudi exports, expanding the US-Iran conflict that has already choked oil supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

Seven of the vessels that passed through Bab el-Mandeb were oil tankers with three of them entering the Red Sea. Two of them are very large crude carriers (VLCCs) heading to the port of Yanbu to load Saudi crude while the third is a Russian-linked ship, the data showed.

The four vessels that exited the Red Sea on Sunday included the Hong Kong-flagged VLCC New Explorer carrying 2 million barrels of Saudi and Emirati crude for eastern China’s Ningbo port, a tanker carrying 1 million barrels of Russian crude for China and a tanker with about 750,000 barrels of Saudi crude onboard for Pakistan, the data showed.

This is the third Chinese VLCC to exit the Red Sea via the Bab el-Mandeb strait. Associated Maritime Hong Kong, the manager for the New Explorer, did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside office hours.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group struck sites belonging to Saudi state oil company Aramco in the cities of Jizan and Yanbu on Saturday.

Hormuz

Fewer than 10 commodity vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz daily over the weekend even though the US and Iran have paused strikes in the Middle East, shipping data from Kpler showed.

Seven vessels transited on Sunday including three Iranian-linked oil products tankers that exited the Strait, the data showed.

On Saturday, there were only three vessels that passed through with their transponders switched off. These include a VLCC heading to Qatar to load oil, a liquefied petroleum gas tanker going to the Ruwais port in the United Arab Emirates to load a cargo and a tanker carrying Qatari naphtha that was heading to Japan, the data showed.

On Friday, seven vessels passed, mostly exiting the Gulf, including two VLCCs carrying crude from Iraq and the UAE and a tanker carrying fuel oil. – Rappler.com

World.title: Can Marcos follow through on flood control promise in penultimate SONA?
World.content:
At 4 pm on July 27, a nation that has spent a year waiting for specifics on the flood-control promise will finally hear the President’s report

MANILA, Philippines — Up until Sunday evening, July 26, to even “one hour before,” President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is likely to be introducing revisions and tweaks to his State of the Nation Address (SONA) on July 27. It will be the penultimate of his presidency.

“I’m never done. Until one hour before the SONA, I’m still changing it, you know. Because, of course, you want it to be perfect,” said Marcos in a chance interview with reporters on Friday, July 24, days before he was set to deliver his annual speech.

Every year, the SONA is a big deal. Officially, the speech is an address to Congress — delivered to both chambers at the Batasang Pambansa in Quezon City with top government officials from all branches and the diplomatic corps present.

In reality, it’s the President’s report to the Filipino people. On July 27, at around 4 om, Marcos will speak to a nation and a people unsettled.

Net satisfaction towards Marcos, according to the Social Weather Stations June 2026 survey, is still in the red at -7 percentage points. It’s an improvement from the -15 he registered in late March 2026.

“I always regard the SONA as a report of the President to the public as to what has happened since the last SONA and that is what we will take up,” said Marcos in the same July 24 interview.

Flood control, corruption at the center

At the center of this year’s SONA will be what Marcos says — or does not say — about how his administration is fighting corruption, which had a rating of 29.8%, according to a late June to early July 2026 survey by Pulse Asia Research. A distant second topic that respondents wanted to hear about was the administration’s “efforts to investigate and hold accountable those involved in the flood control projects scandal (18.9%).”

It’s an agenda that Marcos himself set out, whether inadvertently or not, in his last SONA. In July 2025, as the country was reeling from widespread flooding and its aftermath, Marcos vowed to go after government officials and contractors who had made money out of flood control projects that were either substandard or non-existent.

The 2025 SONA line ballooned into a campaign — that, at times, the Marcos administration seemingly lost control of. In the year since the 2025 SONA, both Marcos’ allies and foes have been dragged into the net that is the flood control corruption scandal.

But actual follow-through — that is, the filing of cases against these personalities — have been inconsistent, at best. The most glaring absence of cases is the one closest to the Marcos home.

The Ombudsman announced in late July that former top Marcos aide and ally, his cousin former House speaker Martin Romualdez, was a “central figure” in the corruption scheme. Yet no case has been filed against the presidential cousin.

Preceding the 2025 flood control corruption scandal was a political disaster that was partly of Marcos’ making, too — the embarrassing showing of the administration-backed Senate slate in the midterm elections that same year.

The political tumult of 2025 was set in motion by the midterm elections and later intensified by the Marcos administration’s decision to arrest former president Rodrigo Duterte and send him to face crimes against humanity charges before the International Criminal Court. Duterte’s trial is set to begin in late November 2026.

Pressure inside and out, too

“I will make sure that people know all of the things that we have done to navigate this very difficult period in our history, where we are buffeted by all of these external forces,” said Marcos in the July 24 interview.

While the president did not say what these “external forces” are, it is easy to deduce that one of them was the swings the Philippine economy — and the Filipino nation — has had to bear as a result of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.

Manila was among the first to declare a national energy emergency, as it scrambled to seek alternative sources of energy.

Affordability of basic goods ranked third in the list of issues Filipinos wanted to hear from the President (18.7%), according to the same Pulse Asia survey.

“Our response has been good, and we have had to make adjustments. But those adjustments have been effective and have served their purpose and I know that it has helped people weather this storm and continue to weather this storm until things hopefully normalize,” said Marcos.

Inflation in the Philippines was at 6.4% in June, lower than the 6.8% in May and the three-year high of 7.2% in April. On average, based on government data, inflation for the first six months of 2026 stood at 4.8%, above the original target range of 2% to 4%.

An issue that has dominated news headlines over the past month is, according to the survey, among Filipinos’ lowest priorities, with the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte registering just 1.2% in the survey.

Vice President Duterte is the daughter of the former president and erstwhile ally to Marcos.

Even as Marcos reckoned last-minute tweaks, the President said at least 90% of the speech was already done. Sources close to the Palace have said that last-minute changes can prove to be the most consequential, the flood control promise being a prime example.

“We’re just fixing it up and making sure that it’s not too long or it’s not too short. That we have everything that we want to talk about is already included,” said Marcos of the speech.

At 4 pm on July 27, a nation that has spent a year waiting for specifics on the flood-control promise will finally hear the President’s report. – Rappler.com

World.title: This Filipino physicist brings outer space closer to home
World.content:
When Dr. Gay Jane Perez was a kid, she never thought that she would grow up to be a decorated physicist, a postdoctoral fellow at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), a leader in the space economy, as well as the director general of the Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA).

“Although much, much younger, I did think about being an astronaut. But not so seriously, just in a way that was, ‘Oh! It would be cool to be an astronaut! I want to be an astronaut.’ But what course would you take to be an astronaut? There’s no Filipino astronaut,” she shared. “So it’s just one of those things that will cross your mind but you don’t have a pathway to get it.”

Perez didn’t even attend a science high school. As a student of the Universidad de Santa Isabel in Naga City, she grew up seeing lawyers, accountants, and doctors at career fairs, not scientists. Her school also focused on developing well-rounded leaders, writers, and public speakers.

Even if she was an active student leader herself, she felt like those skills were her weaknesses, so she gravitated to math instead of words. While her friends were winning extemporaneous speaking competitions, she was winning math olympiads.

She chose to major in physics — the science with the most math, she thought then — at the University of the Philippines (UP) Diliman after the Department of Science and Technology (DOST) offered a scholarship and incentivized the science course.

But while her strength in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) gave her an edge among her high school classmates, all her college peers came from science high schools. She struggled to keep up after everything she knew about physics was covered in the first week.

To her surprise, her perceived weaknesses became her strengths. While applying for a prestigious research lab in her third year of college, her lecture and presentation on the science behind the animation technology of Toy Story captured the attention of her audience.

“Before me, people were chatting during the other presentations. But when I started giving my talk, they all started listening, including the head of the lab, Dr. Caesar Saloma, who eventually became my advisor,” she recalled.

“I guess it turned out that they’re not used to hearing somebody like me. My weakness when I was in high school was my strength when I was in college because I’m more comfortable speaking in front of the class, more than the rest. But it’s all relative, right? So, I thought, if they only knew my high school friends!”

That moment was transformative, especially for a struggling Perez, who was just trying to pass her subjects.

“They must have seen my potential and decided to bet on me, even if I wasn’t as good as those from the science high schools,” she said. “So when they accepted me, I valued it immensely, especially since I ended up doing really well on the research part. I super enjoyed the act of research! Exploring something that you don’t know where it will lead to… I found it very interesting and exciting because every day is unique.”

Mission: Come back home

It was also in college that she found the role models in the sciences that she didn’t have growing up. One of the most influential to her was Saloma, former chancellor of UP Diliman and professor emeritus at the National Institute of Physics.

“He’s the one that really expressed passion for science, and more importantly, doing science in the Philippines. We had some scientists before in the Philippines who are now celebrated scientists out of the country. A few chose to stay and continue to do the science here, and he is one of them,” she said.

“But what I learned from him, which influenced me in my career, is that you can do science in the Philippines and you are most needed here. You can create the highest impact here because the science that you do will help our society.”

ROLE MODEL. Dr. Gay Jane Perez sends a message of inspiration for the high school participants of CanSat 101, a program for hands-on satellite development through the CanSat model. Photo courtesy of PhilSA

After she was accepted into a postdoctoral fellowship at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, she took with her those lessons from Saloma all the way to Washington, DC. Even when immersed in a world-class research center with top-of-the-line equipment at her disposal and Nobel Prize winning scientists down the hall from her office, she never forgot the Philippines.

Throughout her time in NASA, she found herself constantly thinking, “How I wish we have something similar in the Philippines. I want to bring this to the Philippines.” After just a few months, she couldn’t wait to go back home.

At that time, many people were awaiting her return home and counting on her contributions to the country. She made a parallel about how she felt back then in NASA when Christina Koch of the Artemis II mission became the first woman to orbit around the moon.

“During their final burn to go to the moon, the last statement [Koch] said was, ‘We choose Earth.’ So, for me, it was like I went to NASA on a mission to come back home,” Perez said.

NASA on Philippine soil

Back in the Philippines, she applied the research she conducted and data she gathered in NASA by leading the development of the Philippines’ first local microsatellite, Diwata-1, and launched it in 2016. The satellite data was used for drought forecasting, agricultural monitoring, and climate assessment, targeted toward serving farmers and the agricultural sector during intense seasons of El Niño.

Perez, although already a decorated scientist at this point, had a dream she still wanted to fulfill: to have something like NASA on Philippine soil.

The next step was a no-brainer for the scientist as she eventually contributed to the establishment of the Philippine Space Agency. She had first served as officer-in-charge, deputy director general, and finally appointed director general by President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. in January 2026.

LEADER. Dr. Gay Jane Perez takes her oath as director general of PhilSA in January 2026. Photo from Perez’s LinkedIn

As a six-year old government agency, PhilSA is young, new, and exciting. Perez shared that the agency is now 247 personnel strong. Having been involved in its formation since Day 1, she knows that its people are the most crucial in ensuring its effectiveness and sustainability.

But with “brain drain” — Filipino scientists choosing to migrate to countries with better pay, conditions, and research opportunities — the challenge is not to ask them to stay, but to create an environment that makes them want to stay.

“What we are striving for and we think is really necessary is to create the environment for them to thrive, to absorb them. Because otherwise, the same narrative of a Filipino who eventually will seek for greener pastures out of the country, or will find more meaningful things to do outside, will continue,” Perez said.

“[They usually think,] ‘What can I do here? We don’t have the equipment, we don’t have the resources, I’m better off doing my science outside, elsewhere.’ So creating that environment where they can see that they will thrive and excel and do good and do meaningful and impactful science, that’s still a work in progress. Now, in my capacity as the head of the agency, that’s where I’m focusing my energy.”

The Philippine scientific community is resourceful and adaptable amid the lack of funding, equipment, and working “against all odds.” But Perez isn’t one to romanticize struggle. For her, pursuing a career in science shouldn’t always come with so many roadblocks.

The organization’s annual Philippine Space Week is one way they are able to present to stakeholders and the general public why it is worth investing and betting on PhilSA and the Philippine scientific community.

Throughout the week, they present the breakthroughs they achieved that year, the people and partnerships who made it all possible, and the emerging possibilities and opportunities that the space economy has to offer. They also show the problems and issues that space technology and data can help solve and the ways they can be implemented to serve the Filipino people.

Through this event, they not only show what science in the Philippines can achieve, but also why scientists in the country are needed and worth supporting.

Discoveries, adventures

If, growing up, Perez never had a scientist speak at her career fair, it was a full circle moment for her to get invited to be her high school’s commencement speaker. She has now become the role model she never had in her formative years. Now, she’s dedicated herself to showing others that a career in the sciences is full of exciting discoveries and adventures.

“They also used to say that becoming a scientist is like a vow of poverty, that you won’t get rich from the sciences. But I think that is not fair,” Perez said. “It is true in the sense that you won’t get rich, but it’s not like it will make you poor. And while you won’t get rich because you don’t get a lot of money, maybe you don’t need that much, anyway.”

LESSONS. Dr. Gay Jane Perez delivers a talk at the 2026 Annual Philippine-American Academy of Science and Engineering (PAASE) Meeting and Symposium in Bagac, Bataan. Photo from Perez’s LinkedIn

“I also think it’s a very decent and high integrity profession,” Perez added. “Because for one, you disincentivize lying. Because science, right? You need data, facts. So this is a profession where you can earn by simply telling the truth. You can sleep soundly at night.”

To the young Filipinos who are considering a career in the sciences, she wants them to know that, “There’s a future for you here. I’m one of you. Like you, before, I didn’t see a clear [career] path in the sciences. But now you can see me.” – Rappler.com

Quotes in Filipino were translated to English for brevity.

Elise Suarez is a Rappler intern from Puerto Princesa City and a Humanities student of the University of Asia & the Pacific.

World.title: No go for Alex Eala-Venus Williams doubles pairing in Washington Open
World.content:
EAGER. The Philippines' Alexandra Eala reacts during her third-round match against Poland's Iga Swiatek in the 2026 Wimbledon Championships.

Alex Eala will instead focus on singles action as she battles Asian Games tormentor Zheng Qinwen of China in the opening round of the Washington Open

MANILA, Philippines – Plans for a repeat team-up between Alex Eala and tennis icon Venus Williams have fallen through.

The Filipina will instead focus on singles action of the Washington Open in the United States as Williams partners with fellow American Diana Shnaider in doubles play.

Eala and Williams were announced as doubles partners by the WTA 500 tournament and even practiced together days before the start of the competition, but the draw released on Saturday, July 25, showed otherwise.

The development derailed aspirations for Eala and Williams to go on a deeper run after they joined forces for the first time and reached the quarterfinals of the Bad Homburg Open in Germany in June.

Eala opens her singles campaign against China’s Zheng Qinwen in the round of 32 as the two Asian bets meet on the WTA Tour for the first time.

But Eala and Zheng are familiar with each other — the Chinese former world No. 4 beating the Filipina in the semifinals of the 2022 Asian Games on the way to winning the gold medal.

A lot has changed, though, since as Eala now ranks No. 29 in the world while Zheng sits outside the top 100 at No. 123.

Eala is coming off a warm homecoming, where she was honored by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and warmly welcomed by fans.

The 21-year-old hopes to build on the momentum from her splendid grass-court campaign that she capped with a historic run to the fourth round of the Wimbledon Championships as she begins the hard-court swing in Washington. – Rappler.com

World.title: [ANALYSIS] Marcos’ shrinking influence in the legislative
World.content:
The two men seated behind him during the 2025 SONA won't make a comeback on that stage this year. It's a testament to the political upheaval that has reshaped both chambers of Congress over the past year.

When President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivers his fourth State of the Nation Address (SONA) in end-July, he will face a legislative branch that has gone through turmoil in the past year, and he will continue to grapple with his waning — and sometimes underutilized — influence.

On the surface, Congress’ turnaround rate on Marcos’ pet bills this year doesn’t paint a flattering picture. Excluding his inaugural SONA in 2022, this will be the first time he takes the podium with only one priority measure enacted that he can point to as an accomplishment.

That means that out of 52 bills identified as a priority by the Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council, only one — the resetting of the Bangsamoro elections — was signed into law.

That is unlike in previous years, when anywhere from six to 21 pet bills hurdled the legislative branch by the time of his address to the Filipino public. The SONA, after all, is the biggest stage to tout the achievements of his administration.

To be fair to Marcos, the legislative grind typically slows after the midterm elections, as a newly constituted Congress regroups and reassesses which priority bills are worth pushing to the finish line before the next elections usher in the President’s successor.

For the part of the House, whose majority leader is no less than his son Sandro Marcos, 20 out of 51 pending pet bills hurdled the chamber in the past year, but all of them got stuck at the Senate.

The low productivity rate at the upper chamber, however, stems from an unprecedented episode of chaos that Marcos was slow to contain.

Senate

The holdup of bills at the upper chamber took place under the short-lived but destructive Senate presidency of Alan Peter Cayetano.

Virtually no legislative work was accomplished — no anti-dynasty bill, no freedom of information measure, not even the proposed abolition of the travel tax, a relatively easy win that could have earned Marcos goodwill among middle-class voters.

During Cayetano’s weeks-long rule, triggered by a surprise coup, a gun fight broke out inside Senate premises, fugitive Bato dela Rosa escaped from Senate custody, the minority walked out from the session hall in protest, and Cayetano’s majority boycotted the session.

Play Video

It is uncommon in Philippine politics for the Senate president to be a rival of the President, but that’s what Cayetano has been for Marcos.

The President’s recent challenges in keeping the Senate on his side have hardly been a surprise. His slate’s underperformance during the midterms — seen as a referendum on his presidency — resulted in more Duterte-allied politicians winning Senate seats instead of survey-favored administration candidates.

The consequence is an aggressive Senate bloc ready to platform former bodyguards who claimed that top officials, including Marcos, received billions of pesos in kickbacks from public works projects.

The Senate minority now has 11 members, a stark contrast from the two-member minority during the first half of the Marcos administration.

House

Malacañang’s logic has been straightforward: Marcos was the one who exposed flood control anomalies during his SONA last year, so he would not be dumb enough to do that if his hands were not clean.

During that address, he uttered one of the punchiest soundbites of his presidency — “Mahiya naman kayo!” — an emotional warning against people who manipulate the budget for their personal gain.

Play Video

The two men seated behind him at the time suffered the consequences of the scandal: then-Senate president Chiz Escudero for the campaign donation he received from a top contractor in his province, and then-House speaker Martin Romualdez for his role in the passage of what critics described as “mangled” 2025 national budget.

Cousin Romualdez, until his resignation last year, was an effective and efficient ally of the President. Congressmen had little to no complaints, funding poured in for their districts, most of Malacañang’s pet bills cleared the lower chamber, and one of them — the Maharlika Investment Fund — even passed in record time during the early years of the Marcos administration. Romualdez had the ears of the President, he was a companion to Marcos’ foreign trips, and he rallied the troops to impeach Vice President Sara Duterte for the first time in 2025, even if Marcos publicly insisted he had nothing to do with it.

Romualdez’s successor Bojie Dy came from northern Luzon, a bailiwick of the Marcoses. While he is a party mate of the President, the strength of his ties to the President cannot match what the cousins had.

Months into his post, Dy had to contend with growing dissatisfaction from the House’s second-largest bloc, the National Unity Party, which blamed the executive for bottlenecks in the release of district funds, and Dy for failing to effectively press Malacañang to address their concerns.

Privately, some lawmakers, while insisting they had done nothing wrong, also bristled at Marcos’ SONA callout, saying it placed their actions under intense public scrutiny.

The House, however, is still unlikely to turn its back on the President. Earlier this year, it swiftly dismissed an impeachment complaint against Marcos over his alleged involvement in the budget kickback scheme.

Even so, his administration will continue to contend with outspoken lawmakers eager to seize on any perceived misstep — from figures such as Leandro Leviste and Edgar Erice to the Duterte bloc and the usual voices from the traditional opposition.

Marcos is entering the lame-duck phase of his presidency, and the next two years will test whatever political capital he has left: first, whether he can marshal enough support to secure the conviction of a vice president out for blood, despite his apparent reluctance to acknowledge that her permanent disqualification would bolster his family’s political future; and second, whether he can persuade Congress to pass key bills that will ultimately define his legacy. – Rappler.com

World.title: 30 passengers safe after bus plunges down ravine in Bohol town
World.content:
All 30 passengers aboard a Rimon passenger bus were rescued after the vehicle plunged down a ravine along the Loay–Carmen Interior Road in Barangay Villa Aurora, Bilar, on Sunday afternoon, July 26, 2026. INQUIRER FILES

BILAR, Bohol — All 30 passengers aboard a Rimon passenger bus were rescued after the vehicle plunged down a ravine along the Loay–Carmen Interior Road in Barangay Villa Aurora, Bilar, on Sunday afternoon.

The accident occurred around 2 p.m. after the bus, which was traveling from Talibon to Tagbilaran City, reportedly experienced a steering wheel malfunction.

READ: 15 hurt as bus overturns in Bohol town

Article continues after this 

According to the initial investigation, the mechanical problem caused the bus to gradually veer off the roadway before falling down a slope into a forested area.

The Bilar Municipal Police Station confirmed the incident.

Despite the severity of the crash, authorities reported that no fatalities or major injuries were sustained by any of the approximately 30 passengers on board.

Several passengers were assessed and received immediate assistance at the scene.

A total of 25 emergency responders from various agencies were deployed to carry out the rescue operation. These included personnel from the Bilar Fire Station, Loboc Fire Station, the Bureau of Fire Protection’s Special Rescue Force from the 1st and 3rd Districts, the Bilar Search and Rescue Unit, the Bilar Municipal Police Station, and TaRSIER 117.

Article continues after this 

The successful rescue operation highlighted the swift coordination and preparedness of emergency responders and partner agencies, ensuring the safe evacuation of all passengers from the accident site.

Authorities are continuing their investigation to determine the exact cause of the incident, including the reported steering system malfunction./coa

World.title: Marcos, Duterte ratings decline in Q2 2026 —survey
World.content:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Vice President Sara Duterte. PHOTOS BY MARIANNE BERMUDEZ

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Vice President Sara Duterte both saw their performance and trust ratings decline in the second quarter of 2026, according to Octa Research.

The research firm released its latest noncommissioned “Tugon ng Masa” nationwide survey on Monday, July 27, coinciding with the president’s fifth State of the Nation Address. The survey was conducted from July 4 to 11.

In the survey, Marcos’ performance rating plunged by 8 percentage points, from 55 percent in the first quarter to 47 percent in the second quarter of 2026.

Article continues after this 

“The decline more than erased the 4-point gain recorded in the first quarter and left the president without a majority performance rating,” Octa Research said.

The latest survey also showed that 33 percent of Filipinos expressed dissatisfaction with Marcos’ performance.

READ: Octa: 71% of Filipinos want law, evidence to guide Sara Duterte trial

As for his trust rating, Marcos also lost 5 percentage points from his 54 percent rating in the first quarter of the year. He now has a 49 percent trust rating, with 32 percent of Filipino respondents expressing distrust.

Octa Research said Marcos’ ratings fell most sharply in Mindanao, where his satisfaction rating dropped by 25 percentage points and his trust rating fell by 19 percentage points.

Article continues after this 

Balance Luzon, which includes his bailiwick, the Ilocos Region, was “the only major area where the president retained majority trust and performance ratings.”

Meanwhile, Duterte’s performance and trust ratings in July are “both below majority level for the first time since November 2024,” Octa Research noted.

Article continues after this 

The latest performance rating of the vice president—whose impeachment trial started on July 6—is at 45 percent, showing a 5-percentage-point decline from her 50 percent rating in March.

The latest survey also showed that her dissatisfaction rating climbed to 36 percent.

Duterte’s trust rating also fell by 8 percentage points, from 55 percent in March to 47 percent in July, when 33 percent expressed distrust in her.

“The vice president’s trust and performance ratings are both below majority level for the first time since November 2024, but not for the first time in the full trend series,” Octa Research said.

“Both ratings previously stood at 49 percent in November 2024. Nevertheless, her July 2026 trust rating of 47 percent and performance rating of 45 percent are the lowest national ratings recorded for her in the available series beginning in October 2022,” it added.

READ: Survey: 4 of 5 Filipinos doubt senators’ verdict in Sara Duterte trial

Duterte’s drop in performance and trust ratings was “sharpest” in Metro Manila and Balance Luzon, with performance ratings dropping by 15 percentage points and 10 percentage points, respectively, and trust ratings falling by 12 percentage points and 13 percentage points, respectively.

Meanwhile, her bailiwick, Mindanao, still gave her high ratings—90 percent for performance and 89 percent for trust.

The survey was conducted through face-to-face interviews with 1,200 respondents aged 18 and above across the country. /mcm

World.title: Marcos’ agriculture, food security record marked by systemic failure
World.content:
Farmers plant rice in Daguioman, Abra, on July 10, 2025. (Photo courtesy of Neil Clark Onchangco)

The verdict is clear: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr.’s leadership in agriculture has been marked by systemic failure.

Agriculture remains the backbone of Philippine society. Yet under Marcos, who concurrently served as agriculture secretary, the sector has faced mounting crises rooted not only in climate shocks and import dependence but also in a broader debt-and-corruption trap that has eroded fiscal space and undermined farmer welfare.

An estimated ₱8.8 trillion was lost to corruption between 2016 and 2025 — money that could have been used to build classrooms, fund hospitals and protect farmers from traders and import shocks.

Article continues after this 

The leakage has pushed the government into deeper debt dependence. National debt rose from ₱12.79 trillion in 2022 to ₱18.55 trillion by May 2026, crowding out resources for agriculture, irrigation and food security programs.

Although nominal agriculture budgets have increased, real per capita support has stagnated. Filipino farmers receive less than half the support provided to their counterparts in some neighboring Southeast Asian countries.

Import dependence

The Philippines’ return as the world’s largest rice importer in 2024 underscored the depth of its structural weaknesses. Rice imports reached 4.8 million metric tons, with projections rising to 6 million metric tons amid El Niño and global disruptions.

Rice demand has consistently exceeded production capacity. By 2025, total demand had reached 13.8 million metric tons, while production had stagnated at 12.4 million metric tons, leaving a deficit of 1.4 million metric tons.

Imports not only filled the gap but also exceeded it, reaching 4.7 million metric tons in 2025. The imbalance reflects a declining rice self-sufficiency ratio, which fell from 116% in 1960 to 91% in 2025.

Article continues after this 

The erosion of domestic production capacity has been compounded by trade liberalization, climate variability and inadequate farmer support. The Rice Tariffication Law of 2019 dismantled quantitative restrictions, exposing farmers to global competition without sufficient safety nets.

Although imports temporarily stabilized consumer prices, they weakened farmer morale, reinforced middleman-dominated value chains and increased the country’s vulnerability to peso depreciation.

Article continues after this 

The food import burden has grown into a trillion-peso liability. Direct imports of rice, meat, fish, sugar, dairy products and processed food reached $21 billion to $22 billion, or about ₱1.3 trillion, in 2026.

Indirect imports, including fertilizers, pesticides, vaccines, feed grains and machinery, added $8.5 billion, or ₱517 billion. Costs associated with peso depreciation, shipping and displaced labor raised the total burden to an estimated ₱2 trillion to ₱2.2 trillion, equivalent to 31% of the national food economy.

This dependence exposes households to external shocks. The peso’s depreciation from ₱2 to the dollar in 1960 to ₱61.50 in 2026 has increased import costs, while oil price volatility has affected food prices through higher fertilizer and logistics expenses.

The result is a food system locked into external dependence, with an estimated 5 million to 6 million Filipinos displaced or underemployed because of import substitution.

Climate and governance

Climate vulnerability compounds these structural weaknesses. A looming super El Niño in 2026 threatens to reduce rice yields by as much as 30%, possibly cutting palay output to 17 million to 18 million metric tons and forcing rice imports to rise to 6 million metric tons.

Rising oil prices linked to tensions in the Middle East also increase fertilizer and logistics costs, while inadequate irrigation leaves rain-fed areas exposed.

The Marcos administration has failed to articulate a credible adaptation strategy and has instead relied on reactive importation. That approach is increasingly untenable as rice-exporting countries such as Vietnam, Thailand and India face droughts of their own.

The absence of coherent, long-term planning underscores the administration’s inability to balance food affordability with agricultural sustainability.

Governance failures have further aggravated agricultural decline. Technical and physical smuggling continue to destabilize the onion, garlic and sugar markets, while ghost projects in the Department of Public Works and Highways divert funds that could have been used for irrigation and postharvest facilities.

The transfer of ₱60 billion from the Philippine Health Insurance Corp., or PhilHealth, despite Supreme Court rulings, also reflects fiscal management problems that deprive farmers of needed support.

The National Food Authority’s minimum buying price of ₱21 per kilogram of palay remains ineffective because the agency lacks the budget to purchase even 25% of harvests. Farmers are therefore left at the mercy of traders.

Marcos’ pledges to plant 15 million coconut trees and amend the Coconut Farmers and Industry Trust Fund Act also remain unfulfilled, deepening farmers’ disillusionment.

Policy distortions have added to the problem. Inflated estimates placing annual rice consumption at 148 kilograms per person, instead of the reported actual range of 105 to 110 kilograms, were used to justify excessive imports that cost farmers an estimated ₱50 billion a year.

The Filipino diet also remains heavily dependent on rice, imported wheat and processed food. There is no national program to diversify calorie sources toward corn, root crops, vegetables and fish.

This nutritional imbalance weakens the country’s resilience to shocks and perpetuates import dependence. Farmers, whose average age is 57, face declining morale as younger Filipinos leave rural areas, raising a fundamental question: Who will produce food for the next generation?

Declining farm support

The agriculture budget increased from ₱500 million in 1960 to ₱211.3 billion in 2025, but it declined as a share of gross domestic product and the General Appropriations Act.

In real terms, per capita allocations fell from $75 in 1960 to $10 in 2025, partly reflecting the effects of peso depreciation. Even after the increase in the 2025 budget, Filipino farmers received less than half the real per capita support provided in Vietnam and Thailand.

Vietnam’s allocation of about ₱1,200 per capita helped support its 1-million-hectare low-emission rice program, while Thailand’s allocation of about ₱1,800 per capita sustained its export competitiveness.

The Agriculture Orientation Index, or AOI, measures agriculture’s share of government spending relative to its contribution to GDP. The country’s AOI fell from 0.65 in 2005 to 0.48 in 2025, signaling a decline in fiscal priority for the sector.

For a food-insecure country such as the Philippines, this decline is particularly damaging.

Reversing the decline in the AOI would require clear commitments in the national budget. Allocating at least 1% of GDP to agriculture, comparable with levels in Vietnam and Thailand, would signal renewed fiscal priority.

The allocation should support not only production inputs but also marketing assistance, buffer stocks and agricultural cooperatives.

The MSP option

India’s Minimum Support Price, or MSP, system offers instructive lessons. India guarantees farmers a fixed price for rice and more than 20 other crops.

Through the Food Corporation of India, the government procures 25% to 30% of annual rice production, ensuring that farmers have a reliable buyer even when market prices collapse.

The procured crops feed into the Public Distribution System, which maintains large buffer stocks and distributes rice at subsidized prices. This arrangement stabilizes farmer incomes and consumer access by linking production support with marketing and distribution.

Philippine policies, by contrast, have emphasized production inputs such as fertilizers, irrigation and mechanization while neglecting marketing support. The imbalance leaves farmers vulnerable to price volatility, trader dominance and import dependence.

The proposed Philippine MSP Act of 2026 seeks to adopt India’s model with local adaptations. Its main provisions include a guaranteed floor price, set annually by the Department of Agriculture, for rice and at least 20 other strategic crops; government procurement to ensure a reliable buyer for farmers; buffer stocks for food security and price stabilization; and explicit budgetary allocations for MSP operations.

The framework would institutionalize marketing support, reduce import dependence and stabilize farmer incomes. By linking procurement with food security, an MSP law could transform the agricultural sector, as India’s system did beginning in the 1970s.

Implementing an MSP system in the Philippines would nevertheless present several challenges.

Debt service consumes a large share of the national budget, limiting the government’s capacity to finance procurement. Corruption and inefficiencies in procurement agencies could undermine the system’s credibility, while climate-related disruptions could threaten production stability.

Changing diets would also require MSP coverage to extend beyond rice to feed grains and other staples as demand for meat and processed food rises.

Despite these constraints, an MSP system could help reduce import dependence, stabilize the peso, protect farmers and improve health outcomes. It could also strengthen buffer stocks, integrate climate-resilient production strategies and give agricultural cooperatives a larger role in procurement.

Cooperative empowerment is particularly important because middleman-dominated value chains have long weakened farmers’ bargaining power.

By making farmer cooperatives procurement partners, the government could bypass trader cartels, help farmers receive fair prices and provide consumers with more stable supplies. The approach could also strengthen rural employment and help reverse the displacement caused by import substitution.

Dietary diversification offers another opportunity. A national program linked to MSP coverage could encourage the production of corn, cassava, sweet potato, mung beans and tilapia.

Diversification would reduce reliance on imported staples, improve nutrition and reinforce local culinary traditions.

Fiscal discipline and governance reform must underpin these initiatives. Funding an MSP system would require political commitment, stronger budget management and effective safeguards against corruption.

Transparent procurement, digital monitoring and cooperative oversight could reduce the risk of ghost projects, smuggling and the diversion of funds intended for procurement and buffer stocks.

The National Food Authority must also be strengthened and reoriented toward farmer-centered procurement.

Climate adaptation must be integrated into agricultural policy. Research on climate-resilient seeds, irrigation rehabilitation and crop insurance programs is essential to protect farmers from extreme weather.

India’s system shows how buffer stocks can help stabilize food supplies during climate-related crises. By maintaining reserves of rice and other staples, the Philippines could protect consumers from price spikes while ensuring that farmers have a reliable buyer.

Linking MSP procurement with climate adaptation would help keep production and distribution systems functioning during extreme weather events.

Structural reforms

Structural reforms in governance and legislation are equally urgent.

Four measures stand out:

Passage of the National Land Use Act to rationalize the allocation of land among agriculture, industry and housing. Repeal of the Rice Tariffication Law and its replacement with the Rice Industry Sustainable Development Act, which would restore farmer protections while promoting sustainability. Renationalization of the Department of Agriculture, following India’s model of a Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, to strengthen farmer-centered governance. Creation of a Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources to support aquaculture and coastal livelihoods.

These reforms would rebalance policy priorities, institutionalize farmer welfare and align agricultural governance with food security needs.

The cultural dimension of food nationalism is also important. Food nationalism can be defined as growing, eating and protecting locally produced food to reduce dependence on imports and foreign control of the food supply.

It encourages consumers to patronize local dishes such as pinakbet, dinengdeng, inabraw and ginataang lubi-lubi rather than rely heavily on fast-food chains. Such choices can reinforce cultural identity while supporting rural livelihoods.

In this framework, food nationalism is linked to food sovereignty, food security and national security. Agriculture serves as the engine, rural transformation as the road and industrialization as the vehicle toward sovereign development.

By incorporating dietary reform, cooperative empowerment and local consumption into national policy, food nationalism could provide a cultural and economic path toward greater resilience.

Agriculture at a crossroads

In his State of the Nation Address, Marcos must confront the country’s reliance on food imports, the lack of a credible climate adaptation strategy and governance failures that have left food security precarious.

The address offers the administration an opportunity to change direction by committing to structural reform, fiscal discipline and farmer-centered governance.

Food security is not merely an economic concern. It is a matter of national security.

Decades of trade liberalization, currency depreciation and climate shocks have entrenched food import dependence, displaced agricultural workers and exposed households to external volatility.

Although the agriculture budget has increased in nominal terms, real per capita support remains modest compared with support in neighboring countries. The decline in the AOI further reflects agriculture’s diminishing fiscal priority.

The Philippines must rebalance its agricultural policy by institutionalizing marketing support alongside production assistance. The proposed MSP Act of 2026 offers a possible path to stabilize farmer incomes, reduce import dependence and strengthen food security.

By integrating procurement, buffer stocks and distribution, the government could bridge the gap between production and marketing and build a food system that serves both farmers and consumers.

The Marcos administration stands at a crossroads. The debt-and-corruption trap has narrowed fiscal space, import dependence has increased the country’s vulnerability, and climate shocks threaten production.

By adopting an MSP system, promoting dietary diversification, strengthening cooperatives and supporting locally produced food, the Philippines can begin building a more resilient agricultural sector.

Without urgent reforms, the country will remain trapped in recurring food import crises, widening inequality and persistent governance failures. With meaningful reform, it can strengthen food sovereignty and secure a future in which farmers and consumers can thrive. /dm

World.title: In-person classes suspended in Pampanga amid bomb threats
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

MABALACAT CITY, Pampanga — The city government suspended face-to-face classes at all levels in public and private schools on Monday following bomb threats circulated on social media.

“I ordered the suspension of face-to-face classes at all levels in public and private schools on Monday, July 27, 2026, and the implementation of alternative delivery modalities while a thorough security assessment is being conducted,” Mayor Gerald Guttrie Aquino announced through the official Facebook page of the Mabalacat City government on Sunday evening, July 26.

READ: 3 La Union campuses threatened online

Article continues after this 

The mayor was referring to a Facebook account identified only by the alias “Anthony Policarpio,” who threatened on Saturday to bomb several elementary and high schools in the city between Aug. 26 and Sept. 5.

According to the posts, the threats were in retaliation for alleged discrimination in student admissions.

Aquino said he ordered the suspension after consulting with the Mabalacat City Police Station and the Department of Education’s Schools Division Office in the city.

He added that several school principals and barangay officials had also expressed concern over the safety and security of students.

The social media user threatened schools in the villages of Atlu Bola, Mamatitang, San Joaquin, Sta. Ines, Tabun, Camatchiles, and Mangalit.

Article continues after this 

Meanwhile, in nearby Angeles City, three minors were taken to the barangay hall in Barangay Cutud on Saturday for allegedly making a social media video showing a masked person threatening to stab students of Cutud Elementary School.

During questioning, the minors told police officers and barangay officials that the video was merely their “trip,” slang for a prank or deliberately acting out.

Article continues after this 

In a Facebook post, the Cutud Barangay Council said the minors would undergo intervention and counseling and perform community service as part of measures to help them understand the seriousness and consequences of their actions. /mcm

World.title: Marcos to INC: Remain steadfast nation-building partner
World.content:
Members of Iglesia ni Cristo march along Roxas Blvd. to the Quirino Grandstand for the National Rally for Peace in January 2025. INQUIRER PHOTO: MARIANNE BERMUDEZ

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Monday urged members of the Iglesia ni Cristo (INC) to remain “steadfast partners in nation-building” as the religious organization celebrated its 112th anniversary.

Marcos also reaffirmed the government’s support for organizations that promote peace, strengthen families, and serve communities.

READ: Palace warns INC rally should not lead to destabilization moves

Article continues after this 

READ: No politics, just bloc vote, says INC member

“As you gather in thanksgiving, may this milestone deepen your commitment to translating your beliefs into meaningful acts that uplift those in need, comfort the weary, and foster harmony wherever you serve,” he said.

“In this spirit, I encourage every member of the INC to remain a steadfast partner in nation-building, where faith is demonstrated through service and citizenship is expressed through genuine concern for others,” he added.

Marcos noted that for more than a century, the INC has served as “a steadfast guide to a community grounded in faith, discipline, and a shared sense of responsibility.”

He also noted that the religious institution has expanded its presence to communities across the globe.

Article continues after this 

“Your enduring work reminds us that a life rooted in devotion and integrity helps reinforce the moral foundation of society,” he said.

“May this anniversary reaffirm the sacred mission that has sustained your Church through the generations,” he added.

Article continues after this 

The INC made headlines in recent weeks after holding a series of rallies in support of one of its members, Sen. Rodante Marcoleta.

READ: Marcoleta pleads not guilty to plunder, accepting gifts raps

The senator is currently detained at the New Quezon City Jail over plunder charges.

World.title: 3 La Union campuses threatened online
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

CALASIAO, Pangasinan — A bomb threat targeting three college campuses was posted online, prompting the La Union provincial police to deploy its explosive ordnance disposal and canine unit in San Fernando City on July 25.

The police said the unit conducted comprehensive paneling operations (systematic physical checks) and security sweeps across campus grounds but did not detect explosives at the Don Mariano Marcos Memorial State University–Mid La Union Campus (DMMMSU-MLUC), the Saint John Bosco College of Northern Luzon Inc. (SJBCNL), and Lorma College.

READ: La Union school receives bomb threat, adjusts classes, work

Article continues after this 

Police Colonel Redentor Ulsano, La Union police provincial director, assured students, parents, and school personnel that La Union province remains safe, secure, and fully under control.

The bomb threat, as well as provocative slurs, was made through a fictitious social media account, but the police cybercrime unit is tracking the individual or group that made the post, according to Ulsano’s office.

“We urge the public to remain vigilant and refrain from sharing or reposting unverified social media content that incites unnecessary panic. Anyone with information about the individual operating the ‘Britney Madonna Kepya’ account is strongly encouraged to report to the nearest police station or contact the LUPPO Hotline at 0998-598-5152,” Ulsano said in a statement.

Presidential Decree No. 1727 (the 1980 decree that prohibits bomb jokes) declares unlawful and penalizes the malicious dissemination of false information and the willful making of any threat involving bombs, explosives, or any similar device or means of destruction, regardless of the medium used, police said.

Its core policy is to treat false bomb threats or hoaxes as a distinct public safety offense with specific penalties, even if no actual explosive exists. Offenders will also be prosecuted under Republic Act No. 10175 (the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012). /mcm

World.title: Thunderstorms forecast in Metro Manila on SONA Day
World.content:
GRAPHICS BY INQUIRER

MANILA, Philippines — Metro Manila is forecast to experience scattered rains and thunderstorms during President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s fifth State of the Nation Address (Sona) on Monday, July 27, the state weather bureau reported.

READ: More Filipinos want to hear solutions, not achievements in Sona

In its morning update, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) said cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms would affect the following areas due to the continuing effect of the southwest monsoon:

Article continues after this 

Metro Manila

Ilocos Region

Cagayan Valley

Cordillera Administrative Region

Mimaropa

Zambales

Bataan

Bulacan

Cavite

Laguna

Batangas

The southwest monsoon is also expected to bring partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms over the rest of Luzon.

Pagasa weather specialist Aldczar Aurelio said the rain would “not be as heavy compared to the previous days, when tropical cyclone Kiyapo was still affecting the country.”

He also said the habagat is forecast to further weaken in the coming days.

“Tomorrow, this southwest monsoon will affect the western part of Northern and Central Luzon. On Wednesday, the southwest monsoon is expected to move away from our country,” Aurelio said in Filipino.

He added that the easterlies, or the warm winds coming from the Pacific Ocean, would then affect the country until Friday.

Article continues after this 

READ: Agriculture officials fear ‘super’ El Niño

No gale warning is currently in effect for any seaboard of the country, but fishermen are advised to remain vigilant for possible thunderstorms, especially in the afternoon and evening.

Article continues after this 

As for Tropical Depression Noul (formerly Kiyapo), Aurelio said it was last located 1,015 kilometers west-northwest of Extreme Northern Luzon, outside the Philippine area of responsibility.

It carries maximum sustained winds of 55 kilometers per hour (kph) and gusts of up to 90 kph, moving north-northwestward at 20 kph.

World.title: Romblon police, DENR recover abandoned illegally cut tree log
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Police and environment personnel recovered an abandoned, illegally cut Mangkono (Tiga) tree log during an operation in San Fernando town, Romblon province, authorities said on Monday.

The San Fernando Municipal Police Station (MPS) assisted the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) in recovering the Mangkono round log measuring about four feet long and 28 centimeters in diameter in Sitio Talaba, Barangay Taclobo, on July 26.

The timber has an estimated market value of P5,000.

Article continues after this 

The operation was launched after the DENR Sibuyan Field Office sought police assistance.

Police said no individual was found in possession of the log during the operation, and investigators are still determining the identity of the person responsible for the illegal act.

READ: 8 nabbed for illegally cutting trees in Oriental Mindoro, Romblon

READ: P160,00 worth of illegally sourced lumber seized in Mindoro

The recovered timber was turned over to the DENR Guard Post 3 in Sitio Olango, Barangay España, San Fernando, for documentation and proper disposition in accordance with environmental regulations.

Article continues after this 

Personnel from the San Fernando police, led by OIC Police Lt. Romel Rutor, and members of the 3rd Platoon of the Romblon Provincial Mobile Force Company joined a DENR team headed by Protected Area Superintendent Joybert Mijares.

Romblon police director Col. Rexton F. Sawi said the operation supports the Mimaropa police’s Project T.R.E.E. (Take Responsibility for the Enhancement of the Environment), an initiative that promotes environmental protection and the preservation of forest resources through collaboration among government agencies and local communities. /mcm

World.title: Why Almaty’s Fountains Are More Than Just Decoration
World.content:
ALMATY – For generations of Almaty residents, fountains have marked the rhythm of summer. They are meeting places, playgrounds, works of art and fragments of history hidden among the city’s trees.

Today, Almaty operates more than 120 fountains and fountain complexes, making it the undisputed fountain capital of Kazakhstan. Sixty-three belong to the municipality, while the remainder are privately owned. Unlike many cities where fountains exist primarily for decoration, in Almaty they were conceived as part of the city’s environmental infrastructure.

Nestled against the northern slopes of the Zailiysky Alatau mountains, the city experiences long, hot and relatively dry summers. The fountains, together with the famous network of mountain-fed irrigation canals known as “aryks,” were designed to cool streets, humidify the air and make public spaces more comfortable long before air conditioning became commonplace.

Before Almaty became a megapolis

For decades, guidebooks confidently stated that the city’s first fountain appeared in 1948, when ornamental fountains were constructed near the Abai Opera and Ballet Theatre. Local historian Alois Nazarov, however, challenged this widely repeated claim.

According to Nazarov, the 1948 date referred only to the first fountains constructed from durable materials – not the first fountains themselves. The earliest documented fountain connected with the region dates back even further.

According to the archival documents, in 1878, physician, botanist and explorer Albert Regel visited the summer residence of Semirechye Military Governor Gerasim Kolpakovsky near the mouth of the Butakovka River. His travel notes describe a landscaped estate complete with a pond and two fountains.
