This means that if the Kulevi refinery continues processing Russian oil over the next six months, it will become subject to EU sanctions. The refinery’s owner, Black Sea Petroleum, announced on 1 July 2026 that it would begin full-scale processing of non-Russian crude from August or September.

According to Georgia’s National Statistics Office, domestic exports rose sharply in January 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, driven largely by exports of petroleum products.

Petroleum and petroleum products ranked as Georgia’s second-largest export category in January 2026, with exports worth $58.7 million, accounting for 12.2% of the country’s total exports.

Cryptocurrency platforms added to the sanctions list

The EU has imposed transaction bans on 14 cryptocurrency platforms based in Georgia, Panama, the United Arab Emirates, Kyrgyzstan, Belarus and the Marshall Islands.

For the first time, the EU has introduced a mechanism allowing it to impose a complete ban on transactions between EU companies and cryptocurrency platforms that help Russia circumvent sanctions.

The measure also applies to crypto service providers operating in third countries if they facilitate activities that serve Russian interests.

What does the inclusion of Georgian companies in the sanctions package mean for Georgia?

The inclusion of the Kulevi refinery in the EU’s 21st sanctions package has already sparked debate in Georgia.

“The EU’s 21st sanctions package is a national disgrace: Georgian assets are being used as cannon fodder for Russia’s war machine. By allowing the Kremlin to circumvent sanctions, those in power are betraying our sovereignty. Georgia’s place is in Europe — we will never become a loophole for Russian aggression,” Georgia’s fifth president, Salome Zourabichvili, wrote on X.

Analyst Lela Djedjelava said sanctions against such an important economic asset would have an impact on the Georgian economy.

“The consequences will become increasingly visible over time. The reality is that the Kulevi refinery is probably not the only facility that could be exposed for cooperating with Russia. If other businesses in Georgia are also hit by sanctions, it will naturally have a very negative impact on the country.”

Gedevan Popkhadze, one of the leaders of the opposition Coalition for Change, said the EU sanctions against the Kulevi refinery were the result of the Georgian government’s inaction.

“If you are not helping Ukraine, why are you helping Russia? If you do not want war, why are you acting in favour of one of the parties to the conflict? We must clearly understand that these sanctions are not a message to the Kulevi refinery itself — they are a message to Georgia’s de facto government. It should realise that claiming to be neutral is hypocrisy.”

Georgia in the EU’s 21st sanctions package

World.title: Chinese national arrested at airport after alleged $20,000 bribe
World.content:
A Chinese national has been arrested after he allegedly attempted to bribe a public official with a bag of tea containing $20,000 in cash.

The man was apprehended on July 24 as he attempted to board a flight at Sydney International Airport and was extradited back to Queensland on Saturday.

The 39-year-old Chinese national allegedly attempted to bribe a Commonwealth public official during a business meeting in Camp Hill, Brisbane on July 9.

Police have alleged that during the meeting the man handed the woman a bag of tea, which was later found to contain $20,000 cash.

It is alleged the attempted bribery was for business gain.

The woman reported the incident and a joint operation was launched involving Queensland Police, the Australian Federal Police and the National Anti-Corruption Commission.

The man has been charged with one count of gift or offer a secret commission to an agent and will appear before the Brisbane Magistrates Court on Monday.

World.title: Breaking: Seven new suspected H5 bird flu cases detected in SA
World.content:
South Australia has recorded seven new suspected cases of H5 bird flu, including five detections at the same site over two days.

Federal Agricultural Minister Julie Collins said the greater crested terns have been sent to CSIRO laboratory in Geelong to determine if there has been local transmission.

Australia has recorded 20 confirmed cases of the strain so far.

SA authorities are expected to provide an update at 11:30am ACST.

World.title: Community 'shattered' after fire destroys Sikh temple
World.content:
A Sikh leader says the community is feeling "shattered" after a fire destroyed a temple north of Adelaide overnight.

The Country Fire Service (CFS) responded to reports of a fire at Gurudwara Dashmesh Darbar in the suburb of Virginia, about 9:40pm on Sunday night.

About 60 firefighters and 20 trucks attended the scene, supported by the Metropolitan Fire Service (MFS), SA Amubulance Service, SA Police and SA Power Networks.

CFS Incident Controller Gerald Thomson told 891 ABC Adelaide crews worked for three to four hours to extinguish the fire, due to a lack of water in the township.

He said the temple had been established inside a large industrial factory on Old Port Wakefield Road.

The CFS responded to the fire about 9.40pm on Sunday night. (ABC News: Bobby Macumber)

"The fire was burning in what we believe is a kitchen area in that vicinity and got into an industrial part of the factory and because of refrigeration panels, it just made our job very difficult," Mr Thomson said.

"We had gas cylinders in there and the refrigeration panels become quite difficult to extinguish because of the flame in the middle of the panels and once that goes, that burns through the building."

Mr Thomson said one man was "resting" inside the temple when fire crews arrived, but he was evacuated and uninjured.

"We had multiple people from the place of worship standing around outside on first arrival," he said.

He said fire crews would remain on the scene this morning to extinguish hot spots inside the building, while fire cause investigators would also attend the scene.

The CFS estimated the damage exceeded $1 million dollars.

The CFS estimates the damage caused is in excess of one million dollars.

Community 'shattered' by fire

Gurudwara Dashmesh Darbar president Bakshish Singh said the industrial factory was converted to a place of worship for the Sikh community about two years ago.

He said the fire quickly engulfed the building and flames reached as high as the roof.

"This temple is not just a building that has been burnt, people used to find peace there, they used to come there to pray, to serve, meditate, donate groceries, sharing meals together, support one another," Mr Singh said.

" As of now, everything is shattered and we don't really know what to do after this. "

Community members gather outside Gurudwara Dashmesh Darbar this morning. (ABC News: Bobby Macumber)

Mr Singh said the temple also provided important community outreach services.

"Those who come from overseas and they don't have a place to live or food to have straight away, they can come anytime and they can get groceries, food," he said.

"Everything that is inside is gone, the roof collapsed, nothing that could be recovered, there was a lot of equipment there, groceries, everything."

SA Police Senior Constable Matt Hale told 891 ABC Adelaide motorists should expect delays around Port Wakefield Road in Virignia.

"There are lane restrictions in place so the best advise is just to avoid that area if you can," he said.

World.title: Veterinary students denied paid training
World.content:
For Gemima Rahman, completing her studies as a vet meant relocating more than 1,500km from Port Hedland to Perth.

Now in her postgraduate studies, the 24-year-old is specialising in large animals.

Ms Rahman said the financial strain of moving away from home meant missing out on experiences she would have loved to pursue.

Gemima Rahman is a postgraduate student at Murdoch University’s School of Veterinary Medicine in Western Australia. (Supplied: Murdoch University)

"I would have loved to have gone to the Northern Territory, over east to Victoria where there are large animal practices, but in saying that the cost to do so was not possible," Ms Rahman said.

The post-graduate student said a paid prac program would have reduced emotional and financial stress.

"Within our degree, they recommend working 10 hours around your study and practical hours," Ms Rahman said.

"Sometimes I would be at uni 8-4pm then I would work night shift until 1am, so it wouldn't leave much time for sleep and self-preservation."

She said this was another reason burnout was so common in her profession.

Veterinary students have been left out of the Commonwealth Prac Payment. (Supplied: Murdoch University)

"I think if the government were to help students like me, we would see not only a rise in more larger-animals veterinarians, but I also think burnout, which happens in students and graduates, would be reduced because they would have more financial backing," she said.

Veterinary studies not included in expansion

Ms Rahman's comments come after the prime minister recently announced the expansion of the Commonwealth Prac Payment scheme.

The scheme now has an additional 10 university courses, but not veterinary studies.

Students of clinical psychology, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech pathology, paramedicine, radiography, pharmacy, rehabilitation therapies, audiology and podiatry are now eligible for a $338.60 per week payment.

"Paid prac is already making a real difference — it's helping students with cost of living while they train and that's why we're expanding it," Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said.

One of Australia's best-known veterinary schools has since called on the federal government to extend the scheme to include veterinary students.

'Extremely disappointed'

Murdoch University vet school professor and dean of engagement Cristy Secombe said the WA-based school was disappointed veterinary students had been left out of the program, despite facing some of the longest placements.

"We're extremely disappointed we've been left out of the scheme, especially because vets provide an essential service," she said.

Murdoch University says veterinary students should have the same support as other healthcare professions. (Supplied: Murdoch University)

"Students complete 52 weeks of compulsory placements while training for a profession that was recognised by government as an essential service during the COVID-19 pandemic.

" We've got data where students have said it can cost them up to $1,000 a week for them to go out on placement regionally. "

Ms Secombe said she believed the financial pressure of placements was contributing to a shortage in the veterinary workforce regionally.

"The veterinary profession is in its ninth year of shortage, so we are clearly a profession in need," she said.

Murdoch University welcomes the expansion of the payment, but wants vet students to be included. (Supplied: Murdoch University)

" We want more vets out regionally, and want them to experience prac in the rural sectors but it is really hard for them because of financial pressures, so they just don't go. "

Australian Veterinary Association president Diana Barker said the recent emergence of H5N1 avian influenza and the crucial frontline role veterinarians played showed how essential the profession was to Australia's biosecurity.

Vet chanced upon first H5 bird flu case A walk along the beach with a friend turned into the significant discovery.

"Only five weeks ago vets were called to be at the front line of the nation's biosecurity to protect our agricultural industry, and then yet again we are not supported by the government," she said.

"We were in Canberra talking to ministers only a few weeks ago, and had feedback about our possible inclusion, so we fail to understand what it is veterinarians are not doing right."

Education Minister Jason Clare said expanding the prac payment scheme to allied health was the next logical step.

"These are areas where there are big skills shortages and where we expect there will be more shortages in the future," he said.

He did not say whether veterinary students would be included in the scheme in the future.

World.title: Quick hits: Wiggles star's daughter shines, netball 'cleaner' goes viral
World.content:
Two Aussie besties share a podium, a hometown hero fights his way to the final, and a very famous face wiggles his way into the stands.

Here are the quick hits from day three of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Cleaning up never looked so good

Every major sporting event has its surprise star.

Sometimes it's an underdog athlete. Sometimes it's a mascot. And sometimes it's a cleaner with a mop and a sense of rhythm.

A short clip from the Commonwealth Games netball venue has captured exactly why sport is about more than the result.

Loading Instagram content

A cleaner who danced as he mopped the court has become an unexpected crowd-pleaser on social media.

The routine, which was done to I Want To Break Free by Queen, had it all: the splits, the worm and twerking. If there were judges, he would have scored 10 out of 10.

Was the "cleaner" just a dancer with a mop employed to entertain the crowd?

That's for you to judge. Either way, he brought a lot of joy to people in the stadium.

2. Brilliant besties prove the power of friendship is real

With a medal each to their names, attention turned to Aussies Gemma Sellick and Victoria Belando Nicholson as they stepped up to be interviewed after the women's 100m backstroke S9 event.

But the pair had eyes only for each other, their friendship taking centre stage as they gushed about sharing a podium.

"This is my best friend," Sellick said, grinning ear to ear, a question from the media suddenly feeling rather inconsequential.

"This was not even a thought I had; I was not expecting this at all," Belando Nicholson told the ABC.

"To do it with my best friend is actually insane."

As they headed to pick up their medals, the pair were already planning a "debrief later tonight" to celebrate their silver and bronze medals.

3. Silver is sweet for Canada's Dolci after epic gymnastics comeback

The Arena in Glasgow was the venue for one of the maddest competitions at the Games so far: the men's all-around final at the artistic gymnastics.

At the end of the day, Flower of Scotland was on full blast (followed by the latest rendition of The Proclaimers' 500 Miles) as Reuben Ward became the first Scots gymnast to win the competition in Commonwealth Games history.

Jesse Moore also flew the flag, so to speak, as he became the latest Australian gymnastic medal-winner at these Games with a bronze, coming after he had to withdraw halfway through the Games four years ago with a shoulder injury.

But with respect, both these performances were left in the dramatic shadows by the competition of Canada's Felix Dolci.

Felix Dolci was down in 17th place in the men's all-around gymnastics final after falling off the pommel horse twice, before the Canadian made a miraculous recovery. (Getty I,mages: Francois Nel)

The men's all-around features all six disciplines: vault, rings, pommel horse, parallel bars, horizontal bars and floor exercise. Gymnasts are split into groups doing the six in different orders, maximising the drama.

Dolci was in a decent spot when he went on the pommel horse, but everything went pear-shaped as he fell off, twice. He ended up 17th out of 18 competitors after two rounds.

Game over, right? Wrong. A score of 14.200 on the vault, followed by 13.950 on the parallel bars, left him in with a vague hope.

And then he delivered on the horizontal bars, absolutely nailing his landing and scoring a whopping 14.500 to finish with the silver medal. Amazing stuff.

4. Hometown hero Goodburn not done yet

The men's 50m breaststroke is a fairly stacked event, with English legend Adam Ramsay-Peaty, Australia's Sam Williamson and South African speedster Michael Houlie all in the field.

But if you look beyond the very top times, you find Scottish swimmer Archie Goodburn.

The Edinburgh-born Goodburn was the British champion in 50 breaststroke in 2023, and had a chance of going to the Paris Olympics. But then he was diagnosed with three inoperable brain cancers in early 2024.

He was in the eighth and final heat on day three, up against Williamson.

Archie Goodburn of Scotland during the men's 50m breaststroke semifinals in Glasgow yesterday. (Getty: Rob Casey)

The 50m breaststroke is not quite the same "splash-and-dash" as the 50 freestyle, but it's not slow.

Williamson surged through to win in 26.75, with South Africa's Chris Smith second, and Goodburn made the home fans happy coming through for third.

He backed it up in the semifinal to squeeze into the final tomorrow morning AEST in lane one.

Regardless of his eventual placing, you could argue that no-one is flying the Saltire higher at these Games than Goodburn.

5. The Red Wiggle watches daughter star in wheelchair basketball

The Red Wiggle was wearing green and gold in support of daughter Georgia Munro-Cook. (ABC)

The Australian women's wheelchair basketball team notched its first win of the Games on day three, downing South Africa 20-5.

Georgia Munro-Cook was the star for the green and gold, finishing with 10 points in a dominant performance.

Watching on in Glasgow was her father, Murray, who, despite not sporting his famous red skivvy, will be a familiar face to many Australians.

The Red Wiggle was as proud as punch after his daughter's performance.

"She's worked so hard, the whole team has worked so hard, to see them get a win like that is just really exciting," he told ABC Sport.

Munro-Cook was over the moon to have her mum and dad in the crowd, and said it was an interesting role reversal for the family.

"I think it's so funny, I used to go around watching him on stage, and now he's here watching me," she said.

World.title: Deputy premier tells Allan he will run for Victorian Labor leadership
World.content:
Victoria's Deputy Premier Ben Carroll has told Premier Jacinta Allan that he will put his hand up to become Labor leader, as a potential leadership showdown looms.

The ABC understands Mr Carroll has been to see the premier to state his intention.

It comes after a delegation of Labor ministers and MPs met with Ms Allan this morning and urged her to step down, telling her she had lost the majority support of caucus.

Earlier this morning, Ms Allan wrote to the Labor Party's state secretary to indicate she would fight any leadership challenge.

In the letter, Ms Allan said she intended to run as a candidate for the party's leadership "in the event that an election is required".

Under Labor party rules, if there is more than one candidate for the party's leadership, an election must be held among MPs and rank-and-file party members in a process that takes weeks.

The delegation of ministers who met with Ms Allan this morning included Luba Grigorovitch, Enver Erdogan, Lizzie Blandthorn, Anthony Carbines, Gabrielle Williams, Colin Brooks and Ingrid Stitt, as well as MPs Mat Hilakari and Ella George.

The ABC understands Deputy Premier Ben Carroll is seriously considering a leadership tilt. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Labor's Victorian MPs were today at parliament for a pre-planned cabinet meeting.

Labor has struggled in polls in recent months, with News Corp reporting in June that a majority of voters believed it was time for Ms Allan to be replaced as Victoria's Labor leader.

Ms Allan's response to alleged corruption in the taxpayer-funded Big Build scheme has also caused controversy.

There are four months left until the state election in November.

'Too little, too late'

Speaking on the steps of parliament this morning, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said Victorians did not want to see "another un-elected Labor premier".

She refused to say whether she would prefer to be taking on Ms Allan or Mr Carroll at November's election.

"It doesn't matter," she said.

"Ben Carroll is Jacinta Allan's 2IC — he's been sitting next to her in parliament, making the same decisions, supporting her decisions not to call a royal commission [into the Big Build corruption scandal]."

Premier Jacinta Allan has been under mounting pressure to call a royal commission into the Big Build corruption scandal. (ABC News)

Federal Liberal senator for Victoria James Paterson told the ABC this morning that any move to roll Ms Allan would be "too little, too late".

"It sounds like the factional bosses have finally caught up with the sentiment of Victorians, which is they want this premier gone.

" A shift of horse at this very late minute to a new premier is not going to change anything fundamentally. "

While no formal challenger has put their hand up, Mr Paterson said Mr Carroll's role in former premier Daniel Andrew's government would not do him any favours.

"He participated in every decision this government has made over the last few years. He was even a cabinet minister under Daniel Andrews," Mr Paterson said.

"I really think at this late stage it won't change much as Victorians clearly want a change of government."

Jacinta Allan took over the top job after former premier Daniel Andrews announced he was standing down in September 2023. (AAP Image: Daniel Pockett)

Federal Labor MP Kristy McBain said she thought Ms Allan had done a "really fantastic job in the time she's been given".

"I think it is really important at the moment, you know, we're in a situation where we've got a rapidly evolving world out there, and we need strong and steady leadership in each state and territory across the country," she said this morning.

"But ultimately, those questions are for the Victorian parliamentary party."

Jacinta Allan was first elected to the Victorian Parliament in 1999, winning the seat of Bendigo and becoming the youngest female Victorian MP at the age of 25.

Her first ministry was the education services and youth affairs portfolio in 2002.

World.title: 'Weekend DIY' flat-pack homes misleading consumers
World.content:
Steve Harris purchased a prefabricated tiny home for $26,000 in April, believing it was the cheap way to build a small hair salon for his wife's home business in Bunbury, 150km south of Perth.

It was promised to him as a "build-in-a-weekend" job, but it is still sitting deconstructed in his driveway.

"Our engineer rang us yesterday and said the glass on the doors is only four millimetres when it has to be five [millimetres thick]," he said.

"It has been pretty tough going."

The flat-packed home could end up costing him double what he paid, as the Bunbury local battles to get the structure approved under council and Australian building standards.

"I would suggest to anyone doing these prefab builds that they get all their ducks in a row."

An outdoor DIY garden shed for sale online. (Supplied)

The company Mr Harris purchased from appears to be Australian but uses kits made in Europe.

The company, which the ABC has chosen not to name, said DIY assembly varied according to the customer's experience, site conditions and preparation.

"We therefore would not suggest that every customer's installation experience will be identical," a spokesperson said.

Potential consumer law breach

Australia's tiny home industry has seen a 120 per cent increase in sales since 2021, as the housing crisis forces people to look to alternative housing solutions.

Consumer Protection is warning that companies marketing prefabricated flat-pack homes as being "assembled in a weekend" could be in breach of consumer law.

WA's Commissioner for Consumer Protection Trish Blake has cautioned people to be wary of "DIY" or "permit-free homes" claims.

Trish Blake says promises of "permit-free" flat-packed homes should be scrutinised. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"People are looking at quick and easy ways to get accommodation options constructed, and we know that constructing a full home can take a minimum of a year, so these prefab pods and buildings are a great option, " Ms Blake said.

" But I cannot conceive of a prefabricated pod which would be entirely permit-free. "

A major issue with the DIY kits is that they are often made from overseas parts that do not meet Australian building standards.

Owners also need to get proper council building approvals, which can sometimes take months.

"If they are advertising them as permit-free, we will be looking at that very closely and looking at whether they are breaching consumer law for engaging in misleading and deceptive conduct," Ms Blake said.

"Electrical work and all the plumbing work can only be done by licensed electricians and plumbers; these are not the DIY elements of these buildings."

Mr Harris's tiny home was purchased in April but is yet to be unpacked. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

Standards not up to scratch

Bunbury builder Deon Attard said he was seeing increasing issues with tiny homes purchased overseas.

"We just did a commercial project where they brought 12 from China, and the quality just was not up to scratch," he said.

"By the time it's all said and done, they didn't actually save much money at all, and the quality of the finish was not actually delivered."

Bunbury-based builder Deon Attard advises working with professionals. (supplied)

He said "reworks" often needed to be done on houses built overseas, including drilling new holes and places to put electrical outlets and plugs.

"Australian building standards exist for a reason," he said.

Mr Attard is not against tiny homes but says interested buyers should look closer to home.

"Find a local modular or tiny home builder and work with them on the design of the product that suits your budget," he said.

World.title: Mayo wins All-Ireland title, ending 75-year 'curse'
World.content:
In one of the greatest upsets in Gaelic football history, Mayo has beaten Kerry in the All-Ireland football final in Dublin to break a 75-year title drought and end what some people call "the Mayo curse".

Whether the curse was hokum, a story or a real psychological issue that had simply bedevilled generations of Mayo footballers, the victory by 1-20 (23 points) to 1-17 (20 points) at Croke Park immediately drew a line under three quarters of a century of heartbreak and became one of the biggest headlines in Gaelic games history.

And one of the stars of the unlikely victory is a footballer who many think could be a generational talent although he has only just finished school, and is headed to the AFL.

The story goes that after beating Meath at Croke Park in the 1951 All-Ireland final, a jubilant Mayo team travelled home to the western province of Connacht on the back of a truck, celebrating the whole way.

While passing through the village of Foxford though, the players passed by a funeral that was taking place.

The local priest apparently took a dim view of the players continuing to celebrate while the funeral was taking place, placing a "curse" on the county, that it would not win the title again until all the team that played that day had died.

Mayo's 70-year wait goes on amid All-Ireland 'curse' Sporting curse or psychological barrier? Whatever it is, Mayo's All-Ireland Gaelic football title drought reaches 70 years after another final of blown chances against Tyrone at Croke Park.

After 1951, it took the Mayo senior team 38 years to return to the All-Ireland final. In total, before this year, it had played in 11 All-Ireland finals since 1951 and lost them all.

In 2016, Mayo conceded two own goals against Dublin, forcing a draw and a replay, which it lost.

The last of these finals, in 2021, came a few weeks before the final playing member of the original team, Paddy Prendergast, died aged 95.

The team did not make it back to Croke Park for the All-Ireland final until Sunday's decider against defending champions Kerry, who were trying to extend their record by winning a 40th All-Ireland crown.

So this year was the first opportunity to win the biggest game of the season since the elements of the "curse" had been met.

Things did not start well, with Kerry superstar forward David Clifford burying a shot in the net in the 15th minute.

But Mayo fought back to be a point down at half-time, 1-8 (11) to 0-10 (10).

Manager Andy Moran had backed young talent, with 18-year-old Kobe McDonald and 19-year-old Darragh Beirne key to the team's success.

McDonald, who was selected by St Kilda late last year as a Category B rookie and is expected to head Down Under shortly to join the team, would score three points in the final

Beirne's brilliant finish scored Mayo's only goal that sparked the county's run to victory.

Rollercoaster ride to All-Ireland title for Mayo

It had not been an auspicious start to the football season for Mayo, as it was beaten by 10 points by Roscommon in the Connacht provincial championship. The team in red and green was all but written off for the All-Ireland.

Andy Moran (right) got stuck into the media for laughing at long-suffering fans' celebrations. (Getty Images: Sportsfile/Ramsey Cardy)

It entered the All-Ireland Championship series still looking shaky, beating Monaghan by a point before a single-point loss to Tyrone left it on its final chance.

Mayo bounced back with a win over Meath to reach the quarter-finals, then downed Cork at Croke Park to make the last four.

The semi-final turned out to be a one-sided affair against Louth, with Mayo winning by 17 points. But the run was expected to end against Kerry. The questions started after the semi, with Moran asked if fans would lose the run of themselves celebrating given the county's horror record in finals.

Moran hit back hard.

"You laugh at that, lads. I don't laugh at that," Moran said at the press conference.

"I find it very, actually, dismissive, if I'm being honest. I think it's a bullshit question. I think it's a disrespectful question.

"Our county has been starved the last four or five years. If they [fans] go a bit nuts, let them."

He then set his sights on the football reporters present.

"You're going to go to a game tomorrow. Every single one of ye, you're going to write that Kerry or Dublin will go to win the All-Ireland final, right? Right?

"Does anyone here think we're going to win the All-Ireland final? No. Thank you."

Kobe McDonald has just finished school, but the Mayo young gun now has an All-Ireland medal and is set to come to the AFL. (Getty Images: Sportsfile/David Fitzgerald)

When the final siren went on Sunday, it set off emotional scenes at Croke Park among the 80,000-plus crowd.

The Saw Doctors' hit The Green and Red of Mayo, written by a group of Galway musicians about what Mayo means to the people, blasted out of the speakers at the stadium as joy mixed with disbelief for the fans.

After the game, McDonald, like his teammates, was elated and he was trying to focus on the now, rather than what's next.

"Look, to be honest I'm not thinking about Australia right now. I'm just going to soak in every minute of this. To give the people of Mayo something to celebrate, it's special," he told Irish broadcaster RTE.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I know every team probably says it but we're like a family. When we're in training three days a week it's like 40 brothers.

"We know every single person in there has each other's back and whatever is being said outside the group doesn't affect us."

Gaelic games, football and hurling, are amateur sports, and there has been plenty of debate over the years about the loss of talent to the AFL.

The rest of Mayo, and quite possibly the rest of Irish Gaelic games, hopes that McDonald stays with Mayo and doesn't take his skills to Australia.

But whatever happens from here, McDonald and the rest of the team have written their names in Irish sporting history and moved their county forever beyond the ghosts of losses past.

A huge crowd of Mayo supporters travelled to Dublin and were overjoyed after their team's shock win. (Getty Images: Sportsfile/David Fitzgerald)

World.title: Jacinta Allan leadership threat LIVE updates: Ben Carroll tells premier he will contest the leadership as delegation urges her to stand down
World.content:
Deputy Premier Ben Carroll has advised the premier that he intends to be a candidate for leadership in the event of a spill.

A group of ministers and MPs met with Jacinta Allan this morning and urged her to stand down.

Deputy Premier Ben Carroll. Ruby Alexander

Following that meeting, they met with Carroll and urged him to step forward as a contender.

Carroll then advised the premier that he would do so in the event of a spill, likely to unfold at a caucus meeting on Tuesday.

Among those in the delegation were ministers Anthony Carbines, Gabrielle Williams, Ingrid Stitt, Lizzie Blandthorn, Luba Grigorovitch, Colin Brooks, and factional conveners Ella George and Mat Hilakari.

Three Labor sources confirmed the meeting to The Age.

One MP said the delegation included “cross factional ministers and MPs” and they had gone to see the premier “to let her know that she has lost the majority of support in caucus and have urged the premier to stand down”.

Allan was defiant, telling MPs she has no intention to stand down.

One Labor source said the “numbers are overwhelming”.

Cabinet was scheduled to meet at 11am but will be severely compromised given some attendees were part of the delegation.

Ministers have refused to resign their posts.

World.title: I cried when the council cut down my tree. I did not see that coming
World.content:
NationalCity life Opinion I cried when the council cut down my tree. I did not see that coming Melissa Hoyer Writer July 27, 2026 — 11:45am

July 27, 2026 — 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For 27 years, a huge dense-canopied Harpephyllum caffrum, a South African Wild Plum (or a tree with a ridiculous number of leaves that always landed in my backyard), stood on the pavement outside my house. The stump of the tree that stood outside Melissa Hoyer’s house It was, by any measure, just a very, very old and elegant tree, owned by the city long before I arrived, so technically it’s not mine. It gave my house shade, a canopy and some dappled ambience. Turns out it was also propping up something I hadn’t clocked until now: a sense of home. I want to be clear that I did not think of this tree often. I did not hug it. I did not know its Latin name until council’s notice arrived and informed me of it, almost as an afterthought, the way you may meet a friend’s family at their funeral.



A few weeks ago, council decided that my tree was in poor health and, this week, the tree-people took a buzzy chainsaw to it. What’s left is a stump the size of a small car, awaiting its own removal. Soon there’ll be a large hole where a tree used to be. I didn’t expect to feel much about this at all, but I was wrong. Related Article Opinion

Life in the ’burbs Despite what you’ve heard, my suburb’s definitely not grand but at least the bar brawls are gone Diana Simmonds Journalist and writer I’ve been surprisingly, almost embarrassingly, emotional about a piece of municipal vegetation, which made me wonder what exactly I was mourning – because it clearly wasn’t just the tree. Here’s the thing about living somewhere for nearly three decades: you stop seeing the furniture. Not the furniture inside – the furniture of your life outside the front door. The tree wasn’t something I admired each morning like a tourist snapping a photo. It was just there, the way your own reflection is just there. It filtered the light through my windows and into my backyard at a particular hour. It made a particular sound when the wind picked up. I walked past it and its gigantic root system thousands of times without registering it every time. Possums loved it. Birds chirped from it, and they made it their home too. You don’t notice the things that are most obvious in your life until they’re gone. My eye keeps going up to where the canopy was and finding brilliant blue sky instead, which is its own small, repeated joy and a jolt. My brain is expecting one thing and getting another, several times a day, apparently indefinitely.



Scout, my dog, went out to the backyard and just kept barking and barking at the blue sky where my tree used to be. What was that about? I think even little Scout was feeling the loss, a bit like a member of the family having departed. Then there’s the small matter of nobody asking me. I understand councils have arborists and liability concerns and a job to do. But there’s something particular about having a piece of your daily landscape removed by a decision made entirely without you, on a timeline entirely without you, for reasons you’re simply informed of just days before the fact. Even Scout the dog is missing the tree (pictured here with her owner, Melissa Hoyer). It’s not that I think I should’ve had a vote – who am I to argue with an arborist? It’s that grief plus powerlessness is a far more potent cocktail than grief alone. I’m aware this is, in the scheme of life, a very, very minor tragedy. Nobody is sending casseroles or hosting a celebration of life for a stump. Nobody should. I am not asking for sympathy cards or flowers addressed to a tree.



But I’d argue that the loss of a tree that has quietly witnessed 27 years of your life – the comings, the at times sad goings, the baby, the teenager, the BBQs, the excited version of you that moved in and every kooky version since – is not nothing. It’s a legitimate loss, even if the only appropriate way to grieve it is privately and slightly self-consciously, while explaining to bemused friends and family that yes, I am fine at the moment. I’m just very sad about a tree. I’m told the stump goes next week. I’m also told a Weeping Lilly Pilly (Waterhousea floribunda) will be planted in its place. It’s a native evergreen that will, eventually, grow to provide a similar canopy. I will, presumably, not live long enough to sit under its major shade myself. But that’ll be a separate piece of grief for another day.



Melissa Hoyer is a writer and social commentator. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Inner west local gets a $100,000 discount on $2 million semi
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Inner west local gets a $100,000 discount on $2 million semi Carmen Forward July 27, 2026 — 11:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A local upsizer paid $2 million for a small semi in Balmain after the vendor dropped their reserve by $100,000 at auction on Saturday. The two-bedder with stained glass, iron lacework, a leafy courtyard and upstairs balcony at 15 Gladstone Street had clear views across the city, including the Sydney Harbour Bridge. The property was one of 564 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group had recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 53 per cent from 311 reported results throughout the week, while 93 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Three parties registered to bid on the Federation-era property with a $2 million guide. All were young couples or families, but only one made an offer, opening the auction at $1.9 million.



The next bid was a vendor bid of $2 million, then the opening bidder asked the auctioneer if they could match the vendor bid. This was accepted. Related Article Auctions First home buyers pay $2.04m for renovated Sydney house as market drops The vendor then agreed to adjust their reserve of $2.1 million, and it sold under the hammer for $2 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Selling agent Richard Baini of Richard Matthews Real Estate said the street was full of onlookers: “The crowd was easily over 100 people.”



“There’s a lot more buyer confidence coming back into the market,” Baini said. “They’ve gone and reassessed their financial position with their brokers and banks, and the buyers are back out looking and buying again.” The vendor is moving out of Sydney. The house last traded for $463,000 in 1999, records show. In Dulwich Hill, a “shell” of a property in dire need of renovation sold for $840,000. The two-bedroom, top-floor apartment at 8/401 Marrickville Road drew four registrations. Three took part, and all were first home buyers.



Related Article Auctions ‘The worst I have seen it’: Mid-century apartment sells for $785,000 as buyers evaporate Bidding opened at $750,000 and climbed in $10,000 rises, quickly surpassing the $790,000 guide and reserve. Once bidding reached $800,000, two buyers traded alternating bids of $1000 and $5000 until it sold under the hammer for $840,000. Richardson & Wrench’s Aris Dendrinos noted uncertainty in the market. “It’s not a market of fear. It’s a market of uncertainty, and it’s the worst market because when people are fearful, they act. When they’re uncertain, they don’t act,” he said.



“People can panic buy, and people can panic sell because they’re fearful. They want to get their money. They want to move on and do the next thing. But when they’re uncertain, they don’t do much.” The deceased estate last traded for $158,000 in 1994, records show.

World.title: Is London finally winning its mobile phone theft war?
World.content:
WorldEuropeCrime Is London finally winning its mobile phone theft war? David Crowe July 27, 2026 — 11:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Police are claiming progress in tackling mobile phone theft across the capital after years of worsening headlines about thieves who brazenly snatch devices from residents and tourists on the street. A stronger police presence is being named as a key factor in halving the number of phone thefts in the West End over the past year – and many visitors to the centre of the city appear to be more relaxed about the risks. But the new figures show that there are still thousands of thefts from individuals across the city each week, despite years of concern about gangs shipping stolen phones in bulk to markets in destinations ranging from Algeria to China. “The figures are clear: London is safe and getting safer each year,” said the Metropolitan Police Commissioner, Mark Rowley.



Related Article Crime Aussie tourists beware as a mobile phone theft epidemic hits London “Neighbourhood policing is the foundation of what we do – and neighbourhood crime is down 14 per cent across the capital.” The tougher action meant there were 35,000 fewer offences across a range of neighbourhood crimes over the year to the end of June, including mobile phone theft. This means the number of offences each year fell from 250,000 to 215,000. The biggest reduction in neighbourhood crime – 36 per cent – was recorded in Westminster, the area that includes tourist highlights such as Big Ben, the major theatres, Piccadilly and Buckingham Palace.



London became infamous for mobile phone theft over the past few years after videos spread on social media showing young men in black balaclavas, often on e-bikes, grabbing phones from victims on the street. In one case, a victim tracked their stolen iPhone using the “Find My iPhone” feature and located the device in a warehouse near Heathrow Airport. When police gained entry to the warehouse to look for the stolen property, they found it in a box with another 894 phones due to be shipped to China. That led to the arrest of Amir Muhammad Khadikhel and Ismat Miakhel in north-east London last September on suspicion of handling about 2000 stolen phones. The two men, along with an accomplice, pleaded guilty in April. Police said their network trafficked up to 40,000 stolen phones to China over two years. Related Article Travel tips My phone was stolen while visiting London. Here’s how I coped



In a separate case, Algerian national Adel Kerari was convicted of six counts of robbery after he and fellow gang members robbed, assaulted and stabbed victims at stations on the London Underground. He targeted lone passengers to steal their phones and wallets. Kerari was sentenced last month to three years and nine months in prison after prosecutors appealed a lighter sentence he received last year. The impact on victims can be far greater than the loss of the device. In November 2024, four men with ties to Algeria were convicted of smuggling stolen phones out of the UK. They were also found to have used phones to gain access to bank and cryptocurrency accounts, stealing £5.1 million ($9.7 million). The police have been publicising their new methods to disrupt thieves, such as facial recognition cameras and overhead drones that can track offenders on their bikes. “We have momentum which we’re not going to give up on,” Rowley told the BBC last week, when the annual figures were released.



When The Sunday Times investigated mobile phone theft in March last year, it estimated that 28 per cent of the devices were shipped to Algeria, while 20 per cent went to China and 7 per cent to Hong Kong. A phone reported stolen in Britain may still be used in China on networks that do not subscribe to global blocking agreements, and it may have a higher value because it could be used to circumvent Chinese government network controls. London Mayor Sadiq Khan claimed credit for some of the improvement by citing a decision funded by City Hall to set up a “command cell” in the West End to identify thieves and prevent robberies. “In the West End alone, we have seen phone thefts halved and 14,000 fewer neighbourhood crimes, following a doubling of officers on patrol in the heart of the capital,” he said.



Travellers and residents appear relaxed about the risk of theft on the streets of the capital, with many walking while looking at their phones in areas known for theft, such as Oxford Street, Chelsea, and Westminster. Pedestrians carry on scrolling on Oxford Street – the worst in London for mobile phone theft. Bloomberg The headlines about phone snatching have not shifted behaviour for some pedestrians on London streets, with many holding their phones out to check for directions or take selfies, even if they are near passing bikes. Crime rates have fallen across England and Wales over the past decade in categories such as homicide, firearms offences and violence against others. Store owners in London, however, have been worried by a long-term rise in shoplifting and increasing threats against retail workers.



Related Article UK politics Inside the UK town Pauline Hanson cannot stand Under pressure from retailers, the government introduced a new standalone criminal offence for assaulting a retail worker, and it removed a £200 threshold for “low-level theft” – a rule that was blamed for making it too easy for shoplifters to go unpunished for multiple thefts as long as each theft was below the threshold. Police recorded 1.6 million theft offences across England and Wales in the year to March, a fall of 8 per cent. “Following a period of increases in shoplifting, there has been a 4 per cent decrease to 507,086 offences,” the Office for National Statistics said when it released new figures last Thursday. World.content:
Travel newsTours Perfect tour for English Premier League tragics Julietta Jameson July 27, 2026 — 11:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If the FIFA World Cup has left you wondering where your next round-ball fix is coming from, G Adventures has an answer. The small-group tour company is launching Away Games, a collection of football-themed itineraries in England that kick off soon. The tours not only tap into that forlorn post-tournament feeling, but also into one of tourism’s fastest-growing sectors. According to UN Tourism, the United Nations’ specialist tourism agency, sports tourism accounts for an estimated 10 per cent of global tourism. Etihad Stadium, the home ground for Manchester City FC. Increasingly, travellers plan holidays around spectator events from Formula 1 and the Olympics to marathons, cycling and football. And sports tourism now extends well beyond buying a ticket, booking a flight and hotel, then flying home after the final whistle.



Tour companies are building itineraries around fans’ desire to experience the culture surrounding the game, from the pubs supporters frequent to the neighbourhoods that have shaped famous clubs, and local rituals visitors rarely discover on their own. 



Tottenham’s itinerary includes VIP halfway-line seating, premium dining, a behind-the-scenes tour of the stadium’s retractable pitch and time exploring North London’s football pubs and street food. (Tottenham Hotspur: London, Inside the Game, November 20-24, 2026, from $3749 a person.) Arsenal supporters receive guaranteed Club Level seating at Emirates Stadium, alongside a stadium tour, food market visit and a grassroots National League fixture. (Arsenal FC: The Pride of North London, October 9-13, 2026, from $4599 a person.) While each departure is led by a guide who’s a football fan, free time allows travellers to explore beyond the stadium precincts. Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London. The concept is a natural extension for a company that has built its reputation on community-based tourism. Established in 1990 by entrepreneur Bruce Poon Tip, G Adventures aims to connect travellers with local people, cultures, landscapes and wildlife while supporting the communities they visit. It also backs more than 150 community tourism projects through its non-profit partner, Planeterra, and other programs.



In keeping with that philosophy, Away Games uses football as a gateway to the destination rather than treating it as a standalone attraction. Related Article Travel tips Partner loves sport, but you don’t? Five great destinations you can both enjoy Australians are no strangers to sports tourism. Specialist agencies such as Sportsnet Holidays, Events Travel, Australian Sports Tours, Premium Sport Tours and Travel & Sports Australia (TASA) package tickets, accommodation and hospitality for everything from Formula One and the AFL Grand Final to overseas golf, tennis and football events. UN Tourism says destinations are increasingly using sporting events to showcase local culture and create more authentic visitor experiences. G Adventures is responding to the appeal that extends beyond the stadium. Travellers want to better understand the places and communities that give rise to the sporting passions they’re there to witness. Football, that is, the round-ball version we call soccer, the world’s most popular game, is a natural fit.



“Away Games is about much more than watching a match,” says Yves Marceau, the company’s vice-president of product. “It’s about belonging and being part of something bigger. It’s about singing with locals in supporter pubs, celebrating a last-minute goal with fellow travellers, and experiencing a destination through the lens of its football culture.” See gadventures.com

World.title: Adam Doueihi will be at Wests Tigers training on Tuesday after ‘positive’ peace talks
World.content:
Adam Doueihi will report for training on Tuesday after peace talks with the Wests Tigers lasted about an hour on Monday morning.

Doueihi arrived with manager Isaac Moses at the Tigers’ Concord HQ just before 9am, and spent time with coach Benji Marshall, CEO Shaun Mielekamp and football manager Pat Richards.

Adam Doueihi leaves Wests Tigers headquarters on Monday. Nine

There were fears Doueihi had played his last game for the Tigers after a fall-out with Marshall last Thursday, which led to him taking time out from the game. He missed Saturday’s 56-10 loss to Canberra.

Questions were asked about how he could walk back into the side for Sunday’s clash with Parramatta, if he should return via NSW Cup, or would even make himself available at all.

World.title: Victorian premier to fight for job as MPs plan leadership spill
World.content:
Victorian premier to fight for job as MPs plan leadership spill

Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan has insisted she will fight for the leadership of the state Labor Party, despite several of her colleagues telling her she no longer has the confidence of caucus.

World.title: Jacinta Allan leadership threat LIVE updates: Ben Carroll tells premier he will contest the leadership as delegation urges her to stand down
World.content:
Deputy Premier Ben Carroll has advised the premier that he intends to be a candidate for leadership in the event of a spill.

A group of ministers and MPs met with Jacinta Allan this morning and urged her to stand down.

Deputy Premier Ben Carroll. Ruby Alexander

Following that meeting, they met with Carroll and urged him to step forward as a contender.

Carroll then advised the premier that he would do so in the event of a spill, likely to unfold at a caucus meeting on Tuesday.

Among those in the delegation were ministers Anthony Carbines, Gabrielle Williams, Ingrid Stitt, Lizzie Blandthorn, Luba Grigorovitch, Colin Brooks, and factional conveners Ella George and Mat Hilakari.

Three Labor sources confirmed the meeting to The Age.

One MP said the delegation included “cross factional ministers and MPs” and they had gone to see the premier “to let her know that she has lost the majority of support in caucus and have urged the premier to stand down”.

Allan was defiant, telling MPs she has no intention to stand down.

One Labor source said the “numbers are overwhelming”.

Cabinet was scheduled to meet at 11am but will be severely compromised given some attendees were part of the delegation.

Ministers have refused to resign their posts.

World.title: I cried when the council cut down my tree. I did not see that coming
World.content:
NationalCity life Opinion I cried when the council cut down my tree. I did not see that coming Melissa Hoyer Writer July 27, 2026 — 11:45am

July 27, 2026 — 11:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For 27 years, a huge dense-canopied Harpephyllum caffrum, a South African Wild Plum (or a tree with a ridiculous number of leaves that always landed in my backyard), stood on the pavement outside my house. The stump of the tree that stood outside Melissa Hoyer’s house It was, by any measure, just a very, very old and elegant tree, owned by the city long before I arrived, so technically it’s not mine. It gave my house shade, a canopy and some dappled ambience. Turns out it was also propping up something I hadn’t clocked until now: a sense of home. I want to be clear that I did not think of this tree often. I did not hug it. I did not know its Latin name until council’s notice arrived and informed me of it, almost as an afterthought, the way you may meet a friend’s family at their funeral.



A few weeks ago, council decided that my tree was in poor health and, this week, the tree-people took a buzzy chainsaw to it. What’s left is a stump the size of a small car, awaiting its own removal. Soon there’ll be a large hole where a tree used to be. I didn’t expect to feel much about this at all, but I was wrong. Related Article Opinion

Life in the ’burbs Despite what you’ve heard, my suburb’s definitely not grand but at least the bar brawls are gone Diana Simmonds Journalist and writer I’ve been surprisingly, almost embarrassingly, emotional about a piece of municipal vegetation, which made me wonder what exactly I was mourning – because it clearly wasn’t just the tree. Here’s the thing about living somewhere for nearly three decades: you stop seeing the furniture. Not the furniture inside – the furniture of your life outside the front door. The tree wasn’t something I admired each morning like a tourist snapping a photo. It was just there, the way your own reflection is just there. It filtered the light through my windows and into my backyard at a particular hour. It made a particular sound when the wind picked up. I walked past it and its gigantic root system thousands of times without registering it every time. Possums loved it. Birds chirped from it, and they made it their home too. You don’t notice the things that are most obvious in your life until they’re gone. My eye keeps going up to where the canopy was and finding brilliant blue sky instead, which is its own small, repeated joy and a jolt. My brain is expecting one thing and getting another, several times a day, apparently indefinitely.



Scout, my dog, went out to the backyard and just kept barking and barking at the blue sky where my tree used to be. What was that about? I think even little Scout was feeling the loss, a bit like a member of the family having departed. Then there’s the small matter of nobody asking me. I understand councils have arborists and liability concerns and a job to do. But there’s something particular about having a piece of your daily landscape removed by a decision made entirely without you, on a timeline entirely without you, for reasons you’re simply informed of just days before the fact. Even Scout the dog is missing the tree (pictured here with her owner, Melissa Hoyer). It’s not that I think I should’ve had a vote – who am I to argue with an arborist? It’s that grief plus powerlessness is a far more potent cocktail than grief alone. I’m aware this is, in the scheme of life, a very, very minor tragedy. Nobody is sending casseroles or hosting a celebration of life for a stump. Nobody should. I am not asking for sympathy cards or flowers addressed to a tree.



But I’d argue that the loss of a tree that has quietly witnessed 27 years of your life – the comings, the at times sad goings, the baby, the teenager, the BBQs, the excited version of you that moved in and every kooky version since – is not nothing. It’s a legitimate loss, even if the only appropriate way to grieve it is privately and slightly self-consciously, while explaining to bemused friends and family that yes, I am fine at the moment. I’m just very sad about a tree. I’m told the stump goes next week. I’m also told a Weeping Lilly Pilly (Waterhousea floribunda) will be planted in its place. It’s a native evergreen that will, eventually, grow to provide a similar canopy. I will, presumably, not live long enough to sit under its major shade myself. But that’ll be a separate piece of grief for another day.



Melissa Hoyer is a writer and social commentator. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Inner west local gets a $100,000 discount on $2 million semi
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Inner west local gets a $100,000 discount on $2 million semi Carmen Forward July 27, 2026 — 11:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A local upsizer paid $2 million for a small semi in Balmain after the vendor dropped their reserve by $100,000 at auction on Saturday. The two-bedder with stained glass, iron lacework, a leafy courtyard and upstairs balcony at 15 Gladstone Street had clear views across the city, including the Sydney Harbour Bridge. The property was one of 564 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain Group had recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 53 per cent from 311 reported results throughout the week, while 93 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Three parties registered to bid on the Federation-era property with a $2 million guide. All were young couples or families, but only one made an offer, opening the auction at $1.9 million.



The next bid was a vendor bid of $2 million, then the opening bidder asked the auctioneer if they could match the vendor bid. This was accepted. Related Article Auctions First home buyers pay $2.04m for renovated Sydney house as market drops The vendor then agreed to adjust their reserve of $2.1 million, and it sold under the hammer for $2 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Selling agent Richard Baini of Richard Matthews Real Estate said the street was full of onlookers: “The crowd was easily over 100 people.”



“There’s a lot more buyer confidence coming back into the market,” Baini said. “They’ve gone and reassessed their financial position with their brokers and banks, and the buyers are back out looking and buying again.” The vendor is moving out of Sydney. The house last traded for $463,000 in 1999, records show. In Dulwich Hill, a “shell” of a property in dire need of renovation sold for $840,000. The two-bedroom, top-floor apartment at 8/401 Marrickville Road drew four registrations. Three took part, and all were first home buyers.



Related Article Auctions ‘The worst I have seen it’: Mid-century apartment sells for $785,000 as buyers evaporate Bidding opened at $750,000 and climbed in $10,000 rises, quickly surpassing the $790,000 guide and reserve. Once bidding reached $800,000, two buyers traded alternating bids of $1000 and $5000 until it sold under the hammer for $840,000. Richardson & Wrench’s Aris Dendrinos noted uncertainty in the market. “It’s not a market of fear. It’s a market of uncertainty, and it’s the worst market because when people are fearful, they act. When they’re uncertain, they don’t act,” he said.



“People can panic buy, and people can panic sell because they’re fearful. They want to get their money. They want to move on and do the next thing. But when they’re uncertain, they don’t do much.” The deceased estate last traded for $158,000 in 1994, records show.
