While each departure is led by a guide who’s a football fan, free time allows travellers to explore beyond the stadium precincts. Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London. The concept is a natural extension for a company that has built its reputation on community-based tourism. Established in 1990 by entrepreneur Bruce Poon Tip, G Adventures aims to connect travellers with local people, cultures, landscapes and wildlife while supporting the communities they visit. It also backs more than 150 community tourism projects through its non-profit partner, Planeterra, and other programs.



In keeping with that philosophy, Away Games uses football as a gateway to the destination rather than treating it as a standalone attraction. Related Article Travel tips Partner loves sport, but you don’t? Five great destinations you can both enjoy Australians are no strangers to sports tourism. Specialist agencies such as Sportsnet Holidays, Events Travel, Australian Sports Tours, Premium Sport Tours and Travel & Sports Australia (TASA) package tickets, accommodation and hospitality for everything from Formula One and the AFL Grand Final to overseas golf, tennis and football events. UN Tourism says destinations are increasingly using sporting events to showcase local culture and create more authentic visitor experiences. G Adventures is responding to the appeal that extends beyond the stadium. Travellers want to better understand the places and communities that give rise to the sporting passions they’re there to witness. Football, that is, the round-ball version we call soccer, the world’s most popular game, is a natural fit.



“Away Games is about much more than watching a match,” says Yves Marceau, the company’s vice-president of product. “It’s about belonging and being part of something bigger. It’s about singing with locals in supporter pubs, celebrating a last-minute goal with fellow travellers, and experiencing a destination through the lens of its football culture.” See gadventures.com

World.title: Dame Noeline Taurua goes slightly rogue to get critical Comm Games win
World.content:
Knowing the implications of what a loss to Jamaica in pool play at the Commonwealth Games could have meant, Silver Ferns' coach Dame Noeline Taurua didn't mind going a little off-script on Monday morning.

The Silver Ferns passed their first major test of the Glasgow Games by beating Jamaica 53-48, which could prove critical in their path to a potential gold medal match.

A loss would have put the Silver Ferns on course for a semi-final against world number one Australia, with the Diamonds expected to top their pool in the netball programme.

The heavyweights from Pool B were both desperate to avoid a semi-final meeting with Australia, who beat England by 19 goals in the opposite group on Sunday night in a statement performance.

Jamaica beat the Silver Ferns twice at the 2023 Netball World Cup to deny them a medal in Cape Town, and Taurua said Monday's win over the Sunshine Girls was huge for their confidence.

"Knowing that we are progressing in the right direction. It was tough out there, defensively we knew that they were going to be strong. We had a bit of a quiver on the way but to come out with the win is awesome," Taurua said.

To win gold in Glasgow, the Silver Ferns will have to play seven matches in just nine days.

Taurua said given the rigours of that schedule, every player will need to have their loads managed and be given a break at some point.

"With all of them, we know what our loads are, which is why with our first game [against Scotland] nearly everybody got on. I went a bit rogue today in regards to our loads to get that win but thank goodness we've got the day off tomorrow."

Taurua had intended to give Catherine Hall, who is coming back from foot surgery, some time on court today, but with Burger and Kelly Jackson combining well, she resisted putting the exciting defender on court.

Silver Fern Mila Reuelu-Buchanan. Jayne Russell / Photosport

"She will feature when the time is right, I have no issue about her being on but I also know that we've got to make sure we put her in a good position and in an environment that we know she'll thrive.

"Putting her out there today under such huge pressure, sometimes it's a balancing act, but it's also difficult when you've got Karin and also Kelly turning over a lot of ball."

Taurua started Kate Heffernan at centre, Maddy Gordon at wing attack, and sprung a bit of a surprise by starting Mila Reuelu-Buchanan in the unfamiliar position of wing defence.

Kimiora Poi came into wing attack after half-time with Gordon going to the bench.

Gordon came into centre for the final quarter, with Kate Heffernan going to the bench with the game still on the line.

"It's a fine balancing act but how we keep the stability in our team, but also know we've got a few more days of games, so we had that in our mind but I thought with giving Maddy that time off court and to introduce fresh legs, I thought worked really well."

Reuelu-Buchanan usually plays centre/wing attack but Taurua said her personality suited the doggedness needed at wing defence.

"She's a grafter, she's got the voice, she's like a halfback you know coming out of the scrum, she always chats... I thought she played well right through so she warranted to stay out there."

Captain Karin Burger, who is a goal defence-wing defence slide, said Reuelu-Buchanan had embraced the challenge.

"She's done such an amazing job learning that position, she's so eager, she's got the mongrel, she's ruthless when she goes out there and just her energy that she brings, she is so impressive and the versatility she brings to this team is amazing," Burger said.

Karin Burger led the defensive end. Simon Stacpoole / Photosport

Taurua was pleased with the way the Silver Ferns withstood Jamaica's defensive line, which is widely recognised as the strongest in the world.

Grace Nweke put up 47 of New Zealand's goals.

Goal attack Georgia Heffernan was playing Jamaica for the first time, and while she only put up six goals, she was responsible for a lot of goals assists.

"We always knew that Jamaica's defence is a power house, so we were expecting that and really pleased by some of our players. I mean Georgia has never played Jamaica so it's a new experience for her, and also the change-up of Kimiora also going in, just giving ourselves some fresh legs and getting a bit of speed."

Captain Karin Burger said they had done a lot of work leading into the game, aware that a win could set them up well for the tournament.

"Even though we had six months of prep for all the teams we are coming up against, we had a big focus on Jamaica, knowing that they were in their pool. We want to finish at the top," Burger said.

World.title: Sinkhole appears in Auckland street damaged in 2023's floods
World.content:
A large sinkhole has opened up on a street in Auckland's St Mary's Bay.

The area, in a dip in the road on Hackett Street, was badly damaged in the 2023 Auckland anniversary weekend floods and has been covered by a steel plate since then.

Local residents say the hole emerged on Thursday, after which some reported losing water for several hours.

The hole is approximately five metres long, three metres wide and over a metre deep in parts.

Nick Monro

A steady stream of water can be seen running through the hole beneath the street.

Tony Skelton. Nick Monro

St Mary's Bay man Tony Skelton said he was concerned about aging infrastructure that lied beneath the hole.

"All the infrastructure here is 126 year-old clay pipes," he said.

"If there is further damage, that could undermine our properties and could cause considerable problems."

He was particularly concerned about what would happen after the next downpour.

"The next heavy rain event, we don't know what's going to happen."

Nick Monro

Water contractors were at the site on Monday. Hackett Street was closed to traffic.

World.title: Wild deer increasingly encroaching on farms, moving closer to urban areas, hunter says
World.content:
Wild deer are spreading closer to urban areas as they chew through protected pockets of native bush, crops and acres of pine trees.

Kerry Flanders shoots deer for farmers in parts of Hawke's Bay at night using thermal imaging to spot them and says there are a lot more deer migrating from native forests and bush onto farmland - and many people don't realise it's happening.

This follows research from the University of Canterbury showing rising deer numbers are driving a slow decline in native forests as they hollow out forests that support ecosystems.

The paper 'Deer in the Headlights: Sleepwalking Our Way to a Native Forest Catastrophe' warns of a slowly developing crisis that's often hard to see.

It says deer are stripping younger trees and plants sheltered under the canopy of older trees and recommends an urgent national deer management strategy to better control the pests.

Supplied

Flanders says it's no surprise that deer numbers are getting out of control as he sees large numbers where he shoots in the Puketapu and Puketitri areas.

"On a day you might go into a farm and have a look and see one or no deer at all. But later on at night you might see fifty or sixty when it's dark in the same place where during the day you see none."

Supplied

Flanders says the deer wander wherever they want - decimating areas of native trees and plants as well as crops and young pine forests.

He says some young pine forests have needed replanting, as wild deer have eaten them. And fences are no barrier - even the allegedly pest proof ones.

"The deer just go wherever they want to. They even jump deer fences as well. Quite often I've seen it. I'm chasing them and they jump straight over the top of a deer fence! There you go - how did that happen? But it does."

World.title: High-profile sportsperson bitten by police dog, faces series of charges
World.content:
A person accompanying a high profile sportsperson into court has shoved a journalist outside the courtroom.

The man was appearing in Wellington District Court on charges including resisting police in an incident where the man was bitten by a police dog.

He also faces counts of assault with intent to injure, injuring a police dog, and causing loss by deception.

These stem from an incident in Rongotai in the early hours of Saturday morning.

The incident stemmed from an allegedly unpaid taxi fare.

Outside court on Monday morning, a group of reporters and camerapeople were taking pictures of the man as he entered.

A woman who appeared to be with the sportsperson stepped towards media demanding they stop taking pictures.

The man repeatedly asked her to stop interceding.

When a reporter asked the man if he had anything to say, the woman told her to "piss off" before appearing to try bat away the reporter's phone which was being used to record, hitting the journalist in the face.

The reporter did not appear to be injured.

The man was granted interim name suppression and remanded on bail. He will next appear in court on 17 August.

Defence lawyer Phil Mitchell asked for suppression on the grounds of presumption of innocence and that publishing his client's identity could impact his right to a fair trial.

Mitchell said publicly naming the man would also heavily impact his "business interests". Mitchell said the man had "one occupation" which would be affected by his name being published.

Mitchell also opposed applications from the media to take photos inside the court room, saying they had been able to photograph him outside and he felt they would have what they needed.

The police said in a statement neither the victim nor police dog required attention for any injuries.

World.title: PNG's Morea Baru claims Pacific Islands' first medal at Glasgow Commonwealth Games
World.content:
Papua New Guinea weightlifter Morea Baru is the first Pacific Island athlete at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow to win a medal.

The 36-year-old lifted a total of 282 kilogram in the men's 65kg category - 125kg in the snatch and 157kg in the clean-and-jerk.

It is his fourth Commonwealth Games medal and second bronze, with two silvers won in previous Games.

Morea Baru with his bronze medal at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games. Facebook / Team PNG

India's Raja Muthupandi won silver with a total lift of 286kg, while Malaysia's Aznil Biden took his third straight gold, winning with a total of 299kg.

Samoa's Felevaa Tafi was seventh with a total of 238kg, Kiribati's Kaimauri Erati eighth on 215kg, and Fiji's Apakuki Tabuwaiwai Wakanibua was ninth, also with a total lift of 215kg.

In boxing, Fiji's lone female rep Jasmine Daunakamakama scored two knockdowns and the unanimous points decision against Ghana's Adelaide Dede Djabatey in the Round of 16 of the women's 57kg.

The win secures her a quarterfinal spot.

Bowls

Tonga lost 1-0 to Malta in the tie-break after the two teams were tied at the end of the two sets in their women's pair clash.

The Tonga pair of Paris Baker and Milika Nathan won the first set 10-0 but went down 6-4 to Malta in the second set, forcing the tie-break , which they lost in the end.

They then lost 2-0 to Namibia, giving the game away in close sets, going down 4-3 in set one and 4-2 in the second set.

Niue, Cook Islands and Fiji also lost their pool matches.

Niue lost 2-0 to Australia, scoring just one point in the first set as the Aussies dominated 11-1 and 16-0. They also lost to the Isle of Man team 2-0.

Cook Islands were beaten 2-0 by Jersey in their clash, while Fiji also lost 2-0 to New Zealand.

Norfolk Islands pair Ellie Dixon and Christine Jones had a good win over Falkland Islands, winning the two sets 7-3 and 6-4 to claim victory in the end.

In the men's singles, Norfolk Islands Mitchell Graham beat Niue's Frederick Tafatu, 8-1, 9-3 over two sets in their clash, while Cook Islands Royden Aperau also lost by the same margin to Australia's Aaron Wilson.

Fiji's Rajnesh Prasad, who had three previous wins, could not match up with Pakistan's Mohammed Ayub Qureshi, losing 2-0 in a tight contest.

Tonga's Liam Hill also had a tough one against Singapore's Harriman Yuen, losing 2-0, with a tight 6-5 result in the second set of that clash.

Netball

The Tongan Tala had another tough outing on the court, going down to South Africa 96-42.

South Africa dominated the game, winning all the four quarters 26-15, 25-8, 21-12 and 24-7.

That is the second loss they have suffered, following their early result against Australia.

New Zealand defeated Jamaica 53-48 while Australia beat England 66-47.

Basketball

Tough competition for the Pacific Island teams.

The Fiji women's team lost 21-8 to Uganda and 17-15 to Jamaica.

PNG is also competing in the competition.

Meanwhile, PNG Olympic Committee president Mrs. Emma Waiwai OL said the women's basketball team is doing the country proud.

She said the team is the first to represent the country in the Team Sports category after 16 years.

She was on hand in Glasgow to present the team with new uniforms.

Boxing

Kiribati's Eriu Temakau lost his Round of 16 fight after the referee stopped the bout in the first round of the men's 55kg division against Ghana's Amadu Mohammed.

There were losses also for Niue's Phoenix Gataua and Kalani Anitelea-Launiu, Solomon Islands Lio Dicks and Max Makana, Jone Duvale of Fiji, Samoa's Dee Iaopo and Danieele Domonique Holland plus the PNG pair of Bid Michael Inoino and James Paul.

Swimming

Fiji's Reuben Taylor and Tonga's Finau Ohuafi won their heats in the 50m freestyle but failed to make the next round.

Cook Islands Lanihei Connelly qualified for the semis of the women's 100m breaststroke but did not progress to the final.

In the women's 100m freestyle semifinal Fiji's Anahira McCutcheon finished 6th in 55.80s, while teammate Samuel Yalimaiwai made the semi's of the 50m breaststroke but failed to progress.

Fiji's David Young finished 6th in the men's 50m freestyle.

Fiji Swimming said McCutcheon swam in a time of 55.78s, breaking the Fiji record.

Nineteen-year-old Younger clocked a personal best time in the 50m Breaststroke, clocking a time of 29.03s, while Yalimaiwai clocked 28.11s, breaking the Fiji record and earning his place in the semifinals.

PNG Swimming said their teams performed strongly in the individual events and the mixed 4 x 100m Freestyle Relay.

In the men's 50m Freestyle, Josh Tarere recorded a season's best time of 24.40s, while Thomas Chen also posted a season's best of 25.04s.

Joanna Chen swam her best time of 1:12.39s in the women's 100m Backstroke, while Roxanne Kirarock clocked 1:25.82s in the women's 100m Breaststroke.

"All four swimmers finished within striking distance of their personal best times, highlighting their consistency and preparation," PNG Swimming said of the performances.

The mixed 4 x 100m Freestyle Relay team recorded a time of 3:57.71s.

Competition continues throughout the week, with the Games set to close on 4 August.

As of 10:30am (NZ time), Australia continued to lead the medal tally with 17 gold, nine silver and 13 bronze.

England are second with four gold, nine silver and six bronze, while New Zealand is ninth with three silver and two bronze.

PNG is the only Pacific Island country on the medal tally with one bronze.

Ahtletics

The athletics programme gets underway Monday night, with several Pacific athletes in action.

Nauru, PNG, Tuvalu, Kiribati, Fiji and Samoa will be represented when the 100 metres heats get underway.

The Papua New Guinean trio of Pais Wisil, Johnny Bai and Tovetuna Tuna will feature in the men's 100m heats.

World.title: Lifting Pharmac's budget will make healthcare system more efficient  - ACT
World.content:
ACT leader David Seymour is promising no existing services would be cut under its election policy to shift the balance of health funding towards medicines.

And he says Pharmac won't stop being "hard-ass negotiators" either.

On Sunday, ACT announced a pledge to lift Pharmac's budget to 12 percent of total health spend by 2033. It's currently 4.9 percent.

Speaking to Midday Report, Seymour acknowledged that would mean other areas of healthcare would miss out but said "nothing that currently exists will be cut".

David Seymour discusses new ACT Pharmac policy Midday Report Download MP3 7m

He said the shift would bring about a more efficient and effective healthcare system.

Seymour pointed to Pharmac's funding of Trikafta for cystic fibrosis, saying lung transplants, which used to be common, were now "nearly unheard of".

"People have speculated if we were to fund... WeGovy and the like, then we would see, over a decade, less obesity, less diabetes, less kidney disease, less dialysis, less kidney transplants. All of that saves money."

Seymour said Pharmac deserved a share of the continued increase in health spending.

"Pharmac has been punished because they are so tough on their budget. The rest of the healthcare system doesn't do that, and they keep getting these increases.

"If people are worried, oh, Pharmac will will take their foot off the throttle. When they were given $604 million extra after the 2024 Budget, they didn't stop being hard-ass negotiators, I can assure you."

In the 2026 Budget, the health system received a $1.5 billion funding uplift, but Pharmac got just $13.5m.

ACT's costings projected that overall health spending would be between $33.4b and $36.6b in 2027/28. Under its policy, that would put the medicines budget between $2b and $2.2b.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Pacific hope for medals in bowls and boxing
World.content:
There is hope that the Pacific Island contingent at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow will be able to win medals in bowling and boxing.

Top Fijii men's singles player Rajnesh Parasad is the best bet for a medal in the bowls, following his early three round wins so far.

Prasad claimed his first win on Friday morning, when he beat England's top bowler Sam Tolchard in a tie-break, after the two players were tied 1-1 at the end of two sets.

Tolchard won the prestigious World Singles Champion of Champions title in November 2022 in New Zealand, and claimed the top title at the Bowls World Cup in November 2025.

Prasad then defeated Jamaica's Robert Simpson 2-0 in clean sets in his second game. He won 12-1 in the first and 6-5 in the second to wrap the game up.

He also claimed his third win on Sunday morning, taking the tie-break against Scotland's Jason Banks, after the duo had ended the game tied with a set each to their names.

In boxing, male boxers Kiribati's Eriu Temakau won his men's 55kg bout in a split-points decisions against Guernsey's Thomas Teers.

Papua New Guinea's James Paul also got through his first fight, winning a points decision as well over Bahrains Rashield Williams.

Tonga's Josh Tonga is the third Pasifika boxer to win his first bout, defeating Trinidad and Tobago's Jeremiah Thomas in the men's 80kg division.

The three Pasifika boxers will feature in the Round of 16.

Tonga told the media after his win he was excited and looks forward to his next bout.

"Amazing," he said.

"Words can't explain, the atmosphere is insane, and our team is behind me, coaches, families and friends watching as well, it's incredible.

"The game plan was to keep my distance, take little wee steps, keeping it simple in general."

In other results:

Bowls - Women's Pairs

Norfolk Islands pair of Ellie Dixon and Christie Jones beat Cook Islands duo Fa'amanatu Vasie Ngatoko-Oila and Teokotai Rahui Jim 2-0, winning 8-3 and 10-1 in both sets.

Cook Islands returned strong in the second game of the weekend, when they defeated Falkland Islands 2-0, winning 8-2 and 8-2 in the two sets.

Norfolk Islands also did the same when they beat the Jersey pair 2-0 in their clash, winning 7-1 and 7-2..

Niue's Catherine Papani and Christine Ioane lost 2-0 to the Northern Ireland pair of Chloe Wilson and Shauna O'Neill. Northern Ireland won both sets 9-1 and 11-0.

They also lost 2-0 to Singapore, losing both sets 12-4 and 11-2 and went down to Zambia as well.

The Tonga pair of paris Baker and Milika Nathan dropped game two after their first round win, this time losing on tie-break to England. The two teams battled to winning a set each before England took the tie-break 1-0.

They also lost their third game, going down too on tie-break to India in another tight game.

Fijian pair Litia Tikoisuva and Losalini Tukai went down 2-0 to Wales in their second game. Wales won both sets 8-0 amd 5-3.

They did win their next game, beating Kenya 1.5-0.5, claiming the first set 7-2 before the two teams fought to a 5-all draw in the second set.

Bowls - Men's Singles

Royden Aperau of Cook Islands defeated Taylor Greechan of Jersey in a tie-break. Greechan won the first set 5-4 before Aperau claimed the second 9-2 and then won the tie-break 2-0.

He was unlcuky on Sunday morning when he lost 2-0 to Isle of Man's Mark McGreal.

But then came back strong to win 2-0 against Guernsey's Jason Greenslade.

Tonga's Liam Hall won two games after having lost in the first round, defeating Niue's Frederrick Tafatu 2-0. Hall won 11-4 and 8-4 to secure a clean record in that game.

He then defeated South Africa's Wayne Rittmuller in his third game, taking the tie-break in that clash.

Niue's Tafatu, on the other hand, took New Zealand's Shannon McIlroy to the wire in their match before losing on tie-break, after both players had claimed a set each in normal play.

However, he lost to Northern Ireland's Gary Kelly in the tie-break when the two had fought to winning a set each. Kelly took the tie-break 1-0 to claim victory.

Boxing

Fiji's Ben Maukakala lost his first fight and exited the Games after the referee stopped the contest in round two of his men's 65kg clash against New Zealand's Connor Campbell.

Nauru's Vi-J Tebouwa also suffered a loss against Scotland's Leo Church in his opening bout of the same division.

However, not all was good for Vanuatu's Ricksen Nomleas who lost in the first round against England's Ellis Trowbridge and Solomon Islands' Clinton Tetekana, who lost to Bangladesh's Md Rakib Hossan. Both Nomleas and Tetekana were saved by the referee who stpped in to stop their fights.

PNG's Petronella Nokenoke lost by points to England's Lucy Kings-Wheatley in the women's 60kg contest.

On Sunday morning, mixed results were again recorded by Pasifika boxers.

Niue's Phoenix Gataua lost on points to Botswana's Treasure Moremi, followed by loses also to Solomon Islands duo Lio Dicks and Max Makana, Fiji's Jone Davule, Niue's Kalani Anitelea-Launiu and Samoa's Dee Ioapo.

3x3 Basketball

In the women's competition, Fiji defeated Cayman Islands 16-6 in their opening Pool A game but lost 16-14 to Kenya in their second match and Australia 21-3 in their third game.

Tonga beat Scotland 12-10 in their Pool B opener and Papua New Guinea in their third game, but lost 21-8 to New Zealand in their second match.

PNG lost 22-6 to New Zealand and 21-8 to Singapore as well in their Pool G games.

In the men's competition, the Fiji men's team lost 21-16 to Malaysia, 21-13 to England but beat Jamaica 21-13 in their three Pool B games.

The Games media said there was a lovely moment from Tongan sisters Mele Finau and Lesila Finau, who helped the Pacific nation to a surprise 12-10 win over hosts Scotland in their opening match of the Women's 3x3 Basketball, with younger sibling Mele saying:

"She has been my role model for the past 20-something years. It has been great having her by my side and representing our country together. Sibling love can be a bit of tough love at times but it definitely helps on the court."

Swimming

Cook Islands' Carter Makira finished sixth in the heat two of the men's 200 metres individual medley, while Samoa's Christian Toia was eighth in heat three.

Nafanua Hamilton was placed sixth in the women's 200m backstroke heats. She also placed eigth in the women's 200m freestyle.

In the women's 50 metres butterfly heats PNG pair Jhnayali Tokome-Garap and Roxanne Kirarock finished third and fourth respectively in heat one, while teammate Joanna Chew was fourth in heat two, ahead of Vanuatu's Loane Russet, who was at fifth spot.

Fiji's Anahira McCutcheon finished fourth in heat five, while Samoa's Paige Schendelaar-Kemp was eighth in that heat.

PNG's Thomas Chen won heat one of the men's 100m backstroke, while Cook Islands' Carter Makira was third in heat two, ahead of Fiji's Don Younger in fourth.

Heat three saw Fiji's Samuel Yalimaiwai in fifth position while Samoa's Christian Toia was eighth.

In the men's 50m freestyle heats, Tonga's Finau Ohuafi finished first in heat 3 ahead of Vanuatu's Leo Lebot in second, while Fiji's Reuben Taylor won heat 4, which also had PNG's Josh Tarere in fourth and his countryman Thomas Chen in seventh.

Fijian pair David Young and Hansel McCaig both competed in heat 8, with Young finishing second while McCaig was eighth.

The women's 100m backstroke also saw a number of Pasifika swimmers, which included PNG's Joanna Chen claiming third in heat one, Samoa's Hamilton being second in heat two, with Cook Ilands' Mia Laban at fifth.

Netball

Tonga's Tala were thrashed 99-38 by Australia in their opening Pool A clash on Saturday night.

New Zealand defeated Scotland 74-44 in their opener.

The Games continue daily until 2 August.

As of 5pm on Sunday (NZT), Australia led the medal tally with 12 gold, five silver and five bronze.

World.title: Zac Lomax joins PNG Chiefs
World.content:
The Papua New Guinea Chiefs have signed Zac Lomax on a three-year deal from 2028 until the end of the 2030 National Rugby League (NRL) season.

The Chiefs and the former Dragons and Eels player made the announcement during a local rugby league game in Port Moresby over the weekend.

Lomax was in PNG as guest of the Chiefs, arriving in Port Moresby on Friday.

The player is currently with Western Force in the Super Rugby competition, with his contract finishing at the end of the 2027 season.

He joins Jarome Luai, Alex Johnston, Matty Lees and Connor Watson, who have all signed with the Chiefs.

"PNG, thank you very much guys. I just want to say, thank you so much everyone. It's an absolute privilege," Lomax said.

"I am super honoured to be committed to you guys and it's such a great opportunity for all of us boys and everyone that is going to be coming over to the PNG Chiefs.

"We are going to shock the NRL, I am telling you and I can't wait to be apart of it."

World.title: Scottish-blooded Anderson thrilled to win gold in Glasgow instead of Victoria
World.content:
There are a lot of Australians bemoaning the 2026 Commonwealth Games being held in Glasgow instead of regional Victoria, but don't make the mistake of thinking Iona Anderson is one of them.

Anderson emerged as Australia's biggest backstroke star of these Games when undisputed queen Kaylee McKeown withdrew due to glandular fever.

In the 200m, she finished sixth, over two seconds slower than the time she swam at the Australian trials in June.

But in the 100m, she touched first and it could not have been a better place for her first individual gold medal at a senior meet, storming past Canadian veteran and nine-time Commonwealth medallist Kylie Masse.

360 moment for Vicky Belando Nicholson Victoria Belando Nicholson was a baby when she was pulled lifeless from the water after falling from a refugee boat. Now she's a swimming bronze medallist for Australia.

Anderson got it done in the home of her forebears, if not herself, welcoming the controversial late change to the Scottish capital.

"Personally, for me, I think Glasgow's better than Victoria. Sorry," she laughed.

"I love the Scottish. I've got quite a few friends here and obviously my family. So it was great to come back here and do it."

Basically her entire family is from Scotland, Grangemouth on her mum's side and Dumfries and Galloway on her dad's.

Anderson was even named after the small island of Iona off the west coast of the country.

As she took her victory lap, the 20-year-old found her grandma Pam, who had been riding every drop of water displaced by Anderson's furious charge home.

"She was pretty emotional, there wasn't many words," she said.

"She's just really happy and stoked for me. She's always messaging me and always giving me good luck wishes, so that was really special to see her after the race."

The victory was comfortably the tightest of the night by any of the Australian swimmers as the Dolphins took home five more golds and 14 medals in total.

Cam McEvoy completed the full set of 50m freestyle titles by adding Commonwealth gold to Olympic and world titles, baton bearer Tim Hodge enjoyed another moment in the sun with gold in the 100m backstroke S9, Kai Taylor swam a glorious final leg to win the men's 4x200m relay, and Lani Pallister romped home in the women's 1,500m final for her second gold of the Games with the 200m and 800m to come.

Her victory gap of almost 18 seconds was 299 times bigger than Anderson's 0.06 margin over Masse.

A teenage Iona Anderson finished fifth as Kaylee McKeown completed the third leg of her double-double in Paris. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

"I kept my blinders on so I'm really happy I got my hand on the wall," Anderson said.

"I could see some splashes, but to be honest, I closed my eyes at the end and hoped for the best."

The difficulty for Anderson is the spectre of McKeown.

The 25-year-old's double-double – winning the 100m and 200m backstroke at successive Olympics – has raised the bar for how greatness is defined in that discipline for the entire swimming world.

Perhaps that is why Anderson's distant finish in the longer race did not stay with her too long.

"I know I'm capable of more in the 200m but I've got to take away the positive that that's my third best swim ever," she said.

"I really just picked myself up and moved on."

World.title: AFL confirms State of Origin future with Victoria left out of 2027 game
World.content:
The AFL has confirmed the future of State of Origin, with Western Australia to host South Australia in 2027.

South Australia will then host Victoria in 2028 at Adelaide Oval, before Victoria and Western Australia meet again in Perth in 2029.

The State of Origin concept returned to the AFL in 2026, with Victoria beating Western Australia at Perth Stadium.

South Australia and Western Australia last played each other in 1998 at Football Park, with South Australia winning by 36 points in front of 18,000 fans.

No other states have been marked to play in the Origin series, with the Allies concept — Tasmania, New South Wales, Queensland, ACT, and Northern Territory merged together — last used in 1998.

New South Wales joined with ACT and Queensland joined with the Northern Territory in 1993, with Tasmania fielding a standalone team.

"State football is one of the great traditions of our game, and we are pleased to see it continue in 2027 and beyond after the huge success of its return earlier this year which saw more than 58,000 people fill [Perth] Stadium in Perth," AFL boss Andrew Dillon said.



"Origin inspires passion, state pride and draws upon decades of rivalries that are central to the history of our game and our greatest players.



"Locking in the structure for the next three years provides fans, clubs, players and stakeholders certainty on Origin, allowing them to embrace the state rivalry and celebrate our great game."

World.title: 'Don't know how I do it': Pogačar claims fifth Tour de France title
World.content:
Tadej Pogačar confirmed his status as one of cycling's all-time greats after winning a record-equalling fifth Tour de France title in emphatic style.

Daring mountain attacks from deep, multiple stage wins and an ice-cool temperament all helped the 27-year-old Slovenian seal his victory overnight. He joined Belgian Eddy Merckx, Spaniard Miguel Indurain and Frenchmen Jacques Anquetil and Bernard Hinault as the only riders to win five Tours.

"I'm speechless. It's an incredible day, there was an incredible atmosphere," Pogačar said.

"I've ridden seven Tours already, and I've always finished on the podium. You might think this is a fairytale, it's incredible for me too."

After competing strongly in the 21st and exciting final stage in Paris, Pogačar finished 6 minutes, 26 seconds ahead of Belgian rider Remco Evenepoel in the overall standings.

Two-time Tour champion Jonas Vingegaard was Pogačar's main rival heading into the race, but the Dane crashed out on the 15th stage.

"Shame that Jonas and others crashed out of this Tour," Pogačar said.

"I hope we can all fight again next year."

Pogačar's UAE Team Emirates XRG teammate Isaac Del Toro, a 22-year-old Mexican making his Tour debut, was third at 9:42 back from Pogačar, who smiled and held up his hand to signify his wins. His teammates then joined him as they stood proudly on the Champs-Élysées.

"I don't know how I do it," Pogačar said. "I now have to find a new goal to chase. Which goal? Let's just not jump ahead of ourselves, and enjoy this moment."

Pogačar won the Giro d'Italia in 2024 but has not won the Spanish Vuelta, which starts on August 22.

"Will I be at La Vuelta in a few weeks?" he said. "Let's see."

Pogačar won five stages at this year's race to take his impressive tally to 26 overall.

He tried to win overnight too, but victory ultimately went to Dutchman Mathieu van der Poel, who just held off the chasing pack on the home straight for his second stage win at this year's race and fourth overall.

The 88.7km stage looped around Paris and was mostly processional, although less so than in previous years, which were usually entirely flat stages for sprinters and not for the rest of the peloton.

The stage was shortened from 133km, and its starting point in Thoiry, west of the capital, was changed to Paris to reduce pressure on emergency services combating wildfires in the south-west. Some security forces initially mobilised for Paris were redeployed to help response efforts.

For the second straight year the stage featured the hugely popular uphill climb through the Montmartre district, a sharp 1km dash which riders tackled three times before finishing on the Champs-Élysées.

It proved even too much for Pogačar, who could not match Van der Poel's raw power in the closing stages.

Shortly before 6pm local time, Pogačarshook hands at the start line with Evenepoel and Ecuadorian veteran Richard Carapaz, wearing the polka-dot jersey for the best climber.

"I battled hard to win this jersey, it was a great fight," the 33-year-old Carapaz said. "It's the best feeling to win it."

Van der Poel and Dane Mads Pedersen, the green jersey winner as best sprinter, were among the expected contenders for the stage win.

Crowds roared as the riders began the first climb up Rue Lepic in Montmartre, with the famed Sacré-Coeur basilica looming over them.

Pogačar moved ahead after the second ascension of Montmartre, with Van der Poel, Evenepoel and Pedersen alongside him.

Van der Poel attacked on the third and final climb with Pogačar responding well, and the one-day classics rivals surged ahead.

But they were caught with 700 meters left and, after Pogačar faded, the 31-year-old Van der Poel still had work to do.

He got his bike just over the line ahead of Belgian Jasper Philipsen, his Alpecin-Premier Tech teammate, and Pedersen. Pogačar eased up and finished 30th.

"I thought the sprinters would catch us up, so I launched [my attack] from very far away," Van der Poel said. "I gave everything I had left in my legs, and it was just enough."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: From being found lifeless in the water to taking home a medal in the pool
World.content:
When athlete details are listed, Vicky Belando Nicholson's birthplace is "unknown".

We don't know where her journey to Glasgow began, but we do know one of the earliest, terrifying moments when a young baby was pulled lifeless from the Mediterranean after falling off a refugee boat in 2008.

Her sister, Destiny, was aboard. Her birth mother, whose name we also do not know, had died.

Vicky and Destiny were taken to an orphanage in Malta, where they lived for a couple of years.

At the same time, two people just happened to be trying to adopt a child: Australian Ewan and Spanish wife Susana.

"We got a cold call from social services saying: 'We've got two girls here, two and three years old, who are in an orphanage in Malta. Would you be interested in adopting them?'" Ewan told the Sydney Morning Herald this month.

The family lived in Malta, then Spain, before moving to Australia in 2021.

Vicky – who has a condition called fibular hemimelia, meaning she is missing part of the smaller bone in the lower leg – had every reason in the world to never want to see water again.

Belando Nicholson was sixth at the turn and stormed home. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

On Sunday night in Glasgow, she won Commonwealth Games bronze in the women's 100m backstroke S9 with a frankly stunning swim, coming from sixth at the turn to win her first bit of major jewellery.

"It's a bit of a 360 moment," she said.

"When I first started swimming, I was always scared of the water and now to be a bronze medallist for the Commonwealth Games is just absolutely amazing and hopefully there's more to come.

"Coming into this event I wasn't ranked high enough, but I ended up coming third, so anything can happen. Just believe."

To make the moment all the more special, she was joined on her first podium in her first final at her first meet with the Australian team, by her 16-year-old bestie, silver medallist Gemma Sellick.

Besties bound by brilliance. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

"I'm so proud of her," Sellick said.

"I know we've both worked so hard for this and it makes the moment feel even better knowing I can share it with Vicky and very grateful that we got to share our first together."

The moment was almost too perfect to wish for.

"This was not even a thought I had, I was not expecting this at all," Belando Nicholson said.

"To do it with my best friend is actually insane."

For a young woman who has had so much focus on her remarkable history, this feels like the beginning of a spectacular future.

World.title: Luke Bateman earned $400K a year and gambled away every cent
World.content:
During his darkest chapter, things would go missing from Luke Bateman's apartment.

"My partner would come home from work and be like, 'Where's this?'" the former NRL player-turned-fantasy writer tells Australian Story.

"I would've taken it to Cash Converters and sold it for cash so I could go and gamble."

Luke Bateman says in the elite sporting environment gambling was "like breathing". (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

It was 2019, and Bateman was at the height of a debilitating gambling addiction so severe he couldn't afford to feed himself. He was a professional NRL player with the Canberra Raiders at the time, earning $400,000 a year.

"I was so broke … I couldn't pay for anything. I couldn't buy groceries," Bateman says.

"My gambling slowly progressed [until] it consumed my life. Every single thing I did revolved around that gambling app on my phone."

Luke Bateman pictured in a 2016 game against Melbourne Storm, a year after making his NRL debut. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

Bateman says he felt in control of his habit until his gambling saw him lose tens of thousands of dollars in just a few weeks.

" I had $70,000 or $80,000 in my bank account, and in the space of a month, I had nothing. "

Hitting rock bottom with his addiction and mental health, and then finding his way back again, has compelled Bateman to speak out about the federal government's gambling changes, which aim to limit gambling advertising.

He says they would not have helped him through his hardest moments.

Luke Bateman removed himself from temptation when he went bush. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

"I was in so much debt … I was earning $400,000 a year, and I couldn't afford a lollipop," Bateman admits.

"I don't think they [the proposed laws] will move the needle at all when it comes to gambling harm, " he says. "I'd love to call it the bare minimum, but I don't think they got even there."

The legislation, which would cap the number of gambling ads broadcast per hour and ban advertising during live matches, was introduced into parliament earlier this month and is being scrutinised in a Senate inquiry.

Luke Bateman speaks at a panel in parliament house about the role sport, alcohol and gambling play in gender-based violence. (Supplied: Michael Conlin, FARE)

Bateman says the proposed changes do not "even come close" to reflecting community concerns about gambling, with researchers finding that the majority of Australians believe gambling is too easily accessible.

"I would love to see all gambling advertising phased out, and for all incentives that gambling companies can offer a customer [to continue betting] to be banned," Bateman says.

Australia has the highest per capita gambling losses in the world, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.

Bateman's passion for the issue could be enough to see him run for parliament one day. He tells Australian Story that a run at politics is "definitely a possibility".

"I don't think parliamentarians are doing anywhere near enough in terms of protecting … young people from the harms that gambling companies and gambling itself causes."

Loading...

'Rugby league like a religion'

Bateman grew up in the small town of Miles, about 400 kilometres west of Brisbane. He showed exceptional athletic ability from a young age, playing his first game of rugby league when he was four.

"He was probably one of the better players in under-7s at four years old," his stepfather Don Hills says.

"I remember his PE teacher saying to me, 'We'll be reading about this kid in later life. He's destined for big things,'" mother Leanne Bateman recalls.

Luke Bateman (bottom right) with his older brother Sam, twin sister Sarah, mother Leanne and stepfather Don. (Supplied: Leanne Bateman)

By the time he was 12, Bateman had represented Queensland in rugby league, touch football and swimming.

It was around the same time that Bateman was scouted by NRL clubs at the state rugby league carnival.

Luke Bateman was recruited by the Canberra Raiders when he was 12. (Supplied: Leanne Bateman)

"We were approached by a couple of different scouts for different NRL teams. One was the Canberra Raiders," Leanne says.

When the Raiders signed 12-year-old Bateman, it was a big deal, not only for his family, but the whole community.

"Growing up in the country, rugby league is like a religion out there," brother Sam Bateman says.

"It would've been like extremely exciting for him, but also probably a lot of pressure for him as well."

Luke Bateman pictured with Don, Sarah, Leanne and Sam after his first Canberra Raiders game in 2015. (Supplied: Luke Bateman)

Watch Luke Bateman's Australian Story "Turning the Page" Monday 8:00pm (AEST) on ABC TV and ABC iview.

$80k gone: Luke's 'shameful' gambling habit

Despite having an early aptitude for all things sport-related, Bateman says he was a "soft and gentle kid" who found solace in fantasy books.

"I think what really drew me to those specific books was the sense of wonder … my world on the farm is so small, but my world in books is so big."

But Bateman kept his love of reading hidden.

"It was not something that men did. I never saw any of my male role models, my male heroes, reading books."

Luke Bateman had a love for reading from a young age. (Supplied: Leanne Bateman)

So Bateman leant into sport instead.

"Growing up, I saw one dream as possible, and that was the NRL dream.

"I think all the other parts of myself really took a back seat to the athlete and the sporting part of me because they weren't things that received praise," he says.

Luke Bateman says his book collection charts every phase of his life. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

The beginning of his NRL career was an exciting time for Bateman, now 31.

"I was really just happy to be a part of the team," he says.

But a feeling of doubt slowly crept in, and Bateman's 2015 NRL debut at the age of 20 brought up some unexpected feelings.

"I'd worked my entire life to get to this moment … then I played the game, and I remember thinking, 'Huh, that was really underwhelming.'

"I thought that was a thing that would complete me. And then I came off the field, and I thought, 'Oh, I'm still exactly the same.'"

Luke Bateman runs the ball in a match between the Raiders and Dragons in Canberra in 2017. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Bateman was enjoying the benefits of being a cashed-up, young sports star. But his gambling addiction, and the mental health impacts that went alongside it, were getting worse.

After losing nearly $80,000 in one month, Bateman rang his mother and asked her to take control of his bank accounts.

"Luke's gambling got really bad. He had no money. He would literally be borrowing off family and friends. He would regularly ask me to take control of his money and take it back again," she says.

"They were very dark, hard times."

Now back home in Brisbane, Luke Bateman takes time out for himself at the gym. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

Bateman's mental health deteriorated and he contemplated suicide.

"I was just so filled with shame, and I couldn't share it," Bateman says. "I was just in so much pain. I saw no way out."

If you or anyone you know needs help: National Gambling Helpline on 1800 858 858

Lifeline on 13 11 14

Kids Helpline on 1800 551 800

MensLine Australia on 1300 789 978

Suicide Call Back Service on 1300 659 467

Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636

Headspace on 1800 650 890

Leanne noticed the deterioration, too.

"I rang the police in Canberra on two different occasions to go and do welfare checks on him. I rang the Canberra Raiders [welfare officer] on a couple of occasions."

Leanne says Luke "did not appreciate" the checks and was in denial about needing help.

Bateman acknowledges that he hid the worst of his addiction and mental health problems from the Raiders and did not seek support, believing that disclosing them could see him removed from the team.

The Canberra Raiders would not comment on this story.

Luke Bateman says he was the "best liar in the world" when he was hiding the extent of his gambling. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

Bateman goes bush to pay $130k debt

One Monday in 2020, Bateman woke up in Newcastle after a three-day bender with no idea what happened or how he got there.

"Something just broke within me and I [thought] I have two options: I either end my life or I get help," he remembers.

Instead of driving back to Canberra, Bateman headed north to Brisbane, straight to Leanne and Don's house.

"I collapsed into her arms and I said, 'I need help.'"

After shaking off a three-day bender, Luke Bateman drove 8 hours home to his parents in Brisbane. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

After years of resisting and insisting he could cope with his addiction on his own, Bateman agreed to go to rehab. It was about this time that he returned to one of his first loves, books.

"I started reading because I was doing a lot of therapy and I was starting to try and change my life," Bateman says.

After coming out of rehab, Leanne and Don sat Bateman down and gave him an ultimatum: They would absorb his debts and he would go and work for Don in his logging business, which operated in remote locations in Queensland, to repay them.

Bateman estimates his parents took on about $130,000 of his debt, which he recently paid off.

"It was a turning point that he was then out of Canberra, out of the culture [of gambling and drug-taking]," Leanne says.

Luke Bateman and Don chat by the fire. (Australian Story: Shalailah Medhora)

Living outside of the city came with unexpected benefits: it would take several years before Bateman had access to the internet from his campsite.

"All my gambling was done on my phone. So in the beginning, even if I wanted to gamble, I couldn't. [It] was fantastic for my recovery," he says.

Luke Bateman at the family property at Injune. (Supplied: Luke Bateman)

#BookTok success and controversy

Bateman bought a campervan and buried himself in work. To pass the time, he'd listen to audiobooks in his tractor. It was here that his next big career move was made.

He recorded a TikTok video for a part of the platform dedicated to lovers of reading, called #BookTok, from the tractor.

Luke Bateman filmed all his early TikTok videos from this tractor. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

"I made my first BookTok video because I literally just wanted some friends to talk about books with," he says.

He uploaded the video at 8pm, hoping to wake up to a few comments from like-minded people. Instead, his video went viral.

"I woke up the next morning and it had a million views," Bateman says.

Loading...

The #BookTok videos caught the eye of publisher Anthea Bariamis.

"After seeing some of his content for several weeks, I thought it might be worth reaching out to see if he had written or was writing a book," she says.

In the meeting, Bateman and Bariamis ended up speaking for hours about their shared love of fantasy.

"He sent me a sample of his writing, and I could absolutely see the potential … it certainly wasn't something he had come up with on a whim," Bariamis says.

Bateman was working on his tractor when he found out he would be offered a book deal.

"I just bawled my eyes out because I was so happy," he says.

"It was the culmination of decades of something that I kept really secret and felt a lot of shame around."

A hat in Luke Bateman's room displays the phrase "romance reader". (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

Bateman posted the news on #BookTok, eager to share the win with the community.

But the reaction was not what he expected.

"When I first announced my book deal, it received a heap of criticism and backlash," Bateman says. "People filled my comment section with really hateful, spiteful, vile comments."

People had wrongly assumed Bateman was using a ghostwriter for his work and had been offered a deal without a fully sketched-out proposal. They also pointed out how difficult it could be for writers of colour to get book deals, a criticism Bateman acknowledged as fair.

After working all day, Luke Bateman would retreat to the caravan to write his debut novel. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

Bateman now has a three-book deal, with the first novel due in 2027.

He says his "north star" is to help young men and boys through the power of storytelling, and he wants to use his platform to advocate for change, including reducing gambling harm.

"I understand that I have the position, the power, and the voice that can create change, that can change people's lives, and I don't want to squander that."

Luke Bateman is motivated to make real change, even saying politics could be possible" in his future. (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

Watch Luke Bateman's Australian Story "Turning the Page" Monday 8pm (AEST) on ABC TV and ABC iview.

World.title: Diamonds disappointed Glasgow games only live on Seven's streaming service
World.content:
The Diamonds are one of the most successful and beloved teams in Australian sport, but some fans back home trying to tune in to their Commonwealth Games campaign have been left disappointed.

The reigning netball gold medallists kicked off with dominant wins by a combined 80 goals on Saturday and Sunday, but neither match was carried live on any of Seven Network's linear television channels.

The 99-38 victory over Tonga and 66-47 win over England were only shown live on streaming service 7Plus, while Seven carried the swimming heats.

For Sunday's prime-time match against rivals and 2018 champions the Roses, Seven aired 2021 Ryan Reynolds film Free Guy on Mate, and crime drama Vera on TWO.

The Diamonds' Glasgow games have been carried live on 7Plus, but not on Seven's linear TV channels. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Seven's main channel broadcast made clear the Diamonds were live on Plus.

After the swimming finished and the Diamonds had won, the Australia-England game was aired on delay on Seven's main channel.

ABC Sport broke the news to a few of the Diamonds stars after their game.

"That's obviously disappointing, obviously we want to be on TV and have every fan able to watch. I wasn't aware of that," goalkeeper Courtney Bruce said.

"I don't know, hopefully we'll be able to be on the live games [at some point]. It is disappointing, we obviously want netball to be highlighted and want the rest of the sports here at the Commonwealth Games and for Australia to be highlighted too."

Games debutant Jamie-Lee Price said she hopes fans keep making their voices heard.

Sunday's game was between the last two Commonwealth gold medallists. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"I think maybe if we put lots of pressure on maybe we can get there," she said.

"I didn't realise that. We want to be on TV, we want eyes on our sport and if we can get that that's amazing. So, yes please."

The silver lining of the situation is the reminder of the support this team has in Australia and in Glasgow, where the Australians in the Hydro were challenging the English fans for sheer volume and passion.

"We definitely feel the support from home, obviously we're nothing without the supporters back in Australia," Bruce said.

The Diamonds' next match is against Malawi in two days' time. (Getty Images: Rob Casey/SNS Group)

"We definitely feel it today and there's quite a few out there. That was really nice to have them out there today."

A Channel Seven spokesperson responded to requests from the ABC, saying:

"The Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games features multiple events taking place simultaneously, which is why Seven is delivering wall-to-wall coverage across Seven and 7plus Sport — including 15 live channels on 7plus Sport — ensuring Australians can watch every event live and free."

World.title: Piastri blasts '****ing stupid' backmarker, Norris wins Hungarian GP
World.content:
Oscar Piastri was forced to retire from the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix, but not before he blasted a "stupid" backmarker and slammed his team for a poor strategy at the Hungaroring.

Lando Norris claimed his first victory of the season, ahead of Max Verstappen in second and world championship leader Kimi Antonelli in third.

Piastri was left desperately frustrated after a brilliant start saw him overtake his teammate on the opening lap to take the lead from third on the grid.

"It was definitely the highlight of my race," Piastri said of the start.

"And it went pretty downhill from there.

"A lot of things to unpack."

The Australian leaped into the lead but never was able to pull away, complaining of rear tyre wear as Norris was all over the back of his teammate in a clearly faster car.

"The pace on the hard tyres was nowhere," Piastri bemoaned.

At the half-way point, when he was brought into the pits for his second stop in response to Lewis Hamilton doing so.

McLaren, wary of the under-cut, had been pestered by Norris to allow him to pit first and had even told him to box on lap 32, saying he was "miles" faster than Piastri, but the team said the reigning world champion was unable to come in as Piastri had first choice on the pit stop.

Oscar Piastri leads Lando Norris. (Getty Images" Andy Hone/LAT Images)

Piastri did come in, but was then caught behind back markers and, as he tried to complete his outlaps was hit by Carlos Sainz as he battled with the Aston Martin.

"Is he ****ing stupid or what? Get out of the ****ing way, you idiot! Oh my god," Piastri said as Sainz first held him up, then clipped his front wheel.

Piastri's mood did not improve soon after when Norris, having stayed out longer on his second set of tyres, was able to pit and come out ahead of Piastri.

"Oh mate, just don't ****ing talk to me now," he said when told that the Sainz collision had cost them the virtual race lead.

"Nice of you guys to factor that one in by the way, thanks," he added, in reference to the traffic he had to go through.

Already fuming, Piastri was then dealt an even more bitter blow, his gearbox failing on lap 56 forcing him to retire.

After the race though, Piastri said he was simply frustrated by the sequence of events.

"Obviously being taken out by a back marker is never really one of the things you think that can go wrong, but I was proven wrong," Piastri told media after the race.

"I was hoping they wouldn't pit Lando in that moment, to at least give me the chance to stay in the lead," he added.

"But I think that's not very reasonable, so I was more just very upset in the moment about what had happened.

"The timing of my pit stop was fine, we wanted to beat Lewis [Hamilton] and that's what we needed to do."

Lando Norris overtook Oscar Piastri in the opening lap. (Getty Images: Alastair Staley/LAT Images)

McLaren team principle Andrea Stella said he thought both drivers excelled during the race.

"I think today it was actually great racing," he told Sky Sports.

"It was great to see Lando and Oscar fighting at the start for good position, something that was fair.

"Oscar had his own chance to take the lead and see what pace he might have had.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"And how the race unfolded meant that with Oscar we then covered Hamilton and then there was some situation with the backmarkers.

"Lando was very quick once he had the lead and he take advantage of this pace and the fact that there was some delay for Oscar.

"That's racing. We are McLaren racing. It was great racing."

It was also a tough weekend for Ferrari and Lewis Hamilton, who was penalised five seconds for speeding in the pit lane, relegating him to fifth, with his teammate Charles Leclerc in fourth.

Meanwhile, Malaysia's Sepang circuit will host a Formula 1 race for the first time since 2017 as replacement host of the Bahrain Grand Prix.

Liberty Media said in a statement the race will take place on October 4, and would officially be called the 'Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia'.

Follow all the action in our live blog.

World.title: King Cam reigns supreme as distance queen Pallister dominates
World.content:
Cameron McEvoy's Glasgow double whammy has him looking to Los Angeles with confidence as he headlined another big night for Australia's Commonwealth Games swim team.

The sprint ace dominated the 50 metre freestyle final, going under 21 seconds for only the second time.

McEvoy's Games-record 20.97 followed his 20.88 world record in March and continued his remarkable swimming renaissance.

He led home an Australian medal sweep in the event — one of five swimming gold medals on day three — but the time was the bigger deal ahead of defending his Olympic title at the Los Angeles Olympics.

Cam McEvoy, Flynn Southam, and Jamie Jack made it an all-Australian podium for the men's 50m freestyle. (Getty: Rob Casey)

It is McEvoy's first individual gold medal at his third Commonwealth Games.

"It [gold] is really good, but I'm more excited about ducking under the 21-second barrier," he said.

"So, yeah, a double whammy for me. It was a really good night.

"I really wanted to prove to myself that I can consistently get under that [21 seconds]. So to do that for a second time, that brings me a lot of confidence for the world championships next year, LA, moving forward.

"I already know that there's some low-hanging fruit that I can knock off."

After a disappointing Tokyo Olympics, McEvoy took a sabbatical and nearly left the sport. He completely overhauled his training and returned for a stunning Paris triumph in the 50m freestyle.

"Prior to Paris, I still had the, I guess … the demons to work with in terms of my Olympic relationship," he said.

Flynn Southam won silver and Jamie Jack was third to complete the Australian sweep.

Lani Pallister won a dominant gold in the women's 1500m freestyle. (Reuters: Andrew Couldridge)

Just as McEvoy continued to rule the one-lap dash, Lani Pallister remained similarly untouchable in distance freestyle events at the Games and turned the 1500m into a personal time trial and her second Glasgow gold.

After taking out the 400m on day one, Pallister won the 1,500 by nearly 18 seconds as the women's event made its debut at the Games.

But there was no Australian procession in the men's 4x200m freestyle final.

For once, it was a genuine race and England led at the last change before Kai Taylor's blistering anchor leg delivered the last gold medal of day three and another Games record.

Sam Short, Harry Turner, Ed Sommerville and Taylor clocked seven minutes 1.47 seconds to break the Games record Australia set in Birmingham.

Iona Anderson had an emotional hug with her Scottish grandmother after winning the 100m backstroke while opening ceremony baton bearer Tim Hodge successfully defended his Games 100m backstroke S9 title.

Iona Anderson snatched gold at the touch in the 100m backstroke. (Getty: Rob Casey)

Australian swimmers have now collected 16 gold medals in three days, entrenching their country atop the overall Games medal standings.

Also on day three, Australian Matthew Temple suffered a bad case of deja vu, again losing to Canadian star Josh Liendo in a record-breaking 100m butterfly final.

Gemma Sellick (silver) and Victoria Belando Nicholson (bronze) won medals behind England's Alice Tai in the women's 100m backstroke S9 and Harrison Vig won bronze behind Hodge in the backstroke.

Sienna Toohey was third in the 100m breaststroke, while Mollie O'Callaghan, Meg Harris and Shayna Jack were the fastest three 100m freestyle semi-finalists.

Similarly, Alex Perkins and Brittany Casteluzzo were quickest in the 100m butterfly semis.

Scott scores silver ahead of 'idol' Godwin

Australia's star gymnast Georgia Godwin has failed to defend her individual all-around title, but teammate Breanna Scott took silver.

All eyes were on defending champion Godwin, but it was Scott who led the charge for Australia as Canadian great Ellie Black won gold at Glasgow International Stadium.

Breanna Scott claimed silver in the women's all-around gymnastics. (Getty: Naomi Baker)

Black's 16-year-old teammate Lia-Monica Fontaine followed for bronze, while Godwin settled for fifth after guiding Australia to a team gold the day before.

"It's pretty crazy. I don't really think it's sunk in yet," Scott said.

"There's been so much that's happened in the last 24 hours."

The Sydney local credited Godwin and Black for pushing her to the limit in Glasgow.

"They're both like such great role models. Georgia is like basically all of our idols in the team," Scott said.

"We look up to her. She's just so great to have there.

"She's the most supportive person like you could have on the team.

"And obviously Ellie, like she's like an icon of the sport so it was really great to be competing with both of them."

Breanna Scott of Team Australia celebrates after the Women's All-Around Final on day three of the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games (Getty: Francois Nel)

Stealing the headlines after winning two gold and three silver medals at the 2022 Birmingham Games, Godwin was aiming to become the first gymnast in Games history to successfully defend an individual all-around title.

But the tight turnaround proved too much for the 28-year-old, who readily admitted she was struggling with soreness after the team final in her comeback from an Achilles injury.

Godwin had become the nation's most decorated female gymnast at the Games after winning the team gold, surpassing Allana Slater with nine total medals.

The Queensland product will have another chance to win a medal in Glasgow when she competes in the vault and floor finals.

Scott's silver medal comes after Australia's leading male gymnast, Jesse Moore, ended the nation's 16-year medal drought by claiming individual all-around bronze.

Tech.title: Champagne and Bullets belongs on the Mount Rushmore of bad movies
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

There’s something about a movie like The Room, Troll 2, or Fateful Findings that I find irresistible. These sorts of “so bad they’re good” films are marvelous curiosities where ambition far outstrips resources, ability, and self-awareness to become something much greater than the sum of their parts. Champagne and Bullets (also released as GetEven and Road to Revenge) is a film on par with those classics of outsider cinema.

The movie is almost entirely the work of one man, John De Hart. Hart wrote, directed, and stars as Rick Bode in the film. He even performs a musical number early in the proceedings — The bizarre “Shimmy Slide.” During the performance, Hart, who was reportedly pumped full of painkillers after throwing out his back, is stiff and looks around the room as if he’s only performing under threat of violence. And somehow, this lifeless performance of a cringy country rocker isn’t the most awkward scene in the movie.

The relationships and interactions between characters in Champagne and Bullets are just as inexplicable and unnatural as those in The Room. Bode and his partner Huck Finney are cops who lose their badges five minutes into the movie. This precipitates the alarmingly quick mental decline of Finney, who is also going through a divorce after discovering his wife has been sleeping around. He fires a handgun through his bills, drinks bleach to get out of prison, and seemingly starts a cult.

Oh, and speaking of cults, a good portion of the plot revolves around the reemergence of Bode’s old girlfriend Cindy, who is fleeing a satanic coven that “sacrificed a human baby.”

While ostensibly an action film, the fight scenes are few and far between, and staged with all the believability of a theme park stunt show. Hart seemed far more interested in cramming in as much gratuitous nudity as possible. There are three uncomfortably long sex scenes with costar Pamela Bryant, who plays Cindy, all set to songs sung by Hart. In total, they take up 12 minutes of runtime in a movie that is only 90 minutes long. One scene that takes place in a jacuzzi apparently even led Hart’s girlfriend at the time to break up with him. (Warning: One scene not involving Hart and Bryant does depict a sexual assault.)

If you’re a fan of bad movies, cult classics, or the podcast How Did This Get Made, you owe it to yourself to go watch Champagne and Bullets. It’s available on Hoopla, Amazon Prime, and Tubi.

Tech.title: Apple is banking on privacy to set its smart glasses apart
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to Mark Gurman, Apple is planning to reveal its first smart glasses at WWDC next June, with an expectation that they’ll launch by the end of 2027. Part of the hold-up may be around the company’s efforts to get its privacy features and messaging in order. Smart glasses in general, and Meta’s in particular, have ignited controversy over their ability to stealthily capture photos and videos. As Gurman points out:

The company has spent more than a decade making privacy one of its defining product messages. Simply entering the same category as Meta risks undermining that reputation, regardless of how Apple’s approach differs.

Apple is likely to rely on on-device processing and skip out on more controversial features like facial recognition or an always-on-recording similar to Meta’s “super sensing.” Gurman also believes Apple will avoid using customer recordings to train AI models.

Other hardware and software privacy features are also reportedly in the works. It’s also possible that Apple could eventually release a version of its smart glasses without a camera, or with a camera that is exclusively for sensing and won’t be able to capture video or photos at all, similar to what is rumored for Apple’s AI-enabled AirPods.

Tech.title: The US is charging an American citizen for wiping his phone at the border
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

The government is prosecuting US citizen Sam Tunick for allegedly providing authorities with a “duress password” that wiped his phone when they tried to seize it at Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson airport on January 24th, 2025. Federal agents detained Tunick at the airport, allegedly questioning him about child exploitation images. However, a motion filed by Tunick’s lawyers argues this was simply “a pretext for a fishing expedition into Mr Tunick’s connections” to the Stop Cop City movement in Atlanta.

The government is turning to a little-known and rarely-used statute that makes it illegal to destroy or damage property to stop authorities from seizing it. They allege that Tunick used a feature of the privacy-focused GrapheneOS to wipe his phone by giving authorities a duress password, instead of the actual passcode to unlock the phone. The defense has argued that the detention and seizure were unlawful, and therefore all evidence should be tossed.

According to Tunick’s attorneys, agents refused him access to a lawyer, did not provide a warrant, or inform him of his legal rights. They also allege that access to his phone was sought under false pretenses. The government has countered that they were not required to produce a warrant because Tunick had not yet been granted permission to enter the US.

Marlon Kautz, a member of the Atlanta Solidarity Fund, told the Guardian earlier this week that, “we all have a right to secure our private data against unconstitutional searches. And we should — especially in a time of rising authoritarianism.” Under the Trump administration, entering the US has become a much more fraught process, even for citizens who can face hours-long detention and scrutiny of social media accounts. Most agree the only way to protect your data is to delete it.

Tech.title: Carrie is just trying to make a friend in the new trailer
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Mike Flanagan’s latest Stephen King adaptation, Carrie (this will be his fourth), is slated to make its debut on Amazon Prime on October 7th. The new trailer dropped at Comic-Con 2026 and doesn’t contain many surprises. If you’re familiar with Carrie at all, it hits all the expected notes. Though it’s clearly been updated for the modern era.

According to Deadline, Flanagan’s take on the classic King novel will tackle very modern teen challenges like active shooter drills and bullying on social media. The director apparently invited high schoolers into the writers’ room, using their real-life traumas to inform the script:

“They shared shocking one-off situations or constant treatment and microaggressions and things that are not necessarily present themselves as targeted harassment. [We will dive into] the cruelty in today’s world and how the internet has encouraged cruelty, rewards and celebrates and amplifies it. This is awful for adults to deal with, and for teenagers even more so.”

Brian De Palma’s iconic 1976 adaptation of Carrie is iconic and features an unimpeachable performance from Sissy Spacek. But it’s undeniable that Summer H. Howell, who was 21 at the time of shooting, is much more believable as a high school student than Spacek, who was 26 at the time.

Subscribing to Xbox Game Pass Ultimate on a recurring basis has been tough to justify recently, even after Microsoft reduced the monthly cost from $29.99 to $22.99. But you can get a better deal on a three-month subscription (valued at $69) by grabbing a digital code at Eneba that costs $39.01 at the time of publication.

Game Pass Ultimate grants you access to the full Game Pass library on Xbox (compared to a more limited slice with Premium), including first-party titles and online multiplayer access. The subscription also gives PC gamers access to Microsoft’s catalog of Game Pass games through the Xbox app, though the selection differs a bit between console and desktop.

You don’t need me to tell you why deals like these are nice. The costs of subscriptions generally only go in one direction over time, and it is becoming more rare to find worthwhile discounts that give you a break. If you want to jump into Halo: Campaign Evolved when it launches July 28th on Xbox and PC, all you need is this subscription instead of buying the $49.99 re-remake.
